I would still like to have from my hon. friend a clear explanation of the insertion of these words ' eastern or ' before the word ' western.' I would like to know what he understands the effect of that to be.

What I have in mind is this. We are legislating for terminal elevators. They are such public elevators as are located at what may be denominated a terminal point. If a principle is right to be applied to a terminal elevator at Fort William or Port Arthur, it is right to be applied to a terminal elevator doing the same kind of work east of Port Arthur or Fort William or wherever it may be. If, for instance, we come to have terminal elevators at Vancouver, if that is declared by the Governor in Council to be a terminal point, then the same principle would apply to them. I do not see any argument on the ground of consistency which would apply to one terminal elevator and not to another, because one was a few miles east or west of the other.	,
Does my hon. friend speak of terminal elevators in eastern Canada- for instance, on the Georgian bay or at Montreal?

They are not now terminal elevators in the sense of the Act, but it might be that the Governor in Council would declare St. John or Montreal a terminal point, and then the same principle would apply to them that applies to elevators at Fort William or Port Arthur.
I did not think there was any question as to the purchase of grain in the eastern [DOT] inspectional division, but only in the western.
It was in the west that the question arose and that the necessities were pressing; but if the necessity arose in the east, we would have the power to apply the same principle.
It is the purpose to put the purchase of grain in eastern Canada on the same footing as in western Canada?
Yes.

I do not see why this provision should not apply to public elevators as well as to terminal elevators. A public elevator is on all fours with a terminal elevator, except that it Js not at a terminal point. It is under government supervision, under the control of the board, and subject to the provisions of the Act. In every particular, except as to the granting of warehouse receipts, it is in the same position as the elevator at the terminal, and my contention is that, being of the same kind and character as the terminal elevator, so far as the provisions of this Act are concerned with regard to the mixing of grain, the owner or operator of that elevator should be prohibited from the buying and selling of grain just the same as if he were the owner or operator of a terminal elevator. The principle may be right or it may be wrong, but if it is a, sound principle, it is just as sound and just as necessary in the case of public elevators as in the case of terminal elevators.

My hon. friend may be right on the question of principle, and yet there is a difference between what we call a public elevator elsewhere and a great terminal elevator at Fort William or Port Arthur. What we are trying to do in this legislation is to cure what is said to be a very great evil that is concentrated at Fort William and Port Arthur. We are making what my hon. friend says is very drastic legislation, and does he not think that we have gone far enough in confining it to the terminal elevator? What would happen if we attempted to apply the same principle to public elevators? No need has yet arisen, and in legislation of this kind we should not be ahead or needs. If it becomes necessary in the future to apply this principle to public elevators, this House, I suppose, would be prepared to do it; but this House will think a good deal before it does. You go a long way when you eliminate the interest of an eastern man from your western field in the buying of grain. After all, who does the buying of grain, and what is the reason for all this machinery? The love of gain, the speculative interest, on the part of the buyer; yet behind it all is the farmer with his grain to sell. He wants every buyer and every storage facility he can get to ease his position and increase his profit. We do not want to interfere with that more than is absolutely necessary, and the government does not think at the present time that a case has been made out for applying this principle to public elevators.

If public elevator meant only an elevator in the eastern inspection division, I could appreciate my hon friend's argument, and, for my part, I would be quite willing to agree to the clause being framed to give that effect, but, as a matter of fact, there are at the present time, I understand, and the number may be greatly multiplied, public elevators at Winnipeg and at St. Boniface, public elevators that are west of the terminal elevators, and unless these elevators of which I speak are put under the same control as the terminal elevators, the whole position that is in view in the making of this resolution applicable to terminal elevators is lost.
I do not think so.

It is really of no serious *effect. It was proposed to be brought in last session in the Bill which was discussed before the Senate and came down to this

House. It may be that it is not a proper principle, but if it is to be embodied in the Act as a principle 1 am urging that it be made effective with a declaration that it be carried out in fact, not that it will apply only to one section of the trade and not to the other, although the trade will be affected practically just as much in one case as in the other. I do not speak particularly of the public elevators east of Fort William. I am quite willing that they should be excluded on the argument my hon. friend has given. But that is not the case in regard to such elevators west of Port Arthur, and I would still urge that this provision be made applicable to them.

There is one other point that I want to call the attention of the committee to, and I think it is a pretty important one. We may call for railway openings. It takes an immense amount of money and a great deal of time to increase our railway openings from the west. They will come in time, but it will be long, while there is one thing that can come in a very much shorter time, and that is storage facilities. Now the building of storage facilities for western grain has, to a large extent, been at a standstill for the last few years. Why? Because people did not know the ground upon which they were standing, because capital was not willing to put itself into the building of storage elevators. The railroads themselves had not been adding to their storage facilities because they did not know what was going to happen. They have not been building large elevators as they otherwise would have, because they did not know what was going to happen. What was the use of building elevators if the government was going to take these elevators away from them, by expropriating or leasing them and until that doubt is settled you will not have a move forward in the efficient multiplication of storage facilities where large capital is to be invested in order to secure them. Now I think we have gone as far as we possibly can go when we apply this principle, this drastic principle, in an experiment to the terminal elevators only. I would not like to go so far as to apply it to public elevators.
Either west or east?

I look for an increase in the coming year of from seven to ten millions of capacity in the public elevators in the west. That is outside of private enterprise, outside of government elevators in the northwestern parts, outside of the combination or co-operative elevators, whatever you are minded to call them. I want to see them all for my part and I believe everybody in the west wants to see that storage. I would Mr. OLIVER.
like to see storage elevators at all the great strategic points. That matter is now being considered. What will eventuate I do not know, but I think my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) will agree with me that if we could have four, five or six big elevators at strategic points in the west, scattered here and there, it would be a great insurance against what is taking place there this year, and against what may take place other years as the productive facilities increase with such rapidity in a ratio greater than the transport facilities themselves can possibly increase. My hon. friend behind sounded in our ears a note to which we might very well listen and restrain ourselves from attempting to go too far all at once.

I have the same ambition and the same hope for the increase of elevator storage that the minister has. I do not think, however, that we are going to affect the matter detrimentally by putting the trade of handling and storing grain on a strictly well defined basis. Representations have been made to the government that those who handle grain now, and store it, make their money not out of storing grain and handling it, but out of manipulating it. Naturally people may have hesitated in the past few years in putting further capital into this business. I have been told on what I consider good authority that the storing of grain at the prices which are charged, does not pay, that grain and storage men make money out of dealing in grain, and not out of the storing of it. That is what I have been told by an authority as high as there is in any railway company in Canada practically. Now we are going to make it more inviting for men to put their money into the storing and handling of grain by providing that it shall be carried on as a business separate by itself. I think we will make it appeal to the ordinary hard-headed business man better if we divorce that business entirely from the business of trafficking in the grain itself. In any other commodity which railways handle for example, they handle it by itself. I think the grain trade is unique in this: That the interests that handle it, that transport it, and that take care of it on its way to the market are the same interests to a certain extent that make a business of buying and selling the very commodity which is in their custody and in their hands so much of the time. I have understood, and I still understand, that it was proposed to divert these two businesses, to make the storing and handling of grain a separate business from the buying and selling of that grain. I think it will do more to invite capital into the construction of public elevators if you make this a strict business proposition so that those who engage in it will not have to compete with man. who

are skinning and manipulating the grades. It may be there has been a standstill in the past with regard to the increase in our storage elevators. There has been the question, as the hon. minister has said, that it was not known whether these elevators would be expropriated or not, but I have not heard very much talk about public elevators being expropriated. And these are the elevators ot which the hon. minister has been talking to-night. Naturally for a 1 year or two there may be some uncertainty about this business, just as there was when the Bill was brought down, as there was last winter, since the present Prime Minister went throughout the country saying in most unmistakable terms that he was going to put into effect the public ownership of [DOT]elevators now.

Does it not occur to the hon. gentleman that a grain firm engaged in a very large way in the purchase of grain for shipment to the old country, will, from the very necessity of the case, require an elevator of its own. There is a case in Midland where a firm has an elevator with a capacity of 1,250,000 bushels. Probably 5,000,000 or 6,000,000 bushels pass through it every year, but the bulk of this is owned by the company owning the elevator, although it is true they handle grain belonging to other people.

No one has asked that this should apply to the eastern division, which would eliminate the case mentioned, and I do not think any one would abject to placing in the section a clause that it would not apply to elevators handling their own grain.
I said simply that the bulk of it is owned by them.

How would that work in practice? In the west the farmers are building many elevators and they are putting their own buyers on the market. If you applied this you would prohibit them from doing that and thus deprive the farmers of the very best service and protection they are getting. Then the large milling companies afford a great deal of storage capacity to the farmers, but this would prevent them from handling grain for others, and so you would decrease the storage capacity of the west to that extent. This clause would not work out to the advantage of the farmer.
It has not been suggested that this should affect the country elevators.
Would that apply to a firm like the Ogilvies?

If they own terminal elevators, it would. I do not believe the
same people would have the custody of the grain after inspection and also ownership of it.
Subsection 2 of the section covers the case of millers like Ogilvies.

Subsection 2 of section 123 reads:
2. Subsection 1 of this section shall not apply to any person who owns, manages, operates or is otherwise interested in any terminal elevator,-
(1)	which has been leased to the board for
operation, or which has been leased to any person, firm or company for operation with the approval of the board or which is managed and operated by persons approved by the board; or-	.
(2)	which is used or operated in connection with any flour mill situate at the same terminal point as such elevator.
That means that once an elevator is leased, and many elevators are leased, then if that lease is approved- by the board any one who owns or manages or operates it escapes from all penalties of that section. It is too wide altogether. The board must approve in practice of any proposed lease of an elevator. If a man is operator and lessee he is permitted to go out and buy millions of bushels of grain. If the clause means anything it means that once an elevator is leased and the lease has been approved the lessee or any person interested in the elevator can go out and buy and sell all the grain he likes.
Another point affecting the legal interpretation of the section. It says it shall not apply to any person interested in the ownership, management or operation of any elevator the leasing of which has been approved by the board, but it does not say that this immunity is only with regard to that elevator. Suppose a man is interested in the ownership of elevator A, and that is leased to a company. He has only a small interest in it, but he would go into court if charged with breaking this Act and say that subsection 2 savs that this shall not apply to him because he is interested in the ownership of an elevator, the leasing of which has been approved by the board, although he may have a mammoth interest in other elevators. The clause should read so that it protects him only with regard to that one elevator; as it reads he can commit any infraction of the Act so long as he can prove that he is interested in an elevator which has been leased. I would move the following amendment:
No person owning, managing, operating or otherwise interested in any public or terminal elevator shall buy or sell grain at any point in the western inspection division.

Subsection 1 of this section shall not apply to any person by reason only of the fact that he:
(a)	owns or is otherwise interested in the ownership of any such elevator leased to the board for operation, or which has been leased to any person for operation with the approval of the hoard;
(b)	is an owner or holder of stock or shares in any railway eompany which owns or operates such elevator and winch does not as a business buy or sell grain;
(c)	which is used or operated with any flour mill situate at the same terminal point as such elevator. Provided, however, that such elevator shall be subject to such restrictions and regulations as are imposed by the board, with the approval of the Governor in Council.
My first amendment with regard to immunity is meant to apply to those who are interested in the ownership, management or operation of an elevator, the leasing of which has been made. I have made this immunity so that a person shall not come under the penalty of 123 'by reason only of the fact that he is interested in such ownership, that shall not 'be sufficient to penalize him, he shall not be prosecuted for that reason alone. Then there is this further remedy when I say ' owns or is otherwise * interested in the ownership of any such elevator.' The clause as it now reads ' owns, manages or operates ' should not apply when he is only custodian of the grain. He can buy all that grain he likes because he has divested himself of the management or control of the elevator. I put in the clause about owning railway stock for the reason that those who own money in the country, many of them, have stock in railway companies as well as own the elevators; consequently they are interested.
Does *the hon. gentleman think that, were his last exception eliminated there would still be any application to the person who held stock m the railway company?
If the company owned or operated the elevator, I think he would be indirectly interested.
Does he contend that under the wording of the Bill he would be held to be interested?
I think under a strict interpretation of the clause a man who owned or operated an elevator would be debarred from buying or selling grain.

Could not the whole clause be avoided simply by the same company organizing again under another name, that is to say, might there not be two companies taking out separate charters and calling themselves different names? Then Company A, being engaged

in the purchase and handling of grain, and B engaged in the storage of grain, would not that means avoid all the effects of his amendment, and would not it avoid the effect of the clause as it stands?

3788'
]ike little men on each side and vote for and against.

Having admitted that the government are going to either construct or lease some terminal elevators, is the minister prepared to say what charges will be made in the rates for winter storage at government elevators?

Why, bless you no. We shall have a 'commission that will look into that and come to their conclusions from their knowledge. That will be all arranged by the commission with the approval of the Governor in Council.
Are you sure you have all his name?

Yes, Frederick William Gordon. Haultain, and if the minister wants further identification, I will say he is the man who said that reciprocity was a great thing for the country once upon a time. Frederick William Gordon Haultain is British born, and as loyal as the next man on the government benches, but for eight months he supported reciprocity, and on the eve of the election when the whip was laid on his back, the same Frederick William Gordon Haultain came and supported a policy that the people of to-day are finding has put them in the position of being losers of millions of dollars. That is Frederick William Gordon Haultain. I think I have a right to ask, as a member of this House, why that information was sent to Mi. Haultain before we were given the same information, and why, three or four days after the telegram I have referred to was sent, when I asked whether there would be an appropriation for this in the supplementary estimates, the Prime Minister told me as a member of the House that it had not been considered.
What was the question the hon. member asked?
Whether it had been decided to place a sum in the supplementary estimates for the taking over of- the terminal elevators.
Where can I find that?
I do not remember the page, but the minister will find it in Hansard, and I would ask the explanation now which I think I have the right to ask.
I would like to see how you put the question to the Prime Minister?

Well, there are lots of your friends around you there who will find it for you in a few minutes; they are not busy; they are not taking very much part in this discussion. I am sorry to see that, the western members on the Conservative side are not taking the part they should in trying to get this Bill modelled up as they know the great majority of their constituents would like to have it modelled. However, it is not passed yet and I hope they will give us their opinions before the final stage. Wherein does the Minister of Trade and Commerce think my argument was wrong when I said that this Bill would leave it open to anybody who was operating a terminal elevator to buy and sell grain.

I do not intend to make any reference to the celebrated personality who seems to hover around the imagination of my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles), and I apprehend that if he were
present to-night that gentleman would be able to take care of himself quite as well as would the Prime Minister, were he present. However, as to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Moosejaw, personally, in so far as it differs-which is not by a very wide margin-from the Bill as it stands, I would have no objection to it.
It seems to me that it would be well to move very cautiously in this matter. If men wish to evade section 123, I cannot see how they can be prevented from doing so, either under the amendment as moved by the hon. member for Moosejaw or under the Bill as it stands. For instance, suppose five men desire to go into the gram buying business and also in the business of a terminal elevator. They know that under this clause they cannot do it in their personal capacity, nor can any one of them. All they have to do is to form two joint-stock companies, calling the first the Brown Elevator Company, and the other the Brown Storage Company. Under these two names these five men can, in defiance of both the Bill and the amendment, conduct the joint business.
Does not my hon. friend think, that the words ' or otherwise interested in ' would cover the case of holding stock in both companies?

No. The five men are stockholders in both companies, and they own all the stock. ' A ' cannot buy and sell grain while the Brown Storage Company is storing grain because he is interested in that company. But the joint stock company which ' A,' ' B,' ' C,' ' D ' and ' E 5 form, called the Brown Elevator Company, is not interested in the Brown Storage Company, directly or indirectly, and the Brown Elevator Company can go into the field and buy qnd sell grain. I am thoroughly convinced that the whole object of the Bill can be evaded in that way. No individual who is interested in a company doing one line of business can himself engage in the other line of business, but a joint stock company might be formed which as a company" had no interest in the other, and it could do the business. Nor can you get away from that difficulty unless you have legislation that will prevent the interlocking of both directors and shareholders; because, while you might say that no company owned by one set of men could under the name of another company owned by the same set of men perform the two businesses, you would have to say that no man could be interested in two companies which performed as part of their business both of these lines. And suppose we went so far as to legislate that no company which had a shareholder owning even one share of stock could do business as an elevator company if he had also one share of stock in a company doing a grain

business. That would be of course absurd legislation on its face, but we would have to go that far at least to get over the' difficulty; and even if we went that far, all they would have to do would be to put their stock in trust, and the wit of a legislature could never get over that difficulty. 'By means of a trusteeship the law could be evaded in spite of us. I only say this to urge that we had better go slow and see how this works out in practice, and if we find that it is absolutely worthless, we might as well quit. This is not the first time that this difficulty has been encountered. The practice of the interlocking of shareholders and directors is at the bottom of the biggest difficulty in the republic to the south of us. That is the reason of the difficulties in regard to what is called the money trust, which it is so far impossible to get over. The same difficulties exist here in a smaller way. While I appreciate the purpose of the government, and hope that they will have some success, I have great doubt whether the clause as it stands or as proposed to be amended will have very much effect.
I am sure that we have listened with great interest to the very frank statement of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie.
Do you think it is true?

In the last parliament my hon. friend was very much interested in what he and other western members considered to be the only effective remedy for the evils that existed or that were supposed to exist in the terminals at Fort William and Port Arthur. If the hon. member for Portage la Prairie is so frank in expresing his opinion that this clause, or even the amended clause proposed by the hon. member for Moosejaw, will not remedy the evil that we seek to remedy, why does he not state with equal frankness what he thinks would be an effective remedy?
For the simple reason that that is not under discussion now, and I try to stick to the point.

I think it is under discussion. I think the minister by his statement has brought it under discussion. The whole question of the government's intention in regard to taking these elevators out of the hands of the present owners, or rather the operators, is very much the question before us at the present time. I myself was responsible in the last parliament for making certain statements in regard to the situation at Fort William and Port Arthur that brought me a certain amount of criticism, because, like the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, I was somewhat frank in dealing with the subject, and I said on one or two occasions that I Mr. MEIGHEN.
could hardly understand why the present system of supervision of the terminals could not be made effective if it was not effective. Hon. gentlemen opposite found great fault with the position I took at that time-insinuated that I was not fairly representing the farmers of the west. The hon. member for Souris, the hon. member ;or Portage la Prairie, and other gentlemen thought the government should immediately place a sum in the estimates for taking over the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur.
It must be done. The farmers said it was the right thing to d*o, they declared it was the only remedy, and they were the people who knew. And these gentlemen stood right at the farmers back at that time, Mr. Chairman, and they refused to have anything to do with the government legislation until the government of the day would make a pronouncement as to their position on this question of taking over these terminal elevators. Now, look at the situation to-day. The Minister of Trade and Commerce makes a statement to-night as to what so far as he knows, he considers the intention of the government to be. He tells us that they propose to make an experiment, and that experiment is to take over, either by construction or leasing, one or two terminal elevators at Fort William and Po'rt Arthur, and operate them for a year or two alongside of the elevators that are being operated under present conditions, and see by this experiment whether or not this method believed by the farmers of the west to be the effective remedy will have any value or not. In the very next breath the minister tells us that so far as he knows those elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur in the year 1910-11 were operated in a manner that was absolutely above suspicion, and that so far as he knew no fault could be found with the method already in vogue as to government supervision of them. That was the effect of his statement-that in 1910-11 those elevators were operated -without reproof or without cause of complaint. What brought about that change in the year mentioned from preceding years ? We did not hear anything of that in the last parliament. The minister may say that we had not an opportunity because the session was not closed until very nearly August, but a great part of the information as to the operations of 1910-11 at the places in question was available before the close of the last session of parliament, and if the minister and hon. gentlemen from west of the great lakes did not have that information they could have obtained it. Yet that did not make any difference in their attitude of opposition to Bill Q. They said that Bill could not be passed unless the government put so many millions of dollars in the estimates for the

taking o^er of the terminals. Now, what does the minister propose to accomplish ? I am looking for light, I am looking for information. What does the minister propose to accomplish by taking over simply one or two terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur? The shipping season begins in the fall of the year, the government will have one or two of these elevators, and the first thing we know is that the elevators are full. The other ten or twelve elevators are there waiting to do business; and the farmers who cannot get their grain in the government elevators are going to be compelled to send it to the other elevators. How does the minister expect that the operation of one or two elevators at the terminals will enlighten the public as to the benefits to be derived from government operation, especially when he tells us that eo far as he knows in 1910-11 there was no fault to be found with the present system? That is ia sort of piecemeal proposition. My view is that the government should go either all the way or go no way. They should either perfect the present system, or else go the distance of taking over the whole system of terminals. How else can they get any results from government operation ? The whole object of this Bill is to remedy conditions, or supposed conditions, about which we have heard a great deal of fault found-the conditions existing at the terminals. If you are not going to take the radical steps demanded by the men of the west, and the minister evidently considers them to be radical, then I would like to know what sense there is in taking the position at all, and what benefit there is in this whole legislation. I have listened to the member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles), explaining the advantages of tire amendment that he proposes in lieu of this section. I think I am somewhat of the opinion of the member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), probably neither the section itself, nor the proposed amendment, will be efficacious in preventing the men who own the interior elevators throughout the west from also being interested in the operation of the terminal elevators. If the minister, with the aid of his legal advisers-and I am sure the member for Portage la Prairie is willing to give him all the assistance possible in this respect-is unable to draft a section that will prevent the condition complained of, that ia of the men who own and operate lines of country elevators from also owning and operating the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, is unable to bring here a clause that will absolutely commend itself to this committee as meeting this situation, then it seems to me this section is absolutely of no value, and it is only fair and right that 120
the minister should tell us he does not think this section will fill the bill. If the minister does not think he can draft a section to meet the requirements, and if he is going to try any experiment at all, he ought to try the experiment that the farmers of the wresit have asked for, and take over all the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur.

I am rather surprised to hear the member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), confess
that there is a wrong, fox which there is practically no remedy. The government is assuming that there is a wrong, and where there is a wrong, I think-although in this I am contradicting the hon. member for Portage la Prairie-there is a remedy, and this committee should find that remedy. It is all very well to use destructive arguments as the hon. gentleman has done. Destructive criticism is -of very little use, we want constructive criticism. I was also surprised to hear him say that the matter referred to by the hon. gentleman who has just sat down was not in discussion-that is of finding a remedy for these wrongs. If it is not under discussion why waste time, we should not have anything to do with this matter at all. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says there is a wrong, and that he is trying to rectify it; and I think he has satisfied himself-I am sure he must have-that so far as rectifying the wrong complained of, the proposed section 123 is so much useless paper, it is not worth the paper it is written on.	.
The mere fact that he refuses to discuss that section now, and in connection with it the amendment of the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) convinces me of that fact. There' is something in the suggestion of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie and I think he could easily rectify it by the insertion of a word or two in the 4th line, so that it would read:
No person owning, managing, operating or otherwise interested in any public or terminal elevator shall buy or sell or be otherwise interested in the buying or selling of grain, etc.
Let us compare for a moment, the section as it stands, and the proposed amendment of the hon. member for Moosejaw. In the first place you will find that by section 2, subsection 1, it says that section shall not apply by reason only of the fact, etc. The hon. member for Moosejaw has shown the difficulty that will arise as the section is at present drafted. That is, a person may be interested in, or may be the owner of a terminal elevator, which shall be leased in accordance with the provisions of the following subsections. He may own half-a-dozen elevators, but so long as he has one elevator



in which he is interested, leased to some person else, he is exempt. The other subsection (b) should commend itself to the approval of the minister, where the person who is the owner of stock or shares of any railway company which owns or operates any elevator, shall also be exempt. I think the hon. member for Portage la Prairie is satisfied that this can be remedied, and that the minister must see that this clause is defective and can and should be improved.

I think that both of the suggested amendments are perhaps worthy of more consideration than I was at first disposed to give them, and what has been said by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie has also impressed me, as all his utterances on these legal questions do. I would be sorry to have the clause pass without getting as near as possible to the intent of the Act. We might allow this to stand and think it over, and pee if we can get any better construction of this clause. My hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Aikins) has also a suggestion to make I understand.

I would move to add as an amendment at the end of section 123:
But if the person who is mentioned in subsection 2 owns, manages, operates or is otherwise interested in any terminal elevator other than a terminal elevator mentioned in subsection 2, he shall not be exempted from the provisions of subsection 1.
That only covers one of the difficulties.
We will allow this to stand at present, and take it up again.
The minister asked if I would read the question which I had asked the Prime Minister. It is at page 2911 of ' Hansard J February 12.

I would like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister whether any decision has been reached to place a sum in the supplementary estimates for the securing of elevators by lease, purchase, or expropriation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That question has not yet been formally considered. An announcement will be made in connection with the supplementary estimates.

Might I ask the right hon. gentleman if he sent the following telegram to Mr. F. W. G. Haultain:-
F. W. Haultain,
Regina
Telegram received. The statement you bring to my attention is utterly untrue. Bill now before the House includes power for purchase, lease or expropriation of terminal elevators; an appropriation to be placed in the supplementary estimates for this purpose.
(Sgd.) R. L. BORDEN.

speechtext:
