I understood that the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce would give some information as to how this information came to be given to Mr. Haultain several days ahead of the time when the Prime Minister told us the matter had not yet been formally considered in council.
I do not think I promised my hon. friend to give him any explanation at all.
You raised a hope.

I am sorry if I raised a hope that now I shall have to dash to the ground. I quite see what an important influence this has in the proper arrangement of section 123 so as to make it effective. It has been the only little divergence from the straight and narrow path that we have carefully followed, which was to discuss this Grain Bill on its merits. This little episode, however, shows how manfully we have stuck to the right principle. But as there is always an exception, my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) has formed the exception. However, knowing hipn as we do, we will forgive him that breach of the general method which has 'been adopted in the discussion of this Bill. I do not think the Prime Minister was much out of the way. I think he explained himself, he gave an answer, and he gave an explanation. He said it had not been formally considered, and in following up the answer he said that the supplementary estimates had not been considered. This, if it comes in anywhere, as it will come in, will be in the supplementary estimates. I think the Prime Minister was quite consistent in what he said as to why he sent a telegram to Mr. Haultain, and the Prime Minister when he comes will give that explanation himself. I suppose it was to give certain information to Mr. Haultain.

I think I had a perfect right to bring this to the attention of the minister. I contend that we should have been given every particle of information that the government possesses. The Prime Minister was possessed of certain information that he was in a position to impart to a political pet, Mr. Haultain, of Regina. The Prime Minister, I think, had a greater duty to perform to us than he had to perform to Mr. Haultain. Mr. Haultain was told in categorical terms that such money would be in the estimates. I asked: Had the decision been reached to put that in the estimates, and I am told the matter had not been formally consid-Mr. KNOWLES.

ered. Was Mr. Haultain told that it had not been formally considered? No, he he was told in the most formal way that the vote would be in the supplementary estimates for such and such a purpose. I think we are entitled to just as much information as Mr. Haultain was, if not a little more. It is an important matter for us in the west. I have letters upon letters from people in the west, people whose hopes have been raised that they would secure terminal elevators by lease, expropriation or purchase by this neiw government. Perhaps those hopes are to be dashed to the ground. If the minister will be more particular to execute his promise of expropriating the elevators and less particular about establishing a Tariff Commission, he will confer greater benefit on the people in the west. We have been told that the one great reason for the haste of the government in instituting this Tariff Commission was that they made a promise, and the promise was weighing heavily upon their conscience until it was fulfilled. Surely if they are so much in a hurry to fulfil their promise in regard to the Tariff Commission, why should they not be equally in a hurry to keep their promise in regard to terminal elevators? Their rule seems to be that promises to the manufacturers must be kept, but promises to the farmers may be ' chucked.'

I understand the hon member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) to say that although an individual in his private capacity could be prevented from doing a thing that was subject to a penalty, if he were to join a corporation he could secure immunity for doing that very thing which he could not do otherwise. All I have to say is that corporations are subject to the penal laws. In redrafting this section I hope the minister will do it in such a way that it will apply to corporations as well as individuals. The criminal law deals with corporations just as well as with individuals. True, you cannot put a corporation in jail, but you can reach them by heavy fines. As this would be an indictable offence, I would suggest that whatever penalty applies to an individual should be made to apply to a corporation.

The point is that the corporation would not be violating the law, and therefore would not be subject to the penalty. The corporation would be quite within the provisions of the Act. Certainly a corporation under the Act as it stands, if it violates the law, is subject to the penalty the same as any one else, because the word ' person in the interpretation clause covers ' firm "or corporation '. I do not see at present what remedy there 120*
would be that would not make the evil worse, that is to say, that would not entail an even worse confusion. I do not think my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) would advise the government to frame this clause so that no person could be an owner of stock, however small, in one company doing a grain business, and also own stock in another company doing a storage business. If he did that what would happen the unfortunate individual who received by will stock in one business, when he himself owned money in another? He would be violating the law without any act of his own whatever.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 125-security by license,

I propose to amend this section by striking out all the words after ' sum ' in line 24 to ' elevator ' in line 26.
The words struck out will be ' of not less than ten thousand nor more than fifty thousand dollars, in the discretion of the board, for each terminal.' Then I propose to insert the words ' of seven thousand five hundred dollars for each terminal elevator of fifty thousand bushels capacity and under, and of a proportional sum for each terminal elevator of more than fifty thousand bushels capacity.' That puts it upon the basis of $7,500 for a bond for a 50,000 bushel elevator or under, and on the same proportional basis for an elevator of over 50,000 bushels. Seven thousand five hundred dollars is 15 cents per bushel and that is based on the principle of 15 cents for every bushel of capacity in the elevator. That is the same bond that is given in Minnesota; it is not considered too large, and it is cheerfully given there, I understand.
How would that rate compare with the rate actually required now?
It is much larger. We cannot go above fifty thousand. If you have a seven million bushel elevator you get a much larger bond.

I draw the minister's attention to the fact that a little while ago his argument was that the bond was sufficient security and that there was not the necessity of action by the board to close an elevator. I must say that fifteen cents a bushel is not a very adequate security.
If my hon. friend will make the calculation he will find that it gives a very large security.
It is a large security, but it is not an adequate security.

I think it is an adequate security, if you take into

consideration that the grain itself is within the elevator. It is not taken out. Of course, if it were something which was dissipated and if all you had wras 15 cents a bushel, it would not be a very large proportion compared with the price of the grain, but this is a large bond for security.

I am not complaining of the bond, but I am complaining about the application of the minister's argument in a former case.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 57-sale by sample.

Section 57 at present reads as follows:
Nothing in this Act shall prevent any person from selling or buying grain by sample regardless of its grades.
I propose to add the following:
Subsection 2. Notwithstanding any other provisions of this Act that may conflict therewith, sample markets may be established in the cities of Winnipeg, Fort William and Calgary and the mixing of grain permitted in connection therewith under such rules and regulations as shall he recommended by the hoard and approved by the Governor in Council.	.
3. The provisions of section 208, with the exception of subsection 3 thereof, shall apply to sample markets when established.

On the face of it, this amendment would seem to contemplate the mixing of grain at terminal points, or at ainy rate it would contemplate the mixing of grain after inspection. I think that in the beginning of our consideration of the Bill it was generally conceded that that principle was objectionable to the spirit of the Bill; that is to say, that there should be no mixing after inspection. I think the committee would he glad if the minister would give a somewhat full explanation of tihis proposed amendment, because it seems to contradict the principle of the Bill.
I think we do. We want to have a very thorough understanding of this question which is a vital point of the Bill.

Very well, if my hon. friend requires a fairly full explanation he has a perfect right to have Mr. FOSTER (N. Toronto).
it. Perhaps it would be as well to premise the statement in reference to this by a little glance at the history of the grain business in the United States of America, instead of travelling .all over the States and particularizing, it would be just as well for the purposes of this explanation that we should take the state of Minnesota and confine ourselves to that. The facts of the case in reference to the development of grain marketing in the state of Minnesota are briefly these: The time was when they had no sample market 'and allowed no mixing of grains. They had a grade market and a grade market only. Gradually, in the evolution of the grain trade and public sentiment developed and in the course of time, in the early eighties, I think it was, the grade system pure and simple was superseded by the sample market system. For a number of years the sample market system has been the one in vogue in that state. The modus operandi of the system is something like this:	.
Grain coming from the west to Minneapolis, St. Paul and Duluth, is at a certain point outside of Minneapolis sampled by the samplers of the Grain Exchange of Minneapolis and also by the samplers of the state who correspond to our government inspectors. These samples are sent in the one case to the members of the Exchange, and in the other to the proper state officials. The object of the sampling by the state official is to set the grades of the grain; the object of the sampling by the grain exchange is to get from these cars sale samples which -are placed in the band's of the members of the exchange. These samples appear in the exchange when the exchange opens for business. There is a sample of the grain taken from each car, the number of the car, and the district from which the car comes, and these samples are viewed by the buyers, and according to the quality of the samples shown the purchase is made. The samples taken by the state officials, have by an early hour of the day been inspected by the state inspectors and the grades for the cars are fixed and the certificates are sent up to the grain exchange and the buyer then has the advantage of the sample itself which he can see and feel, and of the grade and standard which has been established by the state inspector. The purchases are then made and the cars have gradually made their way down to the city and they are to remain for a certain period. These carloads of grain are bought then by people upon the sample market. They are afterwards taken, if bought by the millers, to their mills, and if bought otherwise they are taken to the warehouses as they call them, or the public or terminal elevators, as we call them. They are inspected into these

elevators and are stored in them and are again inspected out, and are to be inspected out at the same grade and at the same weight as when inspected in.
Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say there were two inspections P
There is a sample inspection by the state and that becomes the inspection into the elevator. I did not mean to say there were two inspections into the elevator.
When the grain leaves that elevator is there a verifying inspection or a different inspection?

am fully convinced, as the result of the tests that I have spoken of concerning different types of wheat, that it becomes absolutely necessary, if we are to have an ideal market, that we must have a sample market to temper the inefficiencies and inadequacies of the grading system, and in order to have such a sample market, we cannot, rely on the western millers, who can place a carload in a special bin, hut we must have the grain specially binned in the terminal elevators .in order to enable the eastern miller and the old country miller to enter into this competition.
I find also, on page 103 of the proceedings of the same conference, a statement from Mr. Henders, who I think is at present the president of the Manitoba Grain Growers' Association, as follows:
We cannot compete under the present existing conditions, but if we could be put in such a position that we were able to go. on a sample market in Winnipeg and select our types of wheat and compel the Ogilvie Milling Company and the Lake of the Woods Milling Company to go on the same market and select their types of wheat the same as we do and compete with us, we could go into the business. On the other hand we put ourselves in this position that we send to the old country the wheat which is not selected by the Ogilvie people or the Lake of the Woods Milling Company, a secondary article which goes into a general bin, and this fixes the price at which we have to sell our good stuff.
In the minutes of the proceedings of the Senate Committee, on page 200, I find in a formal statement put in by Mr. McKenzie, the secretary of the Grain Growers' Association, the following:
There is a consensus of opinion that a sample market established in Winnipeg would be in the interests of the grain producers. In my judgment, that, however, can oidy he made effective by permitting dealers special binning privileges in terminals so as to preserve the identity of their purchases on the sample market. I cannot conceive of a purchaser on a sample market storing his grain in a special -bin in an elevator operated by his competitor. The risk would be too great; his competitor would soon put him out of business. The only effective special binning privilege that could be secured would he in government owned terminal elevators.
I read these as sample statements from those wbo in the west represent the organized grain -producers in the associations known as the Grain Growers' Associations. I might quote from Mr. Fream, of the Alberta Farmers' Union, to the same end, that he is in favour of a sample market, but he wants to see government elevators at the terminals before he would be in favour of having a sample market introduced. Thus much for the opinions of those who represent the grain producers of the Northwest. When we come to other classes who are interested in the Mr. FOSTER (N. Toronto).
grain business, we find probably different views. Many of them are in favour of a sample market; some of them are not. On the whole, I should judge that the preponderating opinion of those most vitally interested in the grain business of this country is in favour of having a sample market in Canada. It is in deference to the course which history has taken in Minnesota and generally in the United States, and also in deference to this opinion, which I believe to be general, that the government has determined to introduce at this time into the Grain Bill a provision under which sample markets can be established at Winnipeg, at Fort William and at Calgary.
The arguments on general principles, without taking up too much of the committee's time, seemed to me in general to be these: The natural method of .buying and selling is for the seller to show and the buyer to examine the article which it is proposed to exchange between them. A man wants to buy a horse, some one else wants to sell a horse. The buyer and the seller come together, and the buyer examines the points of the horse with what knowledge he may have and lie fixes his price for that horse on his own examination. He does not sit in his house and buy a horse by grade or anything of that kind. That is probably an extreme illustration, but what I wrant to come to at first is, that the natural way of buying and selling is to buy and sell by an actual examination of the article of wdiich an exchange is to be made between the two. Now it would seem to be plain that where you have three or four standard grades of grain, the standard 'being fixed as being of a cgrtain weight, of certain texture or kernels of grain, certain colours and so on, that you will have as between the different grades established varying degrees of excellence in the 'grain. You will have a No. 1 which is 'flush and full. You will have a No. 1 which is between that and a hare No. 1 which the inspector looking at in sample, and knowing what the various standards are, will say: 'Yes, that can go into No. 1 '; and so you have these spreads in value between the different grades as far as the grades go. From what study I have given to the matter the impression is strong with me that the farmer gains less and loses more by sales under grade, than he would if he made his sales by sample. If you have a sample market in Winnipeg, where the farmer's grain, sampled from his car, goes on inspection, and the buyers are present in the sample market the grain of the farmer is not simply bought by those who are upon the sample market because it grades No.

2, and the price just given simply on the grade of No. 2, but the price will be proportionate to the qualities within the grade itself. A man will see a plump good quality of No. 2. He will see a less generous quality in No. 2; he will see one that goes down very close to the 'border. In a competition of buyers it is plain to me that the better price will be given for the higher quality within the grade. By the other system it is sold out of sight and by grade. It seems to me that it is rather paid for to the farmer bv the lowest of the grade than by either the average or the highest of the grade. The trouble which is complained of, and it is a grievance, is the spread in price between the different grades. Those who are in favour of a sample market believe that the purchase thereon by the competitors will bring out the value for all these qualities between the grades, and that those values will certainly be shared and gererously shared by the farmers. That is the argument for the sample market so far as that is concerned. The argument against the sample market is one that says: ' Hold by the grades ' and avoid mining. Now it seems to me a necessity for a sample market that you should have mixing privileges as well, and mixing privileges, says the man who stands by the grade, and that alone,	will deteriorate the
grades themselves, and on the ultimate market you will therefore, get a less price than you would if you had no sample market, and no mixing of the grain as a concomitant of the sample market. The man who buys on the sample market with the privilege of mixing in a bin at the terminal elevator or anywhere else, buys the different qualities within the grades and he directs them to his bin. He will buy, for instance, a good grade of No. 1 and he will buy the best grade of No. 2. He will direct both of these-if he buys a carload or two or three carloads of each-to his bin in the terminal elevator. They will go into thiait bin, and the two of them mixing together will make a good grade of No. 1, and before they go into the market they pass the inspection and receive their grade out. That grade out given by the same inspectors is a uniform grade, and the grain goes upon the market with the impress of the grade, with the certificate that the government inspector gives it. I do not know if there are any other points that should be mentioned in giving this very cursory, and of course not very full or complete, description of the sample market as contrasted with the grade market, or the difference between the two. No doubt we shall have some conversation upon this, and other gentlemen will have their views upon it. We will discuss it and I shall
have further opportunity for speaking upon it. Probably I have said sufficient in introducing the question to the committee for its consideration, and by and by for its conclusion.
Is the sample market in the United States under federal control, or state control?
It is under state control.

I am sure the committee is indebted to the minister for the statement he has made on the introduction of this very important amendment. But I am bound to say that the explanation he has so far given does not meet the questions that are in my mind. First let it be thoroughly impressed that for good reason or bad, whether wisely or unwisely, it has been the principle contended for, especially by the western farmers, but acceded to by everybody-that it was in the interests of the trade and in the interests of the grower of grain, that grain should go forward to its ultimate market according to the inspector's certificate.
That has been a cardinal principle of our grain trade which has been held more and more strongly every year, and the desire to maintain that principle is the foundation of the demand for government ownership of terminal elevators, or for the divorcing of the ownership of terminal elevators from the buying and selling of grain. The minister did not make it clear whether this is an amendment that applies in fact cnly to grain bought for local consumption and not in serious measure to grain for export. It seems to me that while ostensibly and according to the argument of the minister it is a provision which will be applied particularly to grain intended for local consumption, as a matter of fact the mixing privileges which this contemplates will apply to grain for export quite as much as to grain for home consumption.
If my hon. friend understood me to limit it to grain for home consumption he took from my words a meaning that I did not intend to convey. They apply generally.

If he had given it to be understood that it applied especially to grain for home consumption I could then have seen the force of the argument, but if it is to apply to all grain I fail to see the logic of his explanation. It is then in direct contradiction to the principle that has been established and carried on for so many years. I am not going to argue for the moment that that principle is right, it may be that in the quotations he has given my hon. friend finds good reason for reversing the principle, but before reversing it there should be the most sub-

stantial reasons and the most complete explanation.
After the grain arrives at an elevator at Fort William it is allowed to be mixed, and a man buying on sample market is allowed to mix it, and the grain is graded out.

That is what is proposed under the amendment and I say that is contrary to the principle which now prevails. To-day the principle is that the grain is inspected as it comes from the country elevator, at Winnipeg; it goes forward under that inspection and it is held most strongly, especially by the farming community, that it should still go forward c.u that inspection, and should not be mixed at Fort William.
Did they not pass a resolution at Brandon last year asking for the establishment of a sample market?

In my humble judgment there is an effort under the name of establishing a sample market to secure unlimited rights for mixing grain for export and that is entirely contrary to our present principles of handling grain.
There can be no question of the advantage of selling grain on a sample market if there is a demand for that grain which demand can handle it without requiring it to be graded or to go through varying channels of transportation. Then, undoubtedly the farmer will get a truer value for his grain. But that only applies and qan only apply so far as there is a consuming market within such range as will allow that grain to go forward without breaking bulk, so that the grain which has been bought on sample will be actually delivered to the place of consumption. Once bulk has to be broken before grain reaches its ultimate point of consumption then, in order that the grain trade may be carried on with facility, it must be carried on under grade and not under sample. You cannot preserve the identity of grain in practice between Fort William and Liverpool.
You must carry on the trade between Fort William and Liverpool on grade and not on sample. You can only carry on the trade by sample where you can reach the point of consumption without breaking bulk from the point of shipment. When conditions in Minneapolis are cited as conditions that might prevail at Winnipeg, you lose sight of the fact that at Minneapolis a large percentage of the wheat is for home consumption, and a small percentage is for export. But at Winnipeg the small percentage is for home consumption, and the large percentage is for export. That makes a radical difference in conditions. In the case of Minneapolis it matters little what Mr. OLIVER.
happens the small proportion of wheat that is exported; the great bulk of it is milled for home consumption, and the great bulk of the mills are right at Minneapolis. But in our case, where only a small part of the whole product is locally milled, the large proportion is for export. Therefore, it makes a great difference to us how that grain that goes to the export market is handled; it makes less difference how the grain that goes for home consumption is handled. Therefore, when a proposition is made which, under the name of giving our farmers the advantage of a sample market, merely becomes a proposition to legalize the mixing of grades for export, it is a matter of a most objectionable character. I wish to place myseif on record as being strongly opposed to the proposition of legalizing the mixing of grain in the terminal elevators, because that is what this proposition is.
It is a proposition for a sample market.

A sample market has nothing whatever to do with the mixing of grain for export, or has no necessary connection with the mixing of grain for export. So far as there is a milling demand which can be centred in Winnipeg for the purchase of the farmers' grain, that milling demand can be exercised without mixing the grades in the terminal elevators. The two things have no necessary connection. Provision can be made in the Bill, if necessary, for selling grain on sample in Winnipeg. The provision exists in the Bill to-day, but it has never been taken advantage of, because I presume, the time has not arrived when conditions were favourable to dealing with it in that way. At present, in the Bill of 1908, provision is made that the shipper of a car of grain can order it stopped at Winnipeg for the nurpose of giving him an opportunity of selling it on sample, and afterwards within six months hie can ship it farther east at the same through rate, a provision absolutely intended to facilitate the establishment of a sample market in Winnipeg. So far as I can see. that is all that is necessary to the establishment of such a market, except the local milling demand, which is the only thing after all, that will create a sample market. When my hon. friend gave notice of the amendment, I -wired Mr. R. McKenzie, at Winnipeg, whose name has been mentioned here, asking him his opinion of the amendment. I will read his reply:
Suggested amendment positively no value to western farmers. Opposed utterly hv our association. Ostensibly to establish sample market, effect will be to enable few' private individuals to make immense profits out of second-class grain at expense of reputation of standard grades, with no advantage to farmers. Conditions essential to establish sample

market at Winnipeg, involve making Winnipeg an order point, and sending samples from points west of Winnipeg in advance of cars, as in Minneapolis, and equal opportunity to all dealers to have identity of grain purchased on sample preserved at terminals.
Tire suggestion of Mr. McKenzie has all been met in making Winnipeg an order point, that is. a point to which cars may be ordered and held for the purpose of the load being sold. In regard to the other suggestions that he makes, they can be dealt with very easily, and in no way do they involve the question of mixing at terminals. I have here a copy of the ' Grain Growers' Guide,' containing -an article by the editor upon the sample market in Minneapolis. I think it was perhaps from this article that my hon. friend got the information that he gave to the House to-night. Mr. Chipman went to Minneapolis for the express purpose of studying the sample market, and his conclusion is this:
It was quite evident from the best advice to be received in Minneapolis that the sample market cannot be created by statute. The only thing that can be done in the matter b.v law is to make the conditions favourable, and the sample market will follow promptly. These conditions will include:
1.	Sampling of cars at divisional points outside of Winnipeg.
2.	Increased terminal elevator accommodation.	.	.
3.	Permission to special bin and mix gram purchased on the sample market.
4.	A prompt and efficient system of handling appeals against the grade given by the government inspector.'
In regard to number 3, I take it that is mixing for the purpose of local use, that is to say, for home milling consumption, which of course must be done. When the grain goes to the ultimate consumer the miller must, of course, mix the grain to suit his particular trade. No doubt the British miller has to do the same. When the grain is bought -on sample and can be delivered with, the package unbroken, it is perfectly legitimate to mix that grain to make it suitable for the miller's market. But that is a different proposition altogether from mixing that grain for the purpose of sending it across the water. _ If the grain to be exported is to be scientifically mixed, it necessarily follows that it will always be only what will pass the grade; it will be of a lower standard than if it were not scientifically mixed, and the result of that is that our trade is affected to that extent in the British market,^ and our home prices are correspondingly affected.
That is necessarily the result of permitting or legalizing the mixing of grain in the terminal elevators for export. Let me draw the distinction absolutely between the question of establishing a sample market
and the question of mixing grain for export. The one has no necessary connection with the other and while the establishment of a sample market in so far as it could be established would necessarily be to the benefit of the farmer, and particularly to the benefit of the farmer producing the highest quality of grain, the privilege of mixing for export would necessarily have the absolute contrary effect and would be a detriment to the good farmer inasmuch as lie would not be getting the grade for the higher quality of grain that he produced.

Mr. Chairman, I regard the amendment moved to-night by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) as being perhaps the most vital feature of this Bill and I welcome with all the earnestness I can the principle launched in this amendment. I believe that it will open up a line of legislation and of grain operating in western Canada that will go far, in the course of time, to get over all the obstacles under which we suffer now. I cannot say that I am surprised that the hon. member foi adnionton (Mr. Oliver) has a telegram in his possession that the clause is absolutely worthless from Mr. Roderick Mackenzie of the Grain Growers' Association. I regret that. the officers of that association cannot see^ their way at the present time to give their assistance to the establishment of sample markets. But while I cannot feel myself to be in touch with them so closely as are the hon. member for Edmonton and his associates I do feel that on this subject I am certainly as closely in touch as I can be with the farmers of my own constituency. I did not learn until I reached this House and knew that sample market provisions were in contemplation by the government that those at the head of the association had become antagonistic to the idea. During and before the last contest I was met by farmers at every point in my constituency and at points in other constituencies in Saskatchewan as well as in northern and southern Manitoba and the desire seemed to be universal that sample marketing privileges and machinery should be provided. I believe that desire is universal to-day and that the gentleman who sent that telegram will become aware of it in due course of time. Why is this proposition made and what is the object to be served? I do not know that I am capable of stating it as it appeals to my mind. I think it appeals to my mind fairly clearly, I will no the best I can to state it and I will be brief. Our grading system is at present in vogue and in order to carry out that system we have to have certain specified and defined grades. We must have a certain number of grades ranging in merit I from the -best to the worst. Each must

be defined in so far as words can define it and the grading is done according to the definition. Let us take the case of wheat in order to make it simple. If in buying all the wheat could be divided into 'certain sections in such a way that each would just reach the grade that is to say if it could be so divided that all in each section would just be No. 1 Hard and no more, all No. 1 Northern and no more, all No. 2 Northern and no more and so on down the list, the farmer would get the full benefit. Then there would be no means of extracting from him a certain amount of the value of his wheat. As the system is operated up to this point, by means of one device or another, the purchaser of the grain, chiefly by mixing, has been enabled-I am dealing now with the export trade because it will make the argument clear-to make the export grade the minimum in each case. By mixing perhaps two different samples of No. 3 Northern he is able to make them No. 2 Northern, the one making up what the other lacks. By mixing a high No. 2 and a low No. 3 he is able to make a No. 2 Northern. At all events he so arranges that, generally speaking, he is able to export different classes of grain, each of the minimum of its grade. He does not buy that grade, On account of the grading system in vogue he is able to buy on one basis and sell on the other and by this means he is enabled to snatch and appropriate to himself the excess of value that comes by reason of the fact that a certain sample of grain stands between the grades. It is to get over that disadvantage under which the farmer labours that this provision is introduced. The question before us is: Does this provision for a sample market get over it? I contend it does. What is the machinery? What does the Minister of Trade and Commerce present to the committee? It is that markets shall be arranged at certain points and it is provided that all that is necessary for that arrangement shall take place there. In addition, in so far as the grain that is bought by sample is concerned it may be specially binned at the terminal elevators or at the public elevator at Winnipeg and may be mixed; that is to say that grain that is bought by a purchaser may all be mixed together and he may do what he likes with it. In so doing he divides it into certain grades and he is able as well to so arrange it that it will be the minimum of its class. But in order that he may do that and get the grade he is bound to pay the farmer what that grain is actually worth because he buys it by sample and his competitor is right there to compete with him. He is therefore bound to give the farmer what he formerly has been able to extract himself. He is bound to pay the farmer every cent that that far-1 mer's grain has in value over and above the Mr. MEIGHEN.
minimum of its class. So that the establishment of a sample market and allowing mixing at the terminals, in so far as the grain is bought by sample, gets over the difficulty under which the farmer has laboured for a number of years as, by virtue of the fact that under these mixing privileges and on account of the practice of purchasing by sample there will be returned to the farmer that which has formerly gone to the purchaser and the operator. The hon. member for Edmonton seemed to argue that this was all right in so far as the home market went, that in so far as grain was bought for milling purpose the sampling provisions were good and would redound to the farmer's benefit, but they had no application to grain bought for export.
In the first place I do not think the practice has iso settled. I have spoken with men in the grain business in Duluth. I refer now especially to one who is on the Winnipeg Grain Exchange at present-and my information is that grain is bought by sample for export just as generally as it is bought for local milling. It appears to me that the advantage to the farmer is just as clear in the one case as it is in the other. The mixing is done when it is bought for milling purposes at home and the sample provisions are provided in order that the farmer may get the benefit of that mixing. It anolies just as well to what is bought for export. The provision must be made that only grain bought by sample can be so mixed, and that it cannot be mixed in such a way that other grain bought by grade under the old system, can be mixed with it. The point that did appeal to me, and I think both the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) raised it, is that mixing being allowed in the elevators at Fort William that contain the grain bought by sample, that mixing will result in enabling the purchaser to ship across the water to the ultimate purchaser the minimum grade of No. 1 hard, and the minimum grade of No. 2. That is to say, that the grain which goes across the water will always be at the minimum, instead of it being, if no mixing were allowed, much of it above what is the minimum of No. I Hard, and much of it above what is the minimum of No. 1 Northern, and so on all the way down. Of course, it is quite clear that if we could provide that our grain should go over there intact, and much of what goes over as No. 1 Hard, is really afcove No. 1 Hard, that would enhance the reputation of our wheat, and if the machinery were just up to that point the farmer would get the benefit. But I apprehend that by the -sampling provision the farmer would have his option to sell one way or the other; the competing buyers are there, the man who is buying by sample and the man who

is buying by grade, and the farmer can sell either way. The man who is buying by sample could get the benefit of the mixing provision, and he will consequently pay a much higher price, and the man who is buying by grade has to pay it or he won't get the grain. It appears to me very much could be done through the machinery provided by this section to meet the difficulty that was in the mind of the hon. member for Edmonton. I do not pretend that I have always understood this question, or even that I fully understand it yet, but I know that a very strong feeling has prevailed that only by government operation can the difficulties be overcome. I am still an advocate of government operation. I earnestly hope that the government shall adopt not only this provision but the other also, and by means of the two together we will I feel certain be able to work out a satisfactory solution. The sample market is certainly popular in the constituency of Portage la Prairie. I have no doubt whatever of that. I would need evidence greater than could be read by the hon. member for Edmonton, to convince me that it is not. I have certainly failed to read the mind of the farmer in my constituency if I have not read it right when I say that he is heart and soul behind the proposed sample clause submitted to this House.
Carried.

I would like to see the Bill in proper form carried very promptly through the House, and to see its provisions, so long as they meet the necessities of the case, become effective at once. But, we are called back to consider this clause for the purpose of considering an amendment, which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen), admitted in his opening remarks, was an absolute reversal of the whole policy of the past in dealing with our grain. The minister makes practically the same admission, and the question is too serious to pass over lightly. We discussed some days ago the value of a sample market, or the possibilities of a sample market under the present conditions. Is the minister going to ask us to insert a provision now which will permit the very thing that is complained of by the men who are asking for this legislation!? There would not be lamy Grain Bill at all before this House if it were not that the farmers of the west have complained in the past that mixing of grades had been carried on in the terminal elevators, and that as the result of that mixing our grain standards had been depreciated especially in the Liverpool market. As we all know, we have a condition in the grain trade in western Canada that is not altogether analagous to the condition in the grain trade of the states across the line. We
know that practically all the wheat grown in Minnesota and the Dakotahs is exported in the form of flour if it is exported at all, and that practically none or it goes to [DOT]the outside world's markets in its 'natural condition. The hard wheat that is graded according to our grading system is almost entirely milled in the mills of Minneapolis. On the other hand, the bulk of the Western Canadian grain is sold in the markets of Great Britain and elsewhere. The present system, whether it is right or wrong, has been the only system in vogue in this country aince we have had a grain trade from the east or from the west. The farmers of the west have made complaints- and that is the cause of this legislation- that until last year the elevator operators at Fort William and Port Arthur had been mixing in their elevators the different parcels of grain shipped into these ele-vatoTs, some labelled No. 1, and some No. 2, or No. 3, as the case may be, and that they have been raising a great quantity of the producer's wheat to a grade higheT than was given to it by the inspector's certificate it received when it passed through Winnipeg. Every year our inspectors select samples of the different official grades, and in every case those samples which are sent to the world's buyers are a better average than the minimum of the grade requires. The western grain producer claims that as a result of the mixing that has gone on in the terminals in years gone by, the Liverpool purchaser of his wheat has not been getting the kind of wheat he might expect to get from the sample furnished him by the government inspector at the beginning of the shipping season. That is why this grain legislation was introduced in the last parliament, and has been re-introduced this year.

This does not prevent that at all. The grain would still be inspected out, and the grain thus inspected, must be equal to the sample in the hands of the purchaser in England. This legislation has no effect whatever on that.

The point I am making is, that if this legislation goes into effect, it will bring about a condition of affairs absolutely identical with that which the farmers have been complaining of in years gone by-that, instead of the Liverpool buyer getting the average of the grade which he might expect to get, judging from the sample which the inspector sends him, he has been getting, as a result of the mixing that has been going on at the terminals, the minimum of the grade, and this has depreciated the standard of our grain in the Liverpool market, and lowered the price. If these practices have not been going on, the farmers are mistaken, and there is no necessity for any legislation, other than what

we have on the statute-books at the present time. If, on the other hand, the farmers have been suffering, as they have been complained of doing, from this very condition at the terminals, what does the minister mean by undertaking to legalize the very condition that has been complained against, and that is the cause of any new grain legislation at all? 1 can quite conceive that a sample market under proper conditions, might be of very great benefit to the grain producer. There is no doubt that the farmer loses and is bound to lose, by having to sell all his grain on the straight grading system, because there is, and must always be, such a difference in the prices paid for the different grades that the man who has a very high average of a certain grade is necessarily losing to some extent; but if the buyer in the world's market could be assured every shipping season, that he was getting something more than the minimum, that he was getting the average of the grade he had been led to expect to get, from the samples he receives from the government inspector at the beginning of every shipping season, the farmer would not be losing as much as he does at the present time. I can quite see, that beyond all that, there are conditions uinder which a sample market might be an advantage; but I dto not think the sample market would be of any advantage whatever iif we are going to insert a clause; such as this amendment is, that will permit of promiscuous mixing at the terminals, and of re-grading the groin out of these terminals for export purposes. If, for instance, a miller from Ontario wishes to go to the sample market at Winnipeg or at Fort William, and purchase a certain brand of No. 3. and a certain quality of No. 2, and intends to take that grain down to his mill in Ontario, certainly if a sample market is going to be of any advantage in that case, you must give him the pr'vi-lege of leasing a special bin in the terminal at Fort William; but if he does so, and the different parcels of grain which he purchases on the sample market are, inspected or not, I say that if you give him the privilege for his own convenience of putting a certain parcel of No. 3 and a certain parcel of No. 2 or of No. 1 into a special bin at Fort William or Port Arthur, you have no right to allow your government inspector to re-grade that grain out of the elevator. Then, if the Liverpool buyer wants to purchase grain and comes over to our sample market-we will sav that he is a miller, or is buying for ia mill or a number of mills-if he wishes to come over and buy certain qualities of grain on the sample market and ship them in one parcel to the mills for which he purchases, there is no reason why he should not have special bin privileges at Fort William and Po't Arthur. There is no reason why you Mr. NEELY
should not have a sample market and the mixing privilege if you restrict them in the ways I have suggested; but there is no evidence of any restriction. If you are going to allow a Liverpool buyer to come to the sample market and take a certain sample of No. 3 and a certain sample of No. 2, and send them to a special bin at the terminal, mix them and have them regraded out, you are going to have continued in the grain trade, exactly the condition which the farmers are complaining of at the present moment. The grain_ dealer is not a philanthropist, and he will deliver to the purchaser, to whom he sells, either in eastern Canada or in Liverpool, a grain not a bit better than what the absolute requirements of the case demand.
1 And what are you going to have with this anomalous mixing privilege as suggested by this amendment? You are going to have continued in existence, only on a much larger scale than at present, the mixing of grain to the disadvantage of our grading system and to the advantage of the man who comes between and sells the farmers' grain to the world's buyers. This, Mr. Chairman, strikes me as being such an important amendment that I do not know hut that the Minister of Trade and Commerce might very well give us a little further time for its consideration. I am not blaming the minister for the fact that on his own side, as well as on this, there is not as full a House at the present moment as there might be. But whether this amendment is carried out or not, I want to say, so far as the position taken by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) is concerned, I think when he says the farmer of the west would like to have a sample market he is perfectly correct, but my hon. friend knows under what conditions the farmer thinks that a sample market oould be safely and properly established.
Does the hon. member not think that the conditions set out by Mr. Chipman are not satisfactory?
Well, Mr. Chairman, I think Mr. Chipman guards his position very thoroughly.
Those conditions are all provided for here.
Does my hon. friend mean to say they are all provided for in this amendment?
I think so.
Then the hon. gentleman's vision is much clearer than mine.
Bead it and see.

I have read it thoroughly again and again, and I can see no safe-

guard in any shape or form for the evils that would be brought into being in my judgment. If the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) takes a different view, his vision is much clearer than mine.

What I stated was that in my judgment the Bill provides the conditions set out by Mr. Chipman, and I think my hon. friend would hardly dare-I am sure he would not dare-to stand up in this House and say there was anything wrong in th.e ' Grain Growers' Guide.'

I will frankly say that I am not the proprietor or publisher of the ' Grain Growers' Guide,' and I aim not a shareholder or stockholder in it or any similar publication. I am not a member of the Grain Growers' organization, or any business concern connected with it.
I do not think that my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen), should take such a position
Hear, hear.

-Because anything that
emanates from the 'Grain Growers' Guido,' or the officials or head men of the Grain Growers' Association in his own province, seems to contain in itself the germ of disapproval so far as the 'hon. gentleman is concerned.
Oh, no, not necessarily.

Apparently sio. It appears that when the minister is making use of a quotation which bears out his argument from some member of the Grain Growers' Executive, or from 'the ' Grain Growers1' Guide,' it is very acceptable, but when anything to the contrary is suggested by way of authority from these very same sources, that is enough to condemn it in the eyes of the hon. gentlemen opposite, including the member for Portage la Prairie. Now, I think hon. gentlemen opposite ought to be reasonable in this matter.
My hon. friend knows the rule, which is a very good principle in law or anything else, that a man's admission can always be used against him, but it can never be used in his favour.

I am not going to split 'legal hairs with the hon. gentleman, because I am not a lawyer, and I do not propose to enter into any fine legal discussion, but I am lawyer enough, I think, to see the effect and the tendency of this amendment, and I fail to see yet-'and I have read the article of Mr. Chipman, editor of the 'Grain Growers' Guide,' who let me say takes no active part in politics whatever-that the article makes any such admission as claimed by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie and the minister in dealing with
this proposition to allow -mixing privileges at the terminals and then grade the grain out again for export purposes.

I am really anxious to h-ave a little light on this question. I listened extremely carefully, with all the care I was capable of, to the minister and my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), but I cannot say that I understood the question much -better after they were done than when they began. It may have been my obtuseness, it very likely was; but -a man rarely gives up some belief in his own judgment, -and I have some suspicion that they do not understand the question themselves as well as they might do. Now, with regard to the minister's statement of the general desirability of buying upon sample there can b-e no two opinions. In the internal markets of the old countries of Europe no other kind of selling of grain is known. The farmer takes his sample to the market, and he sells upon that sample, and he sells the -bulk at the price he has- arranged for. But wliy do w-e h-ave a system of elevators and grades in this country ? I think the answer is very simple and on the surface. It is because we have an en-ormous export trade. We cannot sell our grain to the consumers -as they sell their grain to the consumers in the old countries of Europe. These grades and elevators-, and -all this complex -and large machinery that is unknown in Europe, -are necessary here because of our -enormous -export trade. Now that would seem in itself to cast 'some doubt upon the general argument in favour of this -amendment that -has been presented to this committee by the Minister of Trade and Comoi'erc-e. My horn, friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) does- not agree with the -leaders of the grain growers nowadays. This nonagreement is of somewhat recent origin surely. There was- a time, if my memory serves me right-very likely as my hon, friend's memory i,s younger he may be able to correct -me, hut I am -almost sure I -aim right this time-when there was *mention made by hon. gentlemen on th-e other side of the House of government ownership -and operation of elevators. I am surely right in -that recollection, and -at that time the 'hon. member for Portage la Prairie and Mr. Roderick Mackenzie were absolutely -at -one. The vote of my hon. friend was in -accordance with the opinion of Mr. Roderick, Mackenzie.
Not on reciprocity.

What in the world has that to do with the matter under discussion? When the hon. member becomes a little older and wiser, he may come into accord with Mr. Roderick Mackenzie on reciprocity. If this blockade continues, it will be necessary to find an outlet for

our grain somewhere. There was a time when he. was in accord with Mr. Mackenzie to this extent that he voted for a resolution in favour of government ownership and operation of elevators.
Hear, hear, that is correct.

Then his education has gone on very rapidly in the last few months. I am only sorry that he cannot carry on that education in such a way as to convince me of what he has learned.
He dealt with a matter that is elementary to us who are trying to get to the bottom of this very complex question. For an amateur he gave a fairly good description of what has been the evil with which we are contending, that is the mixing of grain. It is just the description I have heard Mr. Roderick Mackenzie give of that very evil so that on this head also he is in agreement with that gentleman. His peculiarity is that he has voted for an amendment which will allow this mixing to go on. The mixing is the evil we want to get rid of.
The mixing of itself is not the evil we want to get rid of, the evil we want to get rid of is that the grain buyer is getting the benefit of the mixing instead of the farmer.

My hon. friend overlooks one half his case. Canadians have been proud of our grain product and we wanted to preserve that grain product according to its grade on the Liverpool market. If the mixing lowers the character of the grade it lowers the value of the grain at Liverpool and to that extent lowers the price which would be obtained by the farmers at Portage la Prairie as at other places. I contend that the mixing is the evil and that being the case the Grain Growers came here two sessions ago and said that the only way to cure that evil is by government ownership and operation of elevators.
We have now come to this situation that our friends opposite are doubtful about the establishment of government ownership and operation being the cure for this mixing; they tell us that the sample market will deal only with a very small part of the grain that is grown and exported. They will agree only to a sample market in conjunction with the carrying out of the promises which our friends opposite gave and the Grain Growers are looking to hon. gentlemen opposite as they have a right to look for the fulfilment of the promises by which they won the last'election. I would be the last man to say that government ownership is an absolute panacea for all the evils the farmers suffer from, I was brought up in too individualistic a Mr. CLARK (Red Deer)
school for that. But the Grain Growers will be less interested in my opinion than in the vote of hon. gentlemen opposite on this question.
This buying on a sample market in the first part of the amendment cannot be objected to but where we are left in the dark is in the second part of the amendment. I do not see how we can possibly meet the views of the Grain Growers or deal with the admitted evil of mixing by embodying an amendment which allows the very mixing we have been trying to stop.

The minister quotes the Saskatchewan Elevator Commission as authority for the proposed' amendment. I have met within the last few days two members of that commission, Mr. Green and Mr. Langley, and if these gentlemen ever approved of the- mixing of grain under present circumstances, they have since changed their minds, and are now strongly opposed thereto. I don't think they ever approved of allowing mixing under existing circumstances. If these gentlemen could see that we would be allowed to dispose of our grain on the American market, then possibly they would not consider the mixing of grain so great an evil, at least the sample market would be of much more use to us. I do not know that these gentlemen would be so strongly opposed to a sample market, even with mixing, provided) that we had government ownership of all terminal elevators; without that they are as strongly opposed to it as they can be. Mr. Fream is of the same mind. There is no use casting slurs at these gentlemen. They are careful, conscientious men who have gone over this -thing, and know more about it than most of us do. I have listened with attention to the member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen). I do not know how long he has been engaged in farming. I have been at it for over a quarter of a century, and I am beginning to doubt my knowledge of some of these things. My hon. friend, I fancy, thinks he knows all about this question. Perhaps after he has been dealing with wheat as long as I have he will find out that he does not know so much about it. We have a good deal to learn about it yet, even those of us who live in the west. I would ask the minister not to press this amendment.

Will the minister tell the committee on whose recommendation, by whose advice, he has come to the conclusion that it is advisable to legalize the mixing of grain as he proposes to do by this amendment? The member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) tells us that many of the farmers in his constituency are in favour of a sample market. Are they in

favour of mixing as is proposed under this amendment? How many communications can the member for Portage la Prairie give us from farmers in his constituency to that effect? Did the Minister of Trade and Commerce get his advice from the farmers, from the men who came down here and discussed this legislation with him? I would like to know that. The member for Portage la Prairie tells us that it is in the interest of the farmers. Now the farmers should know something about what is in their interest, and will the minister say whether it is the farmers who advised him along this line? Did they suggest this legislation legalizing the mixing, the very thing they have complained of for years, the very thing that this legislation was originally intended to stop? If they did not advise him to do so, then at whose request is he doing it? I cannot forget that a few days ago the member for Rainy River (Mr. Carrick) made a very strong speech in favour of this very provision in the amendment. But what sort of a constituency does that hon. gentleman represent? It is not a constituency of farmers by any means.
The chief interests in his constituency are industrial interests, are terminal elevator men, mill-owners and proprietors, men interested in the buying and selling of grain. That hon. gentleman was strongly in favour of the enactment of just such legislation as the minister proposes by this amendment, and his whole argument, and the argument of the member for Portage la Prairie, are along the same line. The argument of the meuniber for Rainy River was all to the effect that this would be in the interest of the grain producer and not of the men who operate the terminal elevators. Beautiful philanthropy! The hon. gentleman who represents the elevator interests and the milling interests in this House, those interests being the chief industrial concerns in his constituency, advocates this very thing, and his reason is that it is in the interest of the western grain producers. And the member for Portage 'la Prairie, who represents a rural and farming constituency, strange to say, can support that for the very same reason. It is a remarkable state of affairs. No doubt the minister is also legislating in the interest of the grain producers, because they are the men who handle the grain and who take their profit out of it. I say these gentlemen should have some knowledge and some information to show us why the minister is making this proposition, and why he proposes to change the whole current of legislation in this country by this simple looking amendment to clause 57. As I said, certain gentlemen representing the western (grain producers were here, I believe, when this Bill was first brought into committee; they
no doubt made certain representations to the minister. I took an opportunity to discuss this very question of the sample market with some of these gentlemen, Mr. Fream, Mr. McKenzie and Mr. Henders, and they said they did not want a sample market under present conditions.
Under what conditions would they accept it?
Under government operation of terminals at Fort William and Port Arthur.
Suppose you got them?

That is the point. We are legislating so as to legalize mixing, but we are not 'legislating for government ownership or operation. We are making it permissible for the government to do it, but that is all. We had the definite statement from the Minister that he would not lead the committee into any false conclusions by saying the government propose to go into this matter on a wholesale scale.
Is the hon. gentleman in favour of providing sufficient money to buy all the terminal elevators at Fort William?
The question of government operation does not involve the question of buying.
Well leasing then?
I do not know that leasing would be any particular cost at all because the elevators under their present operators are supposed to pay dividends.
Are you in favour of leasing then?	-

Mr. Chairman, I am not a member of the government, but I am willing to say that if the government should stay by the present system, or if they propose, as they pledged themselves to do, to go# into the business of operating the terminals, they ought to do it in a straight, upright manly way by taking over the whole proposition. They cannot show the farmers of the west what they can do by taking over one or two elevators for a season. That particular season the rest of the elevator operators may find it a very useful thing to be on their best behaviour in order to show that the government-operated elevator had not turned out any better results than they had. But, we have had the results of the operation of these terminals year after year. The government cannot carry on a successful experiment unless they take over all the terminals and the handling of the whole year's output. This is not the way by which they can demonstrate the success otherwise of government ownership as compared with private opera-

tion. But, that is not the question under discussion. I do not want to say that my hon. friend was asking me any question to divert my remarks from the line on which I had started out, but I do say again, Mr. Chairman, that it is a strange situation that presents itself. We have one hon. gentleman from Port Arthur and Rainy River telling us that he wants this kind of legislation because it is in the interests of the producer, although he represents an industrial constituency, and the hon. member for Portage ia Prairie (Mr. Meighen) telling us the same thing because he represents a rural constituency. The conditions might be worse than they are at the present time, but if the farmers of the west are not to be consulted with reference to this legislation, if their views and wishes are absolutely to be lost sight of, and if the present conditions of marketing the grain of the west are to be reversed in a way in which the western grain producer does not want them to be, I think it is only fair that the minister should give us the reasons why he desires to make this change, and at whose instigation the change is to be made.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to delay the passage of the Bill. I would like to dispose of this amendment to-night, in fact I would be glad if we could carry the Bill out of committee to-night, but it will not be possible to take the Bill out of committee to-night because section 123 stands for consideration, and while I would not suggest that possibly very much more could be said in regard to this amendment which is now before the committee, it will be admitted by everybody that it is the most important feature of the whole Bill as a matter of policy, and as a matter of legislation. The .membership of the committee at the present time is very small, and I would suggest to the minister that it would not be creditable to pass such an important amendment in such a small committee, and that as the Bill is not going out of committee anyway, and must be considered at another time the amendment be allowed to stand until the consideration of the Bill at a future date.

I do not want to press unduly for the passage of this amendment, or of the Bill, and I do not think that my hon. friends on the other side can say that I have been pressing unduly, but we do want to get the Bill through. I do not know, if we were to let it go until to-morrow, what could be said further than what has been said. The hon. gentlemen who are opposed to this certainly are the pick of their side, and they are the men who have grown up on grain. They come right out of the atmosphere, they have it in their boots, and in Mr. NEELY.
their hats, it is through them all the way. They are the competent ones, they are the ones who have stayed by this Bill manfully as we have been carrying on the discussion for the last fortnight, and I am sure that nothing can be said, but what has been said so eloquently, and so well by the members who have had their full say to-night. The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely), is not satisfied. I would invite my hon. friend to make himself over a little if it is not too late. What is the reason a man who is not a farmer cannot express his views and give his quota to legislation in the interest of farmers, and of the grain producers of the countryP Is it absolutely impossible? The whole argument of my hon. friend was based upon a remarkable conjunction of feelings and of sentiment. The hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Carrick), was in favour of this very thing and he favoured it because it was beneficial to the producer of grain. Why, should the argument prejudice the case? Could not my hon. friend (Mr. Carrick), hold that sentiment, and advance it in this House, and be thoroughly honest in it? Does it depreciate his argument because it is not made by a man who raises grain? Surely that is not what my hon. friend (Mr. Neely), would say. But the strangeness of the thing went still further. There was a complete agreement between the argument oi my hon. friend from Rainy River and the argument of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen). They were on the same line. Mv hon. friend from Portage la Prairie says that his farmers are in favour of it. He advocates it because it is in favour of the grain producer, not of the grain handler. Did my hon. friend mean to throw discredit on that argument because my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie was not a farmer? Here are two arguments, one from a gentleman who is a business, man, who is not a farmer, and one from a lawyer who is not a farmer, but who represents a farming constituency. But the whole point of my hon. friend's argument, if he means to throw discredit on the thesis that was being advocated, because it was advocated by men who were not farmers, falls to the ground when he sees that the arguments, sentiments and reasons of these two gentlemen were exactly in accord with what I have read here tonight as the printed statements of the Grain Growers' Association's officers who are farmers. There is ah argument that compels me, if I were not perfectly clear in my own mind before, to come to the conclusion that this plan must be Tight. These are the sentiments of the men who grow the grain in the west. My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie from his acquaintance with and knowledge of the

farmers whom he represents Is entitled to j give the reason which he has given for supporting this proposal. He believes that it will be a benefit to the farmer.
The man of general business knowledge looks over the whole scene with just as good a business head as my hon. friend has, and he says he advocates it for the benefit of the farmer. There is a concurrence of testimony that must carry weight in this House. The hon. gentleman is anxious to know why I introduced the amendment, and what did it arise from.
I will tell my hon. friend. I have given what study I could to it. I am a novice in the business but I have some power of reasoning and of getting a grasp of facts, and this proposal is here because after a thorough study I believe that the sample market is in the interest of the grain producer. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Neely) admitted it himself to-night; he said: The farmer loses and is bound to lose under the grade system. So did the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) admit it.
Both myself and Mr. Chipman say you cannot create a sample market by statute.

I deny that Mr. Chipman's whole article and the conclusions from it are anything else but an argument in favour of a sample market. I have read it carefully and it seems to me that the whole description is sympathetic to* a sample market. I believe that the main thing to keep our minds on is what is in the best interests of the producer of the grain. The exporter and the buyer will take care of himself. The eternal battle point between buyer and seller is where the farmer comes in and at the present time he comes in at a disadvantage. The sample market to my mind will give him the advantage he has heretofore been deprived of and that is sufficient reason for me to favour the passage of this amendment. I have a good deal of respect for theory. There are just as good men who can be found who out or a life-long experience in the grain business will stand up and say that as far as this whole matter is concerned the buyer on the European market buys by grade under our present system and his price is predicated upon that grade. He buys on grade and he fixes his price according to the grade and whatever is over the grade upon which he buys it, is so much advantage to him and so much taken from the farmer. It is the farmer who has been missing the fatness of the grade and it is the handler and the miller here and the miller in the old country who gets the advantage of the fatness of the grade. To hear some of my hon. friends opposite you would think there was a generic difference between the mil-

I believe that the possibilities of the market in Winnipeg are illimita)ble. You say that Minneapolis has the advantage in the sample market because Minneapolis has the advantage of the millers close by, but Winnipeg has the advantage of the millers on the sample market itself in the person of commission agents who will buy for them. You say that we are perpetuating mixing which we have been trying to minimize by previous legislation. Then ask him:
Mr. Mackenzie, do you believe a sample market is possible without mixing, and he will say I do not. Then ask him are you in favour of a sample market now, Mr. Mackenzie, and Mr. Mackenzie will answer:	I am, provided wTe have the
proper mixing-no, I will not put it in that way: provided we have our mixing in the place where no other mixers will be allowed to meddle with us and provided we do it ourselves. That is what Mr. Henders will tell you, and that is what Mr. Fream will tell you. They are all in favour of a sample market and they will tell you that a sample market is impossible without mixing, but they do not trust their mixing to go on in the other fellow's shop; they want a government shop in which they can do their mixing in their own bin. We will give them a government shop in which they can do the mixing in their own bin. Before next season's grain is ready to be shipped there will be elevators placed under government operation where these gentlemen can have their bins and where they can do their mixing under conditions which they themselves declare will be honest conditions. In the face of this why is it that my hon. friend must seek for reasons for my bringing this proposal in? These are the reasons. I may be in error but my position is that if we have a sample market, then with the other conditions which



will go with it, we will be helping the farmer directly and we will be helping him greatly. You say that the grain out of these bins where grain has been mixed will be degraded on the European markets and so lower the price. Let me take two branches of that argument. Suppose it does slightly degrade, and suppose the English buyer there puts his price down a little the reflection of that fact on the farmer in the west will be something, but a sample market in Winnipeg where his grain is bought on sample will take away the spread that now exists and he will thus get two or three times on the balance of price.
I believe more. Here is the gentleman who inspects the grain out in bodi'ly form. He inspects out the grain which comes from 'the farmer; on that inspection it is put into store on grade, and is inspected out by himself on grade. It comes out as he sees it. It comes out good and easily goes as No. 1. Another lot comes out. He says, I am afraid of that a little; it is very close down to No. 1, the very lowest point of No. I; it is a little shaky; that will go down into No. 2; and so all through. He will not pass a grade to go to the old country market or to the ultimate buyer unless he knows that it is without suspicion of that grade. That is the system on which the grading has been done, and to-day I have talked to one of the best and oldest graders in this country, Mr. Horn, who tells me that the complete testimony from the English market is that the grades of Canadian grain have been remarkably even and satisfactory, and that therefore, there is scarcely any grievance or complaint on the other side. The man who grades out those grades, and sees that they are not skin grades, but are generous grades, is the very same man who will grade out the grain that is mixed in the bin for the sample market buyers, and will see that it goes out on exactly the same level as the others.
