speechtext:
Mr. HUGHES (Kings, Prince Edward Island) moved the adjournment of the House in order to call the attention of the government and of the Minister of Railways to the inadequacy of the train service for the transportation' of passengers between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, ror some years
past it has been the practice of the Prince Edward Island railway to have a special train to meet the winter boats at Georgetown to take passengers who come by those boats from Pictou to Charlottetown without delay. This year that train has been taken off and the consequence is it is exceedingly inconvenient to the travelling public. There is only one train a day between Georgetown and Charlottetown and passengers wishing to go to the mainland from Charlottetown have to leave for Georgetown by the early afternoon train, remain there for a considerable portion of the afternoon and cross to Pictou the following morning. It takes about twenty hours to go from Charlottetown to Pictou, a distance of about ninety miles. Going the other way the conditions are still worse. The boat cannot possibly arrive at Georgetown until after the regular train leaves in the morning. She arrives at Georgetown about two hours after the _ train leaves and, there being no other train, passengers have' to remain there until the following morning, twenty-two hours after they arrive, before they

can go to Charlottetown where business is generally done, or proceed by the regular train to their destination. In_ former years we had the privilege of a special train leaving Charlottetown in the evening about eight o'clock meeting the boat at Georgetown and passengers could go on board and proceed to Pictou the following morning. In the morning the train would take the passengers on the return trip on the arrival of the boat. The train would take the passengers to Charlottetown where they could do business and proceed by the regular train to their destination the same day. This train has been taken off I suppose by the Railway Board or perhaps by the management at Charlottetown for purposes of economy. I do not think there is any economy in it for this reason that under such conditions as I have pointed out, travel would practically cease. The railway management at Charlottetown will give a special train to Georgetown and return at. any time for $40 and, therefore, I presume that $40 will pay the expense and leave something over, probably $30 would be the expense of a special train. As the fare between these two points would be about $1.25 or $1.50. I am sure I shall be well within the mark when I say that an extra fifteen or twenty people would travel by that road per day if that accommodation was given and that this would pay the whole cost of the special train.
I am convinced that no money is saved by this policy. But for some reason or other the Railway Board appointed a few years ago seem to do strange things, they do not seem to take into consideration to any great extent the convenience of the public, but in order to save a dollar they give these peculiar orders or perhaps the management at Charlottetown is to blame. But there is more than that to it. When Prince Edward Island joined the confederation we came in under a bargain and that was that we were to have efficient and continuous steam communication for passengers the year round with the mainland.
I do not suppose that the present hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane), is familiar with that. I do not know that the board of railway management are familiar with it, but they ought to be familiar with it, because it is important. In order that the present minister may have his attention called to it I shall read the clause in the agreement made at confederation which says that we are entitled to have a better train service than we are getting. Then, among other things, the Dominion government undertook this:
.efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers, to he established and maintained between the island and the mainland of the Dominion, winter and sum-Mr. HUGHES (Kings).
mer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial railway and the railway system of the Dominion.
I am sure that no man will say that the service that I have pointed out is either efficient or continuous, for passengers landing at Georgetown have to remain at least 22 hours before being able to proceed to any other point on the island. I would ask that the Prime Minister or the Minister of Railways and Canals take this matter into consideration, and give an order by wire to the management at Moncton, and the management at Charlottetown to put a special train on at once such as we had in former years. This matter has been going on for six weeks. Possibly it has been brought to the attention of the minister because I see by letters and papers, some of which letters I have myself received, that the inconvenience is so pronounced that the people are very much put out by it, and I would ask the minister to send a telegram either to the management at Moncton or at Charlottetown instructing them to remove these grievances immediately. speechtext:
It will be remembered that on the 13th day of July, 1908, the right hon. the then Prime Minister moved certain resolutions in this House with regard to the extension of the boundaries of Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec. The resolution so far as the province of Manitoba is concerned, was in the following words:-
Whereas, petitions have been presented to the government and to this House from the legislative assembly of Manitoba, praying for an extension of the boundaries of the said province northward and eastward, and for an additional subsidy to the said province in lieu of the ownership of public lands in the territory to be so added.
Be it resolved.
That it is expedient that the prayer of the said petition should ho acceded to, and that upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed to by the said legislative assembly and by parliament the boundaries of Manitoba be extended as follows:	_	_
The Northern boundary to he the sixtieth parallel of latitude; the western boundary to he the present eastern boundary line of the province of Saskatchewan to the said sixtieth parallel, the eastern boundary to he the present eastern boundary as far north as the northeast corner of the province, thence on a straight line to the most eastern point of Island lake and thence on a straight line to the point where the eighty-ninth meridian of west longitude intersects the Shore Line of Hudson bay.
And, be it further resolved:
That whereas, notwithstanding the extension of territory above described, the ungranted lands of the Crown in the territory so to he added to the said province will still continue to he administered by the government of Canada, for the purposes of the Dominion ; and the said province will not have the public land as a source of revenue.
It is just and equitable to recognize the increased cost of civil government which such extension of territory will occasion to the province, and in view of the premises, to make to the said province an increased allowance by money payment, the amount of which should be the subject of negotiation between the government of Canada and the government of Manitoba.
For some time afterwards, the question of the financial terms was the subject of negotiations between the government of Canada on the one hand, and the government of the province of Manitoba on the other, but without any definite result. So, the matter stood when the present admin-

istration took office on the 10th of October last. Shortly after we had taken office, the Prime Minister of Manitoba and one of his colleagues, visited Ottawa, and after some negotiations a basis of arrangement was arrived at, which is set forth in a letter which I wrote to the Hon. R. P. Roblin, Premier of Manitoba, on the 20th day of November last. The letter is in these words :-
Ottawa Ont., November 20, 1911. Dear Mr. Roblin,-Referring to our interview, I beg to say that the conclusions arrived at are as follows:
The extension of the 'boundaries of Manitoba has been under consideration at those interviews and a basis of settlement has been reached respecting the financial terms which hitherto have been in dispute.
The basis adopts the principle of equality of terms as between Manitoba and the other prairie provinces. The application of this principle to the details remains to be worked out.
I may add that we shall introduce the necessary legislation at this session.
Believe me.
Yours faithfully,

Hon, R. P. Roblin,
Premier of Manitoba,
Ottawa, Ont.

Mr. Chairman : Whatever there may be in this resolution of a controversial nature, I do not, for my part, intend to advert to upon the present occasion. I think the time of the committee will be better employed in endeavouring to get information, which has been partly presented by my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) in order that we may appreciate the reasons of the policy which has been adopted by the government with respect to this matter, and the basis of the financial terms which they have given to the province. The resolution in that respect is simply meagre, and I am sure

there is further information which could be got, by inquiring for it. I have to observe first of all, that in regard to the territory added to Manitoba the resolution as introduced by the Prime Minister will have to be amended by him, so as to conform to what I understand is now the settled policy of the government, with regard to those boundaries. My hon. friend has based his resolution in that regard, upon the resolution which was adopted by this House in the month of July, 1908, in whicli the boundaries intended to be assigned to Manitoba were thus defined:-
The northern boundary to be the sixtieth parallel of latitude; the western boundary to be the present eastern boundary line of the province of Saskatchewan to the said sixtieth parallel; the eastern boundary to be the present eastern boundary as far north as the northeast corner of the province, thence on a straight line to the most eastern point of Island lake and thence on a straight line to the point where the eighty-ninth meridian of west longitude intersects the shore line of Hudson bay.
The resolutions now proposed, although based upon that of 1908, do not seek to define the boundaries intended to be conveyed to Manitoba. My hon. friend in his resolution simply says:-
Resolved, that it is expedient, (a) to extend the boundaries of the province of Manitoba northward to the sixtieth parallel ot latitude and northeastward to the shores of Hudson hay, upon such terms and conditions as mav he agreed to by the legislative assembly of Manitoba and by parliament.
There never has been any difficulty at all on this question of boundary between Manitoba and the Dominion government, in so far as the western boundary is concerned, because though the province of Saskatchewan made application to have its boundary extended eastward to the shores of Hudson bay, north of the territory whidh now constitutes the province ol Manitoba, the Dominion government of that day could not see the propriety or the justice of this wish on the part of Saskatchewan, but thought, on the contrary, that territory geographically belonged to Manitoba, and ought to be given to her. There never was any difficulty either as to the northern boundary of the province, it was always understood that it should be the 60th parallel of latitude. The difficulty arose with resard to the eastern boundary, and that difficulty was that the province of Ontario made a large claim to have its territory extended north of what is now the present boundary of Manitoba-in fact at the conference which took place between the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta. Manitoba and Ontario, in 1906 the government of Ontario asked to have its boundaries extended up to the Churchill river.
On the other 'hand, the House remembers that- the province of Manitoba asked to have its boom diaries extended eastward over the territory which was claimed by the province of Ontario, north of the Albany river up to about the longitude of Fort William. The government, of that day could not see its way clear to grant either the prayer of 'the province of Manitoba or the prayer of the province of Ontario in its entirety, but thought that justice would he done both if the boundary between the provinces 'were made as described here, that is to say an extension of the present boundary of Manitoba from the northeast comer of that province by Island lake to about the 89th degree of west longitude. I am aware that the province of Manitoba at first demurred strongly to accepting the boundary which we had assigned to them. Several conferences were held between the government of the Dominion and Manitoba. I had the pleasure on more than one occasion of having conference with my hon. friend the present Minister of Interior (Mr. Rogers) when be was a member of the government of Manitoba, not only _ as stated by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden), as to the financial terms, but also <ais to the actual location of the boundary. And I may say that it was only last winter, after the conference we had between the Dominion government and the provincial government, that the boundary which we had offered the province of Manitoba was 'accepted. The record of that .conference is before the House. In the memorial which was sent to my right horn, friend (Mr. Borden) after he bad accepted office, and which also he ha,s laid before the House, the government of Manitoba officially and formally accepted the boundary which had been offered. It is also of record-or, if not of record, it is of public knowledge-that the government of Ontario was not satisfied with that boundary and pressed to have its claims accepted, that is to have its boundary extended northward to the Churchill river, as it nad claimed originally. 1 assume that, as the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) has brought in the resolution in its present form, ' extending the boundaries of Manitoba north-eastward to the shores of Hudson, bay ' without stating precisely the point at which the boundary is to touch the bay, the government have not yet decided Whether they should or should not accept the pretensions set forth by the province of Ontario.

speechtext:
My right lion, friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is mistaken in that regard. The boundaries are the same as those defined in the resolution of '1908, 'except that they have been set forth in more explicit terms by the Dominion geogra-I piher. This more definite and explicit des-

crip'tion was placed in the hands of the proper officer of this House to prepare such resolution as might be necessary, and be has prepared the resolution in the way in which it is set forth, amid which seems to be all that is necessary, inasmuch as the lands 'are not being handed over as th :y are being handed over to Ontario and Quebec.

Whatever may have been the cause which inspired the present resolution, as to the effect of it I am obliged to differ with my right bon. friend. If the resolution were to be adopted as it is, ' to extend the boundaries of the province of Manitoba northward to the 60th parallel of latitude and 'eastward to the shores of Hudson bay,' there would be no actual definition of the boundary. I presumed, am the innocence of my heart, that it was because the boundary had not been decided. For it is reported that Sir James Whitney said no later than last week that he expected that Ontario would have a harbour on Hudson bay. Therefore, I assumed, that the question had not been settled. But, if there is any doubt on this point, a new resolution has been given notice of by my right hon. friend in which it is stated that the eastern boundary of Manitoba shall be that set forth in the resolution of 1908, the production of a line from the north eastern corner of Manitoba to Highland lake and from that to the 89th degree of latitude. I apprehend that the matter has been settled finally and that the province of Ontario has agreed to have its boundary such as was set down in that resolution of 1908, that is to say it will have no harbour at Churchill or Nelson, but is to go no farther northward on the shores of Hudson bay than the 89th degree of latitude. But I persist in saying that if the resolution were to remain as we now have it under consideration, and the Bill were to be put in this form, it would be impossible to say where the boundary of Manitoba was. My right hon. friend (Mr. Borden) will not pretend seriously that there is any definition of a boundary in the resolution we now have before ns. I presume that if he is to introduce legislation that will be effective he must amend his resolution and state that the boundary of the province of Ontario is to be the 89th degree of latitude. If it is the intention of my right hon. friend in this way to settle the boundary of Ontario, it would be preferable to make the matter perfectly clear.

I have no objection to that. But, perhaps the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) did not understand me. For what reason is a resolution necessary at all? The proposed Bill will not alienate any part of the public domain Mr. BORDEN.
of the Dominion, and in that way it will not constitute a charge upon the treasury. It would not occur to me-with all deference to the right hon. gentleman-that any resolution was necessary so far as the question of boundaries is concerned. The resolution is necessary so far as the increased subsidies are concerned, these being a charge' upon the public treasury. If my right hon. friend who has had great experience, thinks it would be better to state the boundaries in the resolution exactly as they are to be defined in the Bill, I should have no objection. But it occurred in the way I have stated. The specific boundary, more definite and more specific than as expressed in the resolution of 1908 but covering exactly the same territory, was placed in the hands of the officer of the House for the purpose of preparing the proper resolution. He has framed it in the way in which it appears before us. But, as I say, if an hon. gentleman of the experience of my right hon. friend thinks it would be better to express it more fully, I have no objection.

I think it ought to be expressed. But, even from the point of view of my right hon. friend (Mr. Borden), I think it essential because the money terms to be granted to the province must depend largely upon what territory is given to the province.
My hon. friend has copied the resolution adopted in 1905, with regard to Saskatchewan. Under the resolutions now before us; the territory of Manitoba will be about the same as the territory of each of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan and, therefore, I do not see how it is possible to offer to the province of Manitoba any compensation in lieu of the lands which are to be retained by the Dominion unless we know exactly the area of the province, and you cannot know what is to be the area of the province unless the boundaries are settled. That is an additional reason why the, boundaries ought to be settled here and now. I am glad that my hon. friend agreed to the suggestion I made which, if there was any doubt, will remove that doubt. So it is settled that the boundaries of the province of Manitoba are to be the boundaries which we offered in 1908.
I said to-day that I did not want to enter into any matter of controversy on the present occasion, I am seeking for information, but I would observe to my right hon. friend that there is no justification that I can see why these four years' arrears set forth in the resolution should be given to the province of Manitoba. What reason can there be? The province of Manitoba has contended that its boundaries should have been extended at the time that the provinces [DOT] of Alberta and Saskatchewan

were created. I cannot see that there is any connection between the two ideas. If Manitoba were entitled to an increase of its territory-and for my part I have always been of this opinion-this question had no relevancy whatever to the creation of the new provinces. Everybody knows that in 1908, when we created the new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan,; the province of Manitoba made a strong effort to have its boundaries extended.! But parliament has not forgotten that the reason we did not extend the boundaries of the province of Manitoba at that time was that we thought it would not be advisable to extend those boundaries unless the two neighbouring provinces of Ontario and Saskatchewan had an opportunity of presenting their claims to us. It was well known to us that the province of Manitoba was making a claim for the extension of its boundaries eastward, and it seemed to us that, although we had not then res ceived any request for- the extension of the boundaries of Ontario, it would not ba in the- public interest, and we would be inviting trouble if we were to attempt to settle the boundaries of the province of Manitoba, where they come in contact with the boundaries of Ontario, unless we had also the opinion of the province of Ontario.
Therefore, we held a conference in 1906, with the three provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario. I stated a moment ago that the government of the province of Saskatchewan, asked to have its boundary extended eastward along the present northern boundary of Manitoba to the! shore of the Hudson's bay. I must say that after having heard what the province of Saskatchewan had to say upon this point I could not see my way to recom-i mend this to my colleagues or to parliament. It seemed to me that that territory belonged to Manitoba and should be given to Manitoba. When it came to the discussion of the eastern boundaries of Manitoba where they touched Ontario we found, as I said, quite a cleavage of opinion between the two provinces, and neither would give way. Ontario insisted on having its territory extended westward as far as the Churchill river, and Manitoba claimed an extension eastward to Fort William. We could not see the propriety of these respective pretentions of either province, and we struck what I then thought was a legitimate boundary of the two provinces, and I am very happy to see that it has been at last accepted.
The province of Manitoba has sought to have these terms date back to the year 1905. This pretension of the province of Manitoba has not been accepted by the government. My hon. friend tells us that after a conference they have determined
to extend the terms back to the time that we made this offer, in July, 1908, and no further back. What reason can there be why Manitoba should be given any terms dating back to 1st July, 1908? The reason which is given us is that at that time the province of Manitoba was offered these boundaries. There was a controversy between the late government and the government of Manitoba as to the financial terms which would be'extended to Manitoba as a consequence of the extension of its boundaries. If that had been the only controversy between us and the government of Manitoba, the government of Manitoba might perhaps say:	We were
ready to accept those boundaries in 1908, and if we did not accept them it was because the financial terms which we asked were not granted, and if those financial terms for which we then made a claim and which have now been granted, had been granted then, we would have had those financial terms since the 1st of July, 1908. If the government of Manitoba were in a position to make that statement there might be some basis for giving the province those terms as from the 1st of July*. 1908, but I have to call the attention of the House to this fact, that the boundaries which we offered to Manitoba in 1908 were not accepted by Manitoba in 1908, or in 1909, or in 1910, or until about the month of March, 1911, and then were not officially recorded until the month of October, 1911. Under such circumstances I fail to see upon what basis it -can be claimed that the trems which are now extended to Manitoba should date back not from the time the statute is passed, but to July, 1908. For my part I repeat that this seems to be a claim for which there is not a shadow of foundation. But I shall not press the point to-day, I said I would not enter into any controversial matter, but would put forth my objection as I conceived it to be, and as I think it must impress the mind of any one who thinks that Manitoba ought to be treated fairly, even generously, but at least reasonably.
I have nothing more to say except that I shall ask the Finance Minister to give us the reasons why he has agreed to these terms which are proposed in these resolutions. These terms were pressed upon us more than once by the government of the province of Manitoba. We have always treated any new province coming into confederation on the terms which are given in the Confederation Act, that, is to say that the province must be given a portion of the revenue of the Dominion to carry on its affairs.
This was done by the Act of Confederation of 1867, the terms of which were revised in 1907 and put upon a new basis.

It seems to be reasonable that if a new territory is to be added to Manitoba where they will have to carry on the civil government, they should be given a reasonable allowance to meet the increased expenditure which this increase of territory will entail upon them. That, I say, seems to be reasonable. But, what is proposed to-day is not to give to Manitoba a sum of money to carry on the civil government in the new territory -which is to be allotted to the province, but the whole financial terms which are now granted to Manitoba are to be revised and Manitoba is to be given compensation in money above anything that it is receiving at the present time". That is my first objection. My second objection is that Manitoba is given a sum of money in compensation for land not only within the extent of the territory which is to be added to its present domain, but over the whole of the province. In other words, Manitoba, which has been for forty years in Confederation, is to be treated exactly as if it were a new province entering to-day the family of provinces. It has been for forty years a member of confederation; it has received the same terms as those which have been given to the other provinces. K has been given special terms from time to time on account of it being a new province and being therefore entitled to special treatment, but to-day it comes in and is treated exactly as if it had been the same as the territory which we are adding to the province. I do not think there is any justification for that. But that point I shall not press any more to-day. I would ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White) what reason there can be for the proposal as contained in clause (b) of the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that the Bill which will be founded upon these resolutions is to establish equality between the province of Manitoba and the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan; in other words to do simple, plain every-day justice to the province of Manitoba, which, I a<m sorry to say, was withheld from that great province by my right hon. friend when he was Prime Minister of this country. What he has said is substantially correct with regard to the principle upon which the allowances were made in lieu of debt, but the situation in regard to the provinces forming the confederation to-day cannot be described as otherwise than anomalous in regard to the amounts which have been given them from time to time. Mr. WHITE (Leeds),. Dominion deductions from provincial subsidy with respect to surveys of swamp lands, &c., amount to $211,942.95; provincial expenditure on account of swamp lands, proportionate estimate, $240,854.60. These two make a total of $452,797.55; leaving the net amount received or to be received by the province from swamp lands at $2,684,601.75. Five per cent of this amount is $134,230.08, which I deduct, as I have previously explained. That would give an average of about $3 an acre for the sw'amp lands already sold by Manitoba. As to the swamp lands, the right to which Manitoba will now surrender, estimated at over 8,000,000 acres, what the value of these is I am unable to say; but Mr. Young expresses the opinion that these lands are of considerably less value than the swamp lands already referred to. Of course, they are not yet surveyed, and it may be a considerable time before they are available for sale.
Were the sales of the swamp lands cash sales or on credit?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On credit, most of them, paid for in instalments.
Is more money expected to he paid on account of these sales?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The figures given represent the principal sum. They will have to be made the subject of an audit. But so far as this Bill is concerned, that makes no difference, for this reason. We charge Manitoba with the total amount for which she sold these lands. Manitoba will continue to hold that amount, and we charge her 5 per cent upon it, and deduct the interest from the amount she would receive if she were placed in the same position as Alberta and Saskatchewan, and did not own swamp lands.
Does the charge of 5 per cent on the proceeds of the sales of swamp lands date from the 1st of July, 1908, or from the time the sales were made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We consider the state of the account as from the 1st of July, 1908.
From the time the sales were made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Up to that time Manitoba had been deriving certain subsidies under statute. Well, we start afresh as on the 1st of July, 1908. We take the total capital amount for which on that date Manitoba had sold the lands-because the province will continue to administer these lands and receive the payments-we take 5 per cent upon that, and deduct from the 5 per cent upon the total capital allowance of $8,000,000, and the result is the balance which Manitoba will receive under the proposed new Bill.

Manitoba, for instance, 10, 15 or 20 years ago received cash from the swamp lands. Why, then, should she not give credit to the Dominion for the interest which she has received upon them in the meantime?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As a matter of fact, whatever Manitoba derived was derived by virtue of the statutes at that time. What we are doing, as I have already said to this committee, is to place Manitoba on a footing of equality with the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and we are commencing to make a fresh start as on July 1, 1908. So far as the suggestion of my hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is concerned, that Manitoba might very well reply-although I do not think it necessary for her to reply-that she would be justified in asking for these increased amounts from July 1, 1905
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think I have answered the questions propounded to me by my right hon. frieua (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), although I do not know whether it is entirely to his satisfaction or not. With reference to the boundaries, I think the leader of the government has mentioned all that is necessary to be stated, namely, that the boundaries are precisely the same as those fixed by the resolution adopted by this House on July 13, 1908. As to a point made by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to the effect, as I understood him, that Manitoba had not accepted the boundaries, my understanding is a little different from his. I believe Manitoba would have been willing to accept the boundaries de-

fined in the resolution of 1908 if the financial terms had been satisfactory. That is my own belief in regard to the matter. The whole question of dispute between the government of Manitoba and the Dominion government related, as I understand, to financial terms; the boundaries proposed would have been entirely satisfactory. In that connection, I will read a letter from the then premier (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to Mr. Roblin, which reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Roblin,-I have the honour to enclose the draft of a Bill for the extension of the boundaries of the province of Manitoba. This Bill is on the line of the resolutions adopted by the House of Commons at its last session. ' The amount of allowance to be paid to the province in lieu of lands has been left in blank. According to the aforesaid resolution of the House of Commons this amount should be fixed by negotiation between the Dominion government and the government of the province.
We will be happy to confer with you at any time that may be convenient to yourself and to your government.
Tours respectfully,

I will now read a letter in answer to that from Mr. Roblin. It is to the following effect:
Winnipeg, March 1, 1909.
My dear Sir Wilfrid,-I am in receipt of your letter of the 26th nit with enclosure as stated. I have read the Bill and, _ as I presume you would expect, I am disappointed. The preamble in the Bill only recites one of our requests, viz., subsidy in lieu of lands, where onr petition also asks for a readjustment of subsidy or capital account; but which I presume, can be dealt with in the conference.
Our legislature has unanimously passed a resolution authorizing the House of Commons and the Senate of Canada to be memoralized along these lines. I presume the material will reaoh you in a day or two, if not already in your hands. In the meantime I enclose yon a copy of the resolution on which the memorial is founded.
I accept the invitation you have extended by your letter to the members of my govern-men to a conference regarding the terms upon which the said extension of boundaries is to he made.
As your parliament is in session I can understand that yonr time is considerably taken up. I therefore will ask you to be good enough to name the day or days that you can give for such conference and in that way avoid the unnecessary and tedious delay of the representatives of Manitoba at Ottawa
You will therefore he good enough to name the day or the days and advise me.
Yours very respectfully,
(Sgd.) R. P. ROBLIN.
It will be seen that the premier of Manitoba raised no question, so far as the correspondence goes at that particular time, with regard to the boundaries. I have Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
understood subject to correction-because I was not in any way privy to the negotiations -and my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) may have a different view, and may recall that some objection was raised with regard to the boundaries-that Manitoba wouild have been willing to have accepted the enlarged boundaries which we now propose, provided the financial terms had been satisfactory. The point as to which the province of Manitoba and the Dominion government were unable to agree was principally with regard to this matter of financial terms, to which I understand. the leader of the opposition now objects. I think that is all that I have to say upon this occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? What explanation has he of the fact that Alberta and Saskatchewan were each allowed 5 per cent on $8,107,000?

Those were territories of the Dominion of Canada. They had no public works. New provinces were being created. The whole territory had to be-developed, and so it was reasonable to give them a certain allowance to construct parliament buildings, to build roads and other public works, and to make the other expenditures necessary to the work of a provincial government. But Manitoba, as I have said, has been forty years a province of Canada. Her people agreed to enter into confederation on the terms arranged at the time she entered. If the hon. gentleman will look at previous legislation he will find that, almost without exception, when it has been deemed advisable to increase the debt allowance of any province, there has been a readjustment in the -case of all the provinces. He will find that some years ago the debt allowance of Ontario and Quebec was increased from $62,500,000 to $73,000,000, and that New Brunswick and Nova Scotia were treated on a similar basis. You are adding to the debt allowance of Manitoba, -one of the old provinces of Canada, to the extent of about $5,000,000, and basing that allowance upon its population. But if you were to do the same with Ontario and Quebec, what would you have? Ontario and Quebec now have a population of about 4,500,000. Give them the same debt allowance per head, as you propose to do in the case of Manitoba,



over and above the cost to them of the assets which they handed over to Canada, and they would be entitled to a debt allowance of about $130,000,000, as against $73,000,000 which they have been allowed. This would at once give to these two provinces an additional revenue of about $3,000,000 over that which they are now enjoying. Take the case of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. If you deduct from their debt allowance this revenue producing property, the railway between Halifax and St. John, which was built by the two provinces and handed over to the Dominion, and treat these two provinces in the same way as you propose to treat Manitoba to-day, you would add a good many hundreds of thousands of dollars to the revenue of these provinces on debt account. And I presume the same would apply to the province of British Columbia.
What I ask is not that the government should decline to take into consideration the necessities of the province of Manitoba, if it is thought necessary to increase her debt allowance. I would not complain if all these provinces were being treated alike. But what I do complain of is _ that the government should come down with exceptional legislation proposing to deal with one of the old provinces of Canada, one member of the family of provinces, upon an exceptional basis, while altogether ignoring the claims of the other provinces. Because Manitoba is close to the other prairie provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and because she has an alleged grievance which has been assiduously cultivated by gentlemen in accord politically with the present government, we are to deal in an exceptional way with Manitoba in order, as it is said, to put her on an equality with Alberta and Saskatchewan. But Alberta and Saskatchewan, as I have said, were created as new provinces. It had always been recognized that in the case of new provinces there should be a debt allowance. There was a debt allowance given to Manitoba, an allowance which was then thought to be fair, and with which the people of Manitoba were perfectly satisfied. In the case of Alberta and Saskatchewan it was thought reasonable to make these debt allowances. When these new provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were_ created from the territories of the Dominion there was every prospect of their increasing rapidly in population. And to-day, Saskatchewan, after having been in confederation only about six years, has a population larger than that of Manitoba. There would be reasonable justification to look forward and make a debt allowance somewhat in accordance with what it was supposed would be the population of the province within a comparatively few years.

!
Cannot my hon. friend see that when you attempt to treat an old province which has been in the Dominion for forty years on a basis which will put it on an equality with two other provinces of the Dominion, utterly ignoring the claims and the position relatively of the other provinces of Canada, you are doing an injustice, and more than that you are creating a source of dissatisfaction which is going to lead to infinite trouble in the future? The idea of the fathers of confederation was that these subsidies should be upon a fixed basis, and if the hon. gentlemen will look back to the legislation which was enacted not many years ago when the debt allowance was last increased, they will find that that was accepted by the province of Manitoba as a full and complete settlement of all claims up to that time. Surely it is better that when there is any proposition for an increase of subsidy to any of the provinces, the negotiating should be done as it was a few years ago by a conference of representatives of the different provinces, so that they might agree upon what would be satisfactory to all, and so that no injustice might be done. It is not in accordance with the scheme of confederation, it is not in the best interests of the country to pick out any one province and attempt to alter the terms of confederation in relation to that province.
But this government is moving along these lines in other directions. The province of British Columbia has made claims which were also submitted to the conference, and the conference unanimously decided that it would be against the interests of the people of Canada to determine the claims of any province by arbitration. Yet my right hon. friend, as reported in the Toronto ' World,' has sent a telegram to the Premier of British Columbia agreeing to refer the claims of British Columbia, which weTe dealt with at the provincial conference, recognition of those claims being then refused, to a commission, on? of whose members is to be chosen by this government, another by the government of British Columbia, and the third by these two, or, in case they fail to agree, by the Colonial Secretary-to all intents and purposes an arbitration, the arbitrators being allowed to determine as to the claims of a province for consideration in a financial way beyond what is provided for by the British North America Act. As well might Saskatchewan make a similar claim now or in the not far distant future, as well might New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario or Quebec. To say that it is unwise, is simply to say what all public men from confederation down to the present time have said should not be done, that whenever there was a proposition to increase the allowance to any one prov-

ince, the subject of the allowances of all the provinces should be dealt with. Surely the province of New Brunswick, for instance, would have as much Tight to have her subsidy readjusted, to have her debt allowance readjusted, and surely Ontario and Quebec would be entitled in the same way to have taken into account the valuable properties which were handed over by those provinces, and which became a part of the assets of the Dominion of Canada. If this Bill goes through, I do not see upon what ground a separate application from any one province could be refused recognition by parliament, if you get away from the well settled principle adopted at the time of the British North America Act which has been recognized ever since.
Let it be well understood that what it is proposed to do by this resolution is to increase the debt allowance of Manitoba, which had no debt at the time of its establishment, after it has been forty years in the Dominion from $3,500,000 to upwards of $8,000,000, and the government base their argument entirely on the fact that they want to place Manitoba on an equality with Saskatchewan and Alberta, altogether ignoring what would be justice to the other provinces of Canada. The Minister of Finance says that we want to do justice to Manitoba in another way, we want to give her territory as large as that of Alberta or Saskatchewan. We often hear of Manitoba being a postage stamp upon the map but Manitoba to-day contains 20,000 square miles more than the three maritime provinces. The three maritime provinces have but 52,000 square miles, while Manitoba has something like 73,000 square miles, and it is proposed at once, without consulting the other provinces, without seeing what New Brunswick or Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island may think, to add something like 200,000 square miles to the territory of the province of Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Was it not proposed in July 1908 by resolution of this House to do that precise thing?
Yes, it was, my hon. friend is entirely right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did you object to that?

I intended to urge certain terms which I thought would do justice to the maritime provinces, and I propose to urge those terms in a little while upon the attention of this government and this committee.
We come now to clause (c) which authorized the Governor in Council:
To pay to the said province, in lien of ownership of public lands, an annual sum based upon the population of the said pro-122i	;	|
vince as ascertained by each quinquennial census thereof, such annual sum to commence with $562,500 (less certain deductions in respect of what are known as swamp lands and university lands) and not to exceed the annual sum of $1,125,000 (less equivalent deductions); the same to be paid as from the first day of July, 1908.
What is the position Manitoba is put in? When she received those swamp lands she was not entitled to any more debt allowance than she then received, that is absolutely clear because she- started with a population of 15,000 when she entered confederation. She had a reasonable debt allowance, I think considerably beyond what she would have been entitled to simply on the basis of population. The Minister of Finance says she has sold the best of her swamp lands at low prices. She does not propose to account for the interest on the moneys she has been receiving during the last twenty-five 'or thirty-five years, but she proposes simply to begin to hand back what is left, the worst of them, and then to begin paying interest as of the first of Juiy, 1908, of $130,000 a year when she is to get from the Dominion something like $700,000 or $800,000 a year or perhaps even more than that. The paragraph contains these words:
The Governor in Council to pay to the said provinces in lieu fof ownership of public lands,
That is not the language which was used by the late government away back some thirty or forty years ago; when an allowance was made to Manitoba it was put in as for want of public lands. This resolution would seem to imply that in some way or other Manitoba is entitled to the public lands within its boundaries and that as it is not intended to give these lands to the province, this large sum of money, $562,500, should be given to her in lieu of public lands. I notice that when the resolution was first placed on the order paper the words were:
-in lieu of ownership of public lands in the added territory.
When my right hon. friend the Prime Minister had the resolution drawn no doubt he saw that the only thing which he could logically ask parliament to do was to make an allowance in lieu of public lands in the added territory.
But that would not suit the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers), because he was wanting a bigger haul out of the Dominion treasury than would be represented by anything commensurate for the loss of the lands in this added territory, and so I take it for granted that he succeeded in getting the resolution altered and that a day or two afterwards, when it appeared again upon the order paper, it

3863
was to authorize the Governor General to pay this amount in lieu of ownership of public lands.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that that is not a correct statement of the case. The change was due to the mistake made by the law' clerk in regard to the matter. The Bill as it now stands is precisely as it was in the beginning.

I am very glad to accept the statement of my hon. friend, but certainly the law clerk has a good deal of ability, and his legal instinct would show him that the right thing to do was to put it in because he would hardly assume it to be possible that my hon. friend would be making an addition of this territory away to the north which will not have very much settlement for a hundred years to come the ground for such a large allowance. Some parts of it will be settled, like the Pas and around the mouths, of the Saskatchewan, Nelson and Churchill rivers, but, speaking generally, it will not be of enormous value to the Dominion or to the province for many years to come. The law clerk would see that it was proposed to do something by reason of adding this territory, and that the words ' in lieu of ownership of public lands ' should be in. But, there is no doubt that the scheme of the government is to make the addition of this new territory an excuse tor altering the whole terms of confederation in so far as Manitoba is concerned, for picking out Manitoba as a favourite child in this family of provinces, and for giving it exceptional treatment, and giving it in such a way that I am sure, if we were dealing -with Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, New' Brunswick, or Prince Edward Island, my hon. friend would be terribly shocked if such a proposal were made. I desire to take the position that these lands do not belong to Manitoba. Those of us who come from the smaller provinces to which no territory can be added, in order to do justice to the people we represent, have to take the ground in the strongest manner possible that neither Manitoba, Ontario, nor Quebec, is entitled to one acre of these lands which are outside the bounds of these respective provinces. These lands formed a part of the Hudson bay territory, they were bought by the original four provinces of Canada, and they paid their hard money for them. While it may be natural and right that they should be added to these provinces, yet if they are to be so added the addition ought to take place upon terms upon which the other provinces have been consulted, and with which they are satisfied. The Act of 1871, I think, provides that the boundaries of a province may be extended. But it expressly Mr. PUGSLEY
provides that in case the rights of any other provinces in the confederation are in any way affected by that extension these provinces shall be consulted, and the government or the legislature-I forget which-of the provinces concerned shall be assenting parties.	_
It is proposed to enlarge the territory of Manitoba. It is proposed to give her $560,000 ai year in lieu of public land. On the order paper also we find a proposition to enlarge the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and to give to them vast tracts of territory which, I say, belong to the whole people of Canada, the people of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island, as well as to the people of other sections of Canada. In regard to the question of representation, I would like to invite the attention of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, to the point as to how this addition to the territory of the province of Manitoba-and of course the same question would come up- when we come to deal with Ontario and Quebec, and more especially in reference to Quebec-will affect the representation of the other provinces. When_ we coine to Quebec the contention, I think, can very properly be raised-and I submit it with all seriousness to my right hon. friend-that the added territory shall form no part of the province of Quebec, so far as the unit of representation is concerned. Quebec, under the British North America Act, is entitled to 65 representatives. I think it is impossible to successfully meet the contention that that means Quebec as it existed at the time of confederation. I observe in the resolution upon the order paper that there is no saving clause in regard to that. If I remember rightly, in the resolution which was passed in 1908, there was a saving clause. My Tight hon. friend the leader of the opposition, then Prime Minister, suggested, or consented to, an amendment by which it was provided that the added territory should not count in the estimate of 65 representatives for the province of Quebec, but that the additional territory should have representation, just the same as if it were another province.
That condition was accepted by the province.
Yes, that condition was accepted by the province.

Does my hon. friend give it as his opinion, that it is within the power of this House to pass legislation limiting the representation of Quebec, as far as added territory is concerned, or would it not require an Act of the Imperial parliament?

I would think not, because I think Quebec means Quebec as it existed at the time of confederation. But, at all events, my own view is, that if the

terms of confederation are to be Te-adiust-ed with respect to Manitoba, there ought to be Imperial legislation and the boundaries should be fixed. But, that is a matter for the legal advisers of the government. What I submit is, that as Quebec is to be the pivot upon which the representation of the different provinces turns, it should be Quebec as it existed at the time that confederation was formed. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, when he was leader of the government, recognized that principle and introduced a saving clause into the resolution. I would like to direct the attention of my right hon. friend the leader of the government to the fact that the boundaries of Quebec have already been enlarged. They were enlarged in 1898. I know the argument has been raised that the statute simply fixed the boundaries. I do not think so. I think that by that statute, there was something like 200,000 square miles added to the territory of Quebec. At the time of confederation, everybody recognized that Quebec extended to the height of land. We know that in the olden days, when the province of Quebec was .owned by the French and Prince Rupert'Land was owned by the English, Prince RupeTt Land was understood to cover all the territory which was drained by the rivers that flowed towards Hudson bay. and in the old geographies, the height of land was shown as the northern boundary of Quebec. This is very important, because all that section of country through which the Transcontinental railway runs from a' point,-I do not know what distance from Quebec, but extending north of Lake Abi-tibi, is included in the territory which was formerly Prince Rupert Land, because, as hon. gentlemen know, the river Abitibi as well as all the other rivers in that territory drain through to Hudson bav.
I would suggest to my right hon. friend that when he comes to consider the question it cannot do much harm to extend the proposition of the right hon. the leader of the opposition a little bit further and as regards the basis for representation leave Quebec as it was at the time of confederation. So far as Manitoba is concerned, and also so far as Ontario is concerned, the subject of representation is also important. As my right hon. friend knows, there is in the British North America Act, section 51, what is known as the saving clause, so far as the other provinces apart from Quebec are concerned. That provides that although relatively to Quebec a province might lose its representation as a result of the census, yet such province shall not lose unless it has fallen a certain percentage behind all of the provinces of Canada. In the case of New Brunswick, after the last distribution, if the computation were confined to the original provinces of .Canada, New Brunswick would not have lost in her representation, but it was because of the new provinces being considered that the effect of this saving clause was done away with and our province lost in representation. In the representation case which came before the Supreme Court of Canada and afterwards went to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and in which I had the honour of being concerned, I took the ground-as the court held that the population of the new provinces should come in against us in considering the effect of that saving clause-that the population of the territories should not count. The point was left undecided. There is no principle upon which the population of the territories should count; it could not be brought in under the terms of section 51 of the British North America Act in any way. You will have this result, that in all these additions to Quebec and Ontario and Manitoba you are bringing in a portion of the territories; you are making them a part of the province, and their population, which, if they had remained territories would not have counted against the older provinces in respect to representation, will count from the day you make them part of a province. Therefore,
I do submit that the provinces ought to be consulted. I do submit that before you strike a blow at the provision of the British North America Act which was intended to save these smaller provinces from the loss of representation, you ought to expressly provide that the population of these added territories shall not at all interfere with the operation of that saving clause or affect the rights of the other provinces so far as representation is concerned. 1 have felt it my duty to mention these matters, which hon. gentlemen may think more especially pertain to the province I have the honour to represent, and I do so-because I believe it is important. I remember very well when the matter was discussed in the New Brunswick Legislature some years ago, when I was Attorney General of that province, that the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries expressed himself as veTy strongly of the opinion that in any redistribution these questions ought all to be taken into consideration. I am relying with the utmost confidence upon his being a strong advocate of the course which I contend ought to be adopted now. I have not dealt very much with the subject of the public lands in the territories because that question will come up more appropriately when we come to deal with the resolution as affecting the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. But, these questions are germane to the subject because it is proposed to give Manitoba this very large allowance in lieu of public

lands to which, the province of Manitoba is not entitled. I am fortified in that view by the statement of Sir James Whitney, Premier of Ontario, made in the legislature a few days ago, when he said that neither Manitoba nor Ontario was entitled to these lands and that they are lands which belong to the Dominion. That is the view I take and that is a view that cannot be too strongly urged. No province ought to be allowed to receive a subsidy upon the theory that it is any more entitled to the public lands of the Dominion than any other province. Whatever else it is deemed desirable to give to Manitoba in order to enable her to carry on government by reason of the added territories and discharge her duties in respect to the people who are there now, or may be there in the future, well and good; and I would not only be just but generous to the province in that respect. But, I do not want to express my approval of taking up the case of any one province and making it a separate case and attempting to take it out of the well settled principles which govern the status of all the provinces under the British North America Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I wish to say a word with reference to the last paragraph of the resolution, which reads:
(d) To authorize the Governor in Council to pay to said province, one-half on July 1, 1912, and one-half on July 1, 1913, the sum' of $201,723.57 towards the construction of public buildings.
The explanation of that is that the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan respectively received under the Alberta and Saskatchewan Act, to provide for the construction of public buildings, the sum of $468,750, the payment of which was spread over five years. The province of Manitoba has heretofore received from the Dominion on account of the construction of the legislative buildings and government house at Winnipeg $267,026 and the sum of $201,723.57 referred to in the resolution is the difference between the two amounts I have mentioned. I have listened with very much interest to my hon. friend and to his expression of opinion that the other provinces will be dissatisfied with what he calls the exceptional treatment of Manitoba. In my judgment, if there has been any exceptional treatment of Manitoba, it has been by the late government and not by this government, and in that connection I would call the attention of the House to the differences between the status of the several provinces of the confederation with regard especially to the ownership of their natural resources. All the provinces of Canada, with the exception Mr. PTJGSLEY.
of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, were made sovereign provinces and the lands belonging to the Crown were vested in these provinces. The result is that they have had the advantage of their lands, their minerals, and the royalties consequent thereon. That is not the case with the three prairie provinces. They have no land, they are not sovereign states in that sense as the other provinces are, and the result is that prima facie they should be entitled to the same treatment. Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba not being sovereign provinces, not being entitled to their lands, minerals and royalties, should prima facie, other things being equal, and having regard to their status in the west, be entitled to precisely the same treatment. That is what we are trying to accord to them. My hon. friend said that no province is entitled to an acre of land without the consent of all the other provinces.
To an acre of Dominion land.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And he was speaking of the extension of the boundaries at the time and I am not sure whether he meant the transfer of lands to the provinces or the extension of t.heir boundaries. I understood him to mean that the extension of boundaries could not take place without-*
Mr. PTTOSL^Y. What I said was that the Dominion lands belonged to the whole Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Which Dominion lands?

Wherever they are in the territory. The lands north of British Columbia belong to the Dominion, the lands north of Ontario belong to the Dominion, and the lands north of Quebec belong to the Dominion and the lands in the prairie west all belong to the Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend to object to the transfer to Quebec of the added territory which is proposed, or was he referring to Manitoba?
Yes, and Ontario too without treating the other provinces fairly and justly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are now dealing with the resolutions regarding the province of Manitoba. As far as the other provinces are concerned, I have no doubt that when they understand the situation they will be satisfied that it is only fair and just to Manitoba that this Bill should be enacted, in order that it may be placed on an equality with these other provinces, because Manitoba, like them, was deprived of its lands, minerals and royalties. Let me point out also that Manitoba under ex-

isting legislation, is entitled to xeeeive about 8,000,000 acres more of swamp lands from time to time as they would be selected. It is getting an increase of about $500,000 a year by way of subsidies, and a total cash payment in respect of arrearages of about $2,000,000.
From the standpoint of the Dominion, would it not be better for Manitoba to keep her swamp lands and sell them, because the Dominion gives away its lands free? .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Manitoba has applied for an extension of her boundaries and for better financial terms. Presumably Manitoba knows her own business. A portion of these swamp lands will not come in for many years. But looking at the question at large and from the Dominion standpoint, having regard to the future as web as the present, the swamp lands represent in value a very large sum of money, which will be a set-off as far as the other provinces are concerned to the increased amount of money that Manitoba is now getting.

Is it the intention of the government of which the hon. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The right hon. leader of the government, I have no doubt will be able to answer my hon. friend; but that question does not arise in connection with the present situation. This matter has been a long-standing sore to Manitoba. She has asked for an extension of her boundaries and a revision of her financial terms, and when we are proposing to meet her in these respects, hon. gentlemen opposite are seeking to confuse the issue by asking such questions as that of my hon. friend. From my knowledge of the right hon. leader of the government I have no doubt he will be prepared in time to carry out explicitly whatever he promised. This question with regard to Manitoba should not be regarded from a narrow point of view. As the hon. member for St. John has said, Manitoba has been virtually a postage stamp on the map. A man has only to look at the map to see that great injustice has been done to Manitoba for years. Manitoba's claim has been soundly based, and everybody now, as in 1908, is in favour of enlarging her boundaries. The west is not entitled to exceptional treatment, but it is entitled to just and generous treatment. I am the first to rejoice that Saskatchewan and Alberta were dealt with so liberally as they were. I like to
see those new children in the confederation treated properly. I have no exception whatever to take to the subsidies that were granted to Alberta and Saskatchewan. But we must go farther and put the pioneer province of the west in the same position ais those favoured children in the confederation. And public opinion in eastern Canada will sustain that position, because it is the application of simple justice to Manitoba. The commercial hope of Canada to-day lies in the great west. There is room there for millions and tens of millions of people, and Manitoba is the pathfinder, the province that blazed the trail and suffered the privations of the pioneer in the early days of the west. We should not approach this question in the spirit of lawyers looking for technical points in sta. utes, but we should approach it in a broad statesmanlike way, with a desire to redress the injustice which Manitoba has suffered, and to put her in the same position as Saskatchewan land Alberta. It would be unfair in the extreme to put the province which has borne the burden and heat of the day in a subordinate position as to her 'territory or financial subsidies. Not only will the other provinces (not be dissatisfied, but they will abundantly approve of the course which this government is taking in redressing the injustice under which Manitoba has laboured, and in putting the pathfinder of the west in as good a position as the two sister provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan.

I want to follow the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance on the point that he made that there should be equality of treatment between the different provinces in regard to subsidies and territory.
I want to point out to him and to the 'Committee that equality of 'treatment does not involve merely an intimate know-

ledge of the multiplication table, or the other rules of arithmetic, but that equality of treatment necessarily involves due consideration of the physical and other conditions surrounding and connected with, the provinces with which it is proposed to deal. For instance, because the province of Ontario has a certain area and receives a certain consideration from the Dominion treasury, it does not by any means follow that part of the territory of Canada, lying ibeneath the Arctic circle and of the same area would fee entitled to receive the same .consideration, if 'erected into a province. That is an extreme illustration, but I want to make a statement of the position, as between Manitoba and Saskatchewan, to which no person can take exception. A provincial government is charged with certain duties of administration in behalf of the people under its jurisdiction, and the cost of that administration depends somewhat upon the area ever which the people are spread, and as well upon their occupations and the means of communication. Now as between the province of Saskatchewan and the proposed province of Manitoba, each province will have an approximate area of 250,000 square miles. Of that area in the province of Saskatchewan it is fair to assume that not less than 200,000 square miles will be occupied by agricultural settlement. I think it is fair to assume that of the 250,000 square miles of the proposed province of Manitoba, that part which will be effectively occupied by agricultural settlement, will not be more than 50,000 square miles. That is to say, the area over which the respective provincial governments will be required to administer justice and deal generally with the subjects which comes within the range of a provincial government, will in the case of Saskatchewan, be over an area of 200,000 square miles, and in the case of Manitoba, over an area of 50,000 square miles. So that if there is to bo equality of treatment in regard to the conditions as they exist, on the face of it, the province of Saskatchewan is unquestionably entitled-if the justice for which my hon. friend (Mr. White, Leeds) clamoured so loudly, is to be done-to receive a larger grant from the Federal treasury than the province of Manitoba. I do not want to be understood as objecting in any degree to liberality being extended by the government to the province of Manitoba. If it were possible to be generous to Manitoba without being unjust to the rest of the Dominion, then there would be no objection whatever to any amount that might be given to Manitoba. I am not even suggesting that the generosity shown in this case is an injustice to the other provinces, but I am bound to place before the committee the fact that what is an adequate and proper payment from the Dominion Mr. OLIVER.
treasury to the province of Manitoba for the services of provincial government in that province, is by all right and reason, not an adequate payment to the adjoining province of Saskatchewan for the same purpose. And the same argument holds good in regard to the province of Alberta, but to an even greater degree, because that province is recognized as being of agricultural capability from north to south and from east to west. So that there is in that case, an area of presumably 250,000 square miles over which agricultural settlement may be spread, and wdiich will require the administration of the provincial government which will have to incur corresponding expenses because of that. Therefore, if this question is to be decided as a matter of strict justice, and only as a matter of justice, I submit to the committee that that is not the basis upon which it is being decided now.
There are two features of provincial subsidies which are being dealt with in this arrangement: One is the feature in regard to the debt, and the other is the feature in regard to lands. The feature in regard to debt is dealt with by simply doubling the present debt allowance of Manitoba, or placing it on an equality with the province of Saskatchewan. I take a somewhat different ground, possibly, from my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), and I offer no criticism against that increased debt account. I offer no criticism of the increase of debt account, because of equality of population between Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Be it remembered that the debt account is adjusted by population and not by territory, and that the addi-i tion of the new territory to the province of Manitoba has nothing whatever to do, either nearly or remotely, with the question of debt account. If Manitoba is entitled to an increased allowance of debt account it is entitled to that because of its population, and not because of its territory. But if I say that I am not exactly in accord with the remarks of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), I want to follow it with a statement that will be absolutely in accord with what he savs. It cannot be held to be reasonable that there should be a readjustment of debt account in regard to any province without the consent of the otheT provinces. So when this government undertakes to readjust the debt account of the province of Manitoba, admitting that it is in itself a fair adjustment, it is taking upon itself the responsibility of disturbing the fundamental elements of confederation, and giving good and sufficient reason for some, at any rate, of the other provinces to come forward and demand a similar readjustment of debt account ; and if the plea as to justice is to obtain, as my

hon. friend the Minister of Finance insists that it is, then the other provinces have just as good a right to claim justice
as Manitoba has. That is a matter that I think the committee should consider very gravely; that it is not for any government to gratuitously disturb the basis of confederation and introduce an element of discord 'when that condition could toe avoided.
This should certainly never be done under the conditions that exist at the present time, where a government deliberately comes forward and, under a plea of doing (justice to one province takes it upon itself to readjust the debt account of that province-at once holding out to the other provinces the promise, or at least making the suggestion, that if they will only bring sufficient pressure to bear, their debt accounts may be readjusted as well; placing a premium-absolutely placing a premium-upon agitation against the fundamental basis of confederation. I think that a government which takes that attitude has something to answer for to the people of this country, altogether of more importance than the doing of what may be called justice in this particular to one province. The government has a duty to perform and a responsibility to bear, to the whole Dominion of Canada which weighs as heavily upon it as its duty and responsibility to the province of Manitoba. There is a proper way to secure a readjustment of the debt account of the province of Manitoba, but I submit that this government has not taken that proper way.

I hardly think I would be discharging my duty to my constituents, and to those who have placed this Bill in my charge if I allowed the hon. member's motion to go without challenging the correctness of his statement. In order that the House may adequately understand the relation of this institution to the national life, it is necessary that I .should go into its history, take the House into my confidence and explain to them what legislation nas been passed in this House affecting the university that now presents this Bill for consideration. In 1849 Queen's University was incorporated, not by an Act of the parliament of Upper Canada, but by virtue of Her Majesty's prerogative. From 1841 until 1874, the original charter granted toy Her Majesty continued unchanged and under it the university was governed. In]

1874, after the union of the Free Church of Scotland and the old Kirk in Canada, it was necessary to make application for fresh powers and at that time the legislature of the province of Ontario passed an Act in regard to the matter, which was then thought to be constitutional. However,	a case commonly called the
Temporalities Fund Case, was taken to the Privy Council, and that body laid down the principle that in the case of any corporation or institution enjoying privileges that affected the citizens of the two provinces, it would be ultra vires of either , province to legislate away the rights of citizens of the other province. Believing that decision to be good law, the trustees of the university in 1882, made application to this parliament for a confirming statute and this parliament passed such an Act. Again in 1889, when fresh powers were required, application was made to this parliament and a most vigorous debate took place in this House, participated in by men like Sir John Thompson, Hon. David Mills, Sir John A. Macdonald, Mr. Weldon, of St. John and other eminent constitutional lawyers, after which by a vote of 104 to 35 this House decided that it had authority to deal with this question, because the rights of citizens of Ontario and Quebec were at issue. Again in 1906 the trustees came to this House for legislation when this House took the responsibility of passing legislation affecting Queen's University.
