I have not forgotten the other incident referred to, when the opinion of Sir John Thompson was given that this parliament had jurisdiction. The matter presents itself in this way. The university was in need of legislation, and it had to decide whether it would go for it to Toronto or to Ottawa, and I presume that, following the prece 1-ents of 1882 and 1889, it decided to come to Ottawa. In my judgment this parliament has certainly jurisdiction, because we have these two precedents. Under such circumstances I would be loth for my part to vote to kill the Bill for want of jurisdiction. I understand that the motion made by my hon. friend from the St. Lawrence division is that the committee rise. If this motion were carried, the Bill would be killed. I would be averse, for my part, to take such a course, and I think the House should be chary about doing so. I think my hon. friend from the St. Lawrence division will agree that it would be hardly fair to the university to kill the Bill. My hon. friend may be entitled to information, and I am sure that the hon. member for Kingston would not object to giving it. For these reasons I could not vote for the Mr. WILSON (Laval).
motion that the committee rise; but in the meantime parliament will not be prorogued for some time yet, and it should be possible to furnish the information asked for by my hon. friend from the St. Lawrence division.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What has been pointed out by my right hon. friend had already been pointed out by the hon. member for Kingston. It seems perfectly clear that parliament has dealt with^ Queen's University on two previous occasions, and no less eminent a jurist than Sir John Thompson expressed the opinion that this parliament had jurisdiction over the subject matter of this Bill. The hon. member has pointed out that this legislation is of supreme importance to this university and to its adherents and supporters, who are a large and influential body of people, and it seems to me that we should proceed with the Bill and the question_ raised as to section 20 or any other section may he discussed afterwards in the committee or in the House. There is no question involved in this Bill that cannot be discussed apart from the question of jurisdiction. This parliament would stultify itself if it decided that it had not jurisdiction in this matter. I entirely concur in the view of the right hon. the leader of the opposition.

I do not wish to kill the Bill, but I have endeavoured on three occasions to -get the opinion of the Justice Department on this question. My hon. friend from Kingston states that the Private Bills Committee has had that opinion. I am not a member of that committee, and I think we are entitled to have that opinion laid on the table of this House. There are some clauses in the Bill that we have pleaded with the promoters to leave out, because they are insulting to a large number of people. As long as clause 20 remains in the Bill, I will take every chance to defeat it. I stated to the promotor of the Bill that if that clause were struck out, I would not raise the question of jurisdiction.

The hon. member for the St. Lawrence division evidently feels strongly on this matter, and I understand he is speaking from information given to him by people who are supposed to have some authority. Personally, I do not think there is anything in the objection as to the jurisdiction of this parliament, and that opinion is fortified by the fact that on two previous occasions parliament has exercised jurisdiction by dealing with Queen's College. But the law officer of the Crown is the Minister of Justice, and I must say that he does not honour us with his presence in parliament or in parliamentary committees as frequently as -he ought. When hon. members raise a

serious question, I think the committee is entitled to know what the Minister of Justice thinks of it, just as a few years ago when a question was raised on a similar Bill, Sir John Thompson as Minister of Justice gave his opinion and settled the question. While not agreeing with my hon. friend from St. Lawrence in the objection he has raised, I think the promoters of the Bill would be well advised if they allowed it to remain in committee until the Minister of Justice stated to the House the opinion which he is said to have given.
Lost.

Hon. members know that it is near nine o'clock. I say that the Minister of Justice should be in his seat to give his opinion on a serious question raised in this committee, and that question will not be settled by the hon. gentlemen saying ' lost.' Hon. members who do not belong to the Private Bills Committee, and who had not an opportunity to hear the discussion theTe, cannot form an intelligent opinion on the legal question from the short discussion we have had to-night.
All I wish, with the desire of assisting the Bill-not believing in the point raised by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike), because there is no political question involved in this matter, not the *slightest in any degree-is this: that my friend from St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) having raised .a question upon which the opinion, of the Minister of Justice ought to be given; that he is not unreasonable, 'and that he is not stating a position which is untenable, when he suggests to the committee that we should have an opinion from the Minister of Justice before a conclusion is reached upon the matter. Can any reason be seriously urged in opposition to that course ? Hon. gentlemen want to rush the Bill through without giving those who apparently have some ideas upon the subject, time or opportunity to present those views, without giving them an opportunity of having the legal question determined which they are instructed and advised is a very serious and important one. That is the whole issue and that is the question. Therefore, I would ask my hon. friend, from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) to recognize that it is impossible for the Bill to go through at this sitting of the House and to accede to. the request of my hon. friend, Mr. Bickerdike.
I want to make my position very clear on the question, and I desire to state that I do not want to kill the Bill.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen may protest; they seem to be in a great
burry. If the ministers had been in their seats at eight o'clock, instead of 8.15, we would have been able to proceed very well with the business before the House. I remember in the old days when we on this side occupied the seats 'to the right of the Speaker, and) those gentlemen who now sit there were sitting on this side, that a certain hon. gentleman who was a plain member of parliament and not a minister, took very good care when the member for Laval was absent from his seat, to express deep sorrow that that hon. gentleman was not in the House when a public question of interest to his riding was being considered. I shall not mention the hon. gentleman's name.
He is not in his seat now.

No, he is not in his seat now. I do not know whether that hon. gentleman wishes to refrain from giving his opinion on this Bill. At any rate the position I am taking now is the position that every member of the House, in my opinion, should take. I want to know whether the hon. member for Kingston is sure of his ground, or whether he is afraid to knock again .at the door of the Minister of Justice in order to have his opinion confirmed and submitted to the House ? I think, Mr. Chairman, my demand is a reasonable and just one and should have been accepted by my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle).

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hour for Private Bills having expired, the House will go into Committee of the Whole on the resolution in regard to the Manitoba boundaries.
House again in committee on resolution respecting the boundaries of Manitoba.

When the House rose at six o'clock I was discussing that part of the resolution which deals with the question of debt account. I want to point out to the committee, that the question of the readjustment of the subsidies to the provinces was dealt with in the conference that was held, I believe in 1906, and the conclusion of which conference was afterwards embodied in an amendment to the British North America Act. At that conference a change was made in the basis of two features of the subsidy allowance, namely, in regard to civil government, and in regard to payment per head of the population. It was arranged at that conference, and afterwards sanctioned by the Imperial authorities, that hereafter the allowance for civil government, and the allowance on account of population would increase

from time to time with the increase of population. There was no such readjustment in regard to debt account. But in my humble judgment, Mr. Chairman-and I am speaking now on behalf of the western provinces-such a readjustment would have been right and proper at that time, and not having take place at that time would 'be right and proper and would be in order to toe taken into account at some future conference. The idea of the subsidy is for the purpose of enabling the provincial governments to discharge the responsibilities which iconifederation lays upon them, and it is an evident fact that these responsibilities, speaking generally, have increased with increase of population, so that, however the original basis of subsidy was arrived at, or for whatever reason a *certain sum was fixed upon, if the population has .increased largely then that fixed sum becomes inadequate and should, outside of the question of law, as a matter of-equity, be subject to readjustment. What has occurred in the case of Manitoba is liable to recur in the case of that province, and still snore liable to occur in the case of the three provinces farther west: That is, that their debt accounts being adjusted on the basis of present population, the population of those provinces is liable to increase so very rapidly that the provision towards their total subsides on debt account is certain to be .inadequate. It is I presume, that reasoning which leads the government - to make provision for an increase of Manitoba's subsidy on debt account by doubling the calculation, that is to say increasing the population basis from 135,000 to 250,000, the basis of population adopted in the case of Alberta and Saskatchewan. But the arbitrary adoption df the same basis of population as was adopted in the case of Albeita and Saskatchewan does not by any means settle the question, does not by any means bring it to finality. Once the government undertakes to depart from the original fixed basis without consultation with the other provinces there i.s no finality. And in my judgment there should not be a finality so long >as the population is increasing, but there .should not toe action by the government dealing with the case of a single province, unless there is an arrangement and understanding with all the other provinces, so that every province shall feel that when a 'certain province has received an increase of subsidy the other provinces have been fairly dealt with at the same time. With our vast area of agricultural land in Alberta and Saskatchewan, with the increases of population that have taken place since these provinces were organized, it is clear to-iday that the subsidy allowance on debt account is not adequate, and is not fair to those provinces of Canada.

Now, to repeat. The population of Alberta, Saskatoliewam and Manitoba is a larger precentage greater than the basis of the debt account, than is the population of any of the eastern provinces. Therefore, if I were making an argument on the grounds of pure justice, I would claim at onbe that the debt allowance of these provinces should be increased in order to put them on an equal footing with the eastern provinces so far as population is concerned. But I have taken the ground that the government should not interfere with the basis of calculation of subsidy on its own initiative and should only interfere with it with the consent of all the provinces.
To emphasize the point, let me illustrate: Take the case of the province of British Columbia. That province to-day receives a smaller allowance on debt account in proportion to its present population than any other province in the Dominion. If there were any ground for increasing the payments on debt account to the province of Manitoba, that reason is just as strong or stronger in the case of the province of British Columbia; and by making the increase that has been made in the case of the province of Manitoba, I take it, the government is thereby compelled to make a similar increase to the province of British Columbia,-or, if they do not, the .province of British Columbia will rest under a sense of injustice at the hands of this government.
I have gone into this in detail for the purpose of demonstrating that this portion of the subsidy grant in regard to debt allowance should not have been interfered with by this government except as part of a general scheme in which the rights of the provinces should have been considered and, as far as possible the consent of the provinces obtained. Again I say that I deal with this question at such length because I am .quite aware that the late government will be subjected to adverse criticism because of the cash payments proposed to be made by that government in connection with the proposed extension of the boundaries of Manitoba as compared with the cash payments proposed to be made by this government; and I point out that in my judgment the late gevernment had good and sufficient reason, and was well advised, in not undertaking of its own motion to increase the subsidy of the province of Manitoba on debt account as this government has seen fit to do: I do not speak of the matter with any idea of preventing the province of Manitoba from setting a larger payment on debt account, but in order that there may be -a square deal amongst all the provinces; so that there may not be raised a sense of irritation on the part of any of the provinces which, I as I have pointed out, is bound to occur

in the ease of British 'Columbia at any rate and which would .not have oocured had not the government taken the course it has taken in this connection.
Now, as to the item in the resolution in regard to subsidy in lieu of land: The resolution 'before the House sets out that there is to be paid each year $562,500 on account of land, less certain deductions; and I am informed in reply to a question that the actual cash payment less the deductions to be made is $413,270 a year. This is $313,270 more than the province is now receiving on land account and $113,270 more than the province would have received under the arrangement offered by the late government which involved practically a payment of $200,000 on land account. The deductions that have been made from the nominal sum placed in the resolution, we have been informed by the Finance Minister, are deductions on account of swamp and university lands handed over to the province by the Dominion and disposed of, either in whole or in part, by the province and charged up to the province. On that point, I think my hon. friend is hardly dealing fairly with the Dominion in the calculation that has been made so far as the university lands are concerned. It is true I have not had very much time to consider the figures, but if this land transaction is to be a purely business transaction, and if the province is to account to the Dominion for that which it has received and the amount thus accounted for is to be deducted from the cash to be paid, then it is fair and reasonable that we should consider whether the calculation has been rightly made or not. The province is charged with $15,000 a year, presumably interest on the value of the university lands, none of which are to be returned to the Dominion. The quantity of university lands is 150,000 acres. These were selected lands, selected as being farming lands. Being within the province of Manitoba and being selected, they must have a very fair market value; and as they are acquired by the province for the purpose simply and solely of securing a revenue from them for university purposes, of course the province is entitled to dispose of them so as to get out of them the last cent of value that is in them. Now, I think it would not be an unreasonable valuation to put on these lands to say that they were worth $10 an acre. In fact, it is in my mind-having had some occasion to go into this matter in the past-that an actual accounting giving all the sales of these lands would indicate that the price at which they had actually been sold was in the neighbourhood of $10 an acre.
One hundred and fifty thousand acres of land at $10 an acre would mean $1,500,000, and if interest is computed on that at 5 per cent, it would make an interest value of $75,000 a year which has accrued to the province of Manitoba in respect of the university lands on the calculation which I think it is fair to make, while the Dominion is only credited and the province is only charged with $15,000 a year. Of course, the expense of handling, selling and selecting these lands is properly chargeable to the amount received from them, but I do not think that even under the able administration of my success _r in office, who may be supposed to have had something to do with the management of these lands, it can be presumed that the expenses of sale would make the difference between the $15,000 and the $75,000 per year. It is only fair that the minister should at a later date give us the grounds upon which he arrived at the calculations by which he charges the province and credits the Dominion with $15,000 in respect of 150,000 acres of selected lands in the province of Manitoba, the interest upon which is, according to his own figures, computed at 5 per cent.
In regard to the swamp lands, 836,430 acres realized $3,137,389. It will be observed that the swamp lands have not brought the returns per acre that I have placed as a valuation upon the university lands, but the swamp lands are not selected lands; they are taken because they are swamp lands, and they must be sold as swamp lands, but I submit that if the swamp lands are sold as they have been to the extent of over three quarters of a million acres at $3 an acre, they not being selected lands, surely the university lands, which were selected, were worth a great deal more. I am not objecting to the calculation in regard to the swamp lands, as far as I can see it appears to be a fair calculation of value.
I observe, however, that the Dominion is charged with the cost of sale amounting to something like a quarter of a million dollars. I have not the figures absolutely correctly, but it is over $200,000 a year and something less than $250,000, so that undoubtedly the Dominion is being charged up with every expense that can reasonably be charged against it. Thus, as far as the swamp land is concerned, it must be presumed that it is a business transaction as set down here and that the Dominion has got no advantage in it.
On land account, as I have said, the province is to get, over and above what it now receives, $313,000, and over and above what it would have received under the offer of the late government $113,000. The figures I have been dealing with have been the figures which were used by the
Why did not the hon. gentleman work along this line at the creation of Saskatchewan and Alberta?

I do not know what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Staples) is worrying about. Conditions in Alberta and Saskatchewan are not the same as they are in Manitoba. In a large part of Alberta and Saskatchewan the trouble is to get water on the land, whereas, in a large part of Manitoba, the trouble is to get water off the land. That is the difference between the two conditions. Just as irrigation is an important question in parts of Alberta and Saskatchewan, drainage is an important question in a large part and a very v_aluable part of Manitoba.
I think the government of Manitoba, if I am permitted to criticise it, as well as this government, in this transaction whereby swamp lands are returned to the Dominion in consideration of a money payment, has made a mistake because this is not good business either for the province or for the Dominion, it does not tend to the development of the province and it does not tend to the progress of the Dominion.
As to the amount of money that is provided for in the last part of the resolution, a sum of $201,723 to be paid to the province in two annual payments, that is a small amount and it is not perhaps necessary to delay the committee in discussing it. So far as this resolution goes with regard to the increase of subsidy to the province of Manitoba, either on deist account or land account, I have no objection to it. I think the government are ill-advised in dealing with the debt account as they do. I think it would have been very much wiser, if it were desirable to increase the allowance to Manitoba, that the whole sum should have been put on land account and that the question of debt 'account should not have been raised. But, the government has seen fit to take the responsibility and, of course, it will have to take the' consequences of what it has done. I am prepared to support the resolution so far as the debt account is 123J
concerned as a western man believing that the debt account of all the provinces should be subject to a readjustment with the increase of population just the same as the per head allowance and just the same as the allowance for civil government. If Manitoba is satisfied with the arrangement in regard to land account I have no reason to complain except in so far as the handing back of the swanp lands to this government will be a detriment to the development of the province, as I see it.
But, there is one feature of this resolution, as it is brought out in the speech of my hon. friend and as I find it in answer to the question which I placed on the order paper, that I must take very strong exception to. I refer to the arrearages which are paid there. I find that an arbitrary sum under the heading of arrearages, amounting to $2,179,000 is to be paid to the province of Manitoba aside from and over and above the increase of subsidy on debt account, the increase of subsidy on land account and the special allowance made in regard to 'buildings. It is not because1 the sum is very large, it is not that anybody would wish that Manitoba should not 'have that beyond the grant which it gets now, if it had a right to it, but the principle of this payment is, it seems to me, absolutely objectionable.
Mv hon. friend has said that the province of Manitoba has claimed the payment of these so-called arrearages from the date of the organization of the two new provinces, but the government compromised with the provinces by giving payment for one-half that period. Well, if the province of Manitoba is entitled to arrears for a period of three years, or, as they claim, for a period of six or seven years, why were not the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan entitled to arrearages upon their being organized into provinces, because of the subsidy payments that the adjoining province of Manitoba had received during the previous thirty years, as against the amount that had been paid in regard to these provinces. If the principle of arrears is good in one case, it is just as good in the other. But the fact is that there is no ground for it in either case. This proposition to pay a bulk sum of two million dollars to the province of Manitoba is not a proposition that can be justified on any ground of fair-play to any other province in the Dominion, nor can it be justified on any argument of the right of Manitoba to that payment. If I appreciate the meaning of the payment, it is, on the one hand to compensate the province for the loss of its swamp lands, to make the people of the province feel that because they are getting a great big bulk sum in cash, therefore they are getting a great deal the best of this bargain.

And particularly, that they are getting a much better bargain out of the present Conservative government than they were offered by the late Liberal government. Or, on the other hand, it is to stand in the place of the granting of the demand that was made by the opposition in the Manitoba legislature, and that has been made by a large number of the people of the province. That demand, as I understand it, was absolutely conceded and promised by the Prime Minister no later than last summer, namely, that the natural resources of the province would be handed over to the province. This appears to be a proposal to pay two million dollars in a bulk sum without justification, without rhyme or reason, to the province of Manitoba, and I can only conclude it is done for a purpose. The only purpose I can see in it is to make the people believe they are getting value in the case of the swamp lands and to keep them from complaining because the leader of this government, who is the maker of this bargain, has not in the bargain implemented the promise he definitely made only last summer.

I would ask the Prime Minister for a little information. I would be glad to know if the government of the province of Ontario has been consulted in regard to -the proposed boundary line and has it assented to the line which is set out in the resolution in the amended form in which it was proposed this afternoon by the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When we dispose of this resolution which is concerned purely with the financial terms and come to the Bill, I will give to my hon. friend information with regard to that. I would like to say to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) and to other hon. gentlemen who have discussed this question at great length, that I do not want them to understand that I refrain from answering all the arguments they have addressed to the committee for any reason of discourtesy but because I realize these matters must be gone into probably at considerable length on the second reading of the Bill and when the Bill is in committee. It is purely with a desire of not repeating arguments and to save the time of the House that I refrain from going into all these matters now. I am very glad indeed that these gentlemen have put forward their views and they are certainly deserving of consideration and a reply, and they will be replied to in due course so far as we are able to. I would say one word in answer to my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) with regard to the restoration of their lands to the prairie provinces. I understand perfectly the promise I made in that regard and I Mr. OLIVER.
want to assure my hon. friend that that promise will be carried out. But I want to tell him this: that I do not think it could have been carried out at this_ session, nor could the necessary consideration have been given to it, nor the necessary inquiry made. This question of extending the boundaries of Manitoba has been before parliament for a very long time and therefore it seemed to the government, whether rightly or wrongly, that the best course now was to put the province of Manitoba as nearly as might be in the position of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan and then take up after due consideration, and upon proper inquiry, the question of restoring to all these three provinces their natural resources upon terms that would be just and reasonable. I would like to point out to my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) that one of his own colleagues on that side of the House has raised an important question this afternoon, and has expressed views with which perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) may not be inclined to concur; namely, that when this question does come to be considered, some regard will have to be given to the claims of some other provinces in Canada and especially the three maritime provinces whose boundaries have not been increased, whose boundaries cannot very well be increased on account of their natural situation. That is a matter that will have to be taken up in connection with the handing over of their natural resources to the three prairie provinces. 1 would like my hon. friends from the maritime provinces to understand that that is a matter which has not escaped the attention of the government. But, I want to say that I realize the importance of getting through with this session as soon as may be after the very considerably large dose of politics we have had for the last eighteen months, and in that view we realize that it would be utterly impossible to deal with all these matters if we are to prorogue at a date when most hon. gentlemen of this House would like to be rid of political affairs for an interval.
Would the government think of increasing the representation of the maritime provinces even if the number of sixty-five representatives was not increased in the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
For the time being I do not wish to be understood as dealing with the question of representation; I was dealing with the question of the financial terms. The point was very distinctly made by my hon. friend from St. John as to the necessity of some consideration being given to the other provinces in Canada, particularly the maritime provinces; because the provinces of Ontario and Quebec are getting an extension of their boundaries and are re-

ceiving the public lands within those boundaries, while the maritime provinces have no opportunity to extend their boundaries; and some consideration must be given to the feeling on their part, that when the public domain of the western provinces, a very valuable public domain, is being taken into consideration, they have a right to be consulted and to have some voice in regard to it. All of us, I am sure, will agree that they should not be permitted to labour under any sense of injustice in that regard. The proposal before the committee, so far as Manitoba is concerned, is to retain the public domain in the Dominion and to take back that portion already handed over to Manitoba in the shape of swamp lands. At the same time, in connection with the extension of the boundaries of Ontario and Quebec, the public lands within the extended boundaries will naturally follow under the terms of the proposed resolution, the lands already within the existing boundaries of Ontario and Quebec, as indeed was the case in 1898 when the bound>aries of the province of Quebec were extended by ian Act of this parliament. If the resolution is permitted to pass, I will endeavour to give to my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) on the first reading of the Bill the information to which he has just allliulded.

I do not want to continue the discussion, but it is rather important to those of uis who represent Ontario . constituencies to know whether the government of the province of Ontario has been consulted by this government in regard to 'the line which it is now proposed to lay down as the extended boundary line of Manitoba. The resolution upon the order paner was indefinite upon that point. As pointed out by the right hon. leader of the opposition, it did not show at what point the boundary line would strike Hudson bay; but in. its amended form it is to a point on the shore of Hudson bay at or near the 89th parallel of longitude. That is a reasonably definite point, and, in view of the fact that the discussion this afternoon and this evening has Deen almost entirely upon the financial aspects of the question, I think it would be well to have it pointed out as clearly as possible to those hon. members who represent constituencies in the province of Ontario, that the line proposed as the extended boundary line of Manitoba is an absoilutely arbitrary line, and reaches a point on the shores of Hudson bay below both of the ocean ports of Fort Churchill and Port Nelson. That is the point which I think we in Ontario are chiefly concerned about. It may be said that in July, 1908, this House unanimously adopted that line, and that I, as a member of the House, while I did not dissent, must have assented to
the proposal. Well', if I did, I have certainly had more light upon the subject in the meantime, and I most emphatically dissent from the proposal at the present time. Now, the shore of Hudson bay, upon which both of these harbours are to be found, is in territory which should really belong to the province of Ontario and not to the province of Manitoba, if you go upon geographical lines. If you draw a merely arbitrary line, as is proposed in this resolution, you may give those ports to Manitoba) But the natural boundary line of the extended province of Manitoba would be a straight line northward, following, not the 89th parallel, but the 95th parallel of longitude up to the 60th parallel of latitude. If that were done, the province of Ontario would get the ocean ports on Hudson bay. I think that we from the province of Ontario should bear this in mind in this discussion. I have always understood that the government of the province of Ontario had contended, and would continue to contend, for those ports, or one of them at least, but I see no reason why both of them should not be in Ontario, and, with a representation of 86 members in this House, I should think that we ought to be able to hold for the province of Ontario one or both of these ocean ports.
Besolution as amended reported, and amendments agreed to.
Mr. BOEDEN moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 115) to provide for the Extension of the Boundaries of Manitoba. He said: I will proceed to give my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) the information he asked for a moment ago, as to whether or not the province of Ontario had been consulted with respect to the line which will constitute the eastern boundary line of the province of Manitoba and the western boundary line of the province of Ontario. I would say, in the first place, that before this administration assumed office, I understand that the province of Ontario was consulted, and I think the return already brought down to the House in connection with this 'matter will show that I am not mistaken in that regard.
I would also like to inform him that the province of Ontario has been consulted since the present administration took office; and so far as that is concerned every hon. gentleman in this House who has given any attention to this country knows that there was a difference in the views put forward by the province of Manitoba, and the views which were put forward by the province of Ontario in that connection, and particularly in regard to the question of ports on Hudson bay. Negotiations have gone on in regard

to that matter. The importance of a port on Hudson hay to the province of Ontario was this:	That province at the
present time owns and operates a railway known as the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway. It is anticipated that that railway will be extended still farther to the north, or to the north and west, and it is expected by the government of Ontario, as I understand it. that one day that railway may require an outlet on Hudson bay, and, therefore, a port. The boundaries of Manitoba, of Ontario, and of Quebec, we are presenting to the House to-day are those which were agreed upon unanimously by the House of Commons on the 13th July, 1908. Now, it is apparent that boundaries so agreed upon unanimously by both sides of the House, should not be departed from lightly by a succeeding administration, and so, after a good deal of negotiations and consideration of claims which had really been passed upon by the administration which the hon. gentleman supported-and I would like to observe that, as he himself has said, he is one of those that assented to the boundaries of Manitoba, of Ontario and of Quebec exactly as they are proposed by this Bill and the other Bills which are to be brought before the House later on-the question arose as to how Ontario might -be granted a port on Hudson bay, because it was desirable in the interest not only of Ontario but of the province of Manitoba and of the Dominion of Canada as a whole, that if Ontario desired to extend its railway to Hudson bay it should be given every opportunity of doing so. That is to the advantage not only of Ontario but likewise of Manitoba, and every hon. member in this House, whether representing Ontario, Manitoba, or any other province, will agree at once in the truth of what I have just stated. It is apparent to every hon. gentleman that the lands within the extended boundaries of Manitoba are to be retained by the federal government, so it was suggested, and eventually the suggestion was carried out, that a grant of certain lands, within the ownership and control of the government of Canada, might be made to the province of Ontario sufficient for the purpose of . extending the Ontario government railway to a port on Hudson bay if it should desire in future to adopt that policy. In that view the Governor in Council passed on the 20th of February an order in council, which I will lay upon the table of the House for the information of hon. members, couched in the following terms:
The Committee -of the Privy Council have had before them a report from the right hon. the Prime Minister submitting,- in connection with the proposed extensions of the limits Mr. BORDEN.
of the respective provinces of Ontario and Manitoba as defined by resolutions of the House of Commons passed on the July 13, 1908, -that -the government of Ontario represents that upon the enlargement of the territory of the province as proposed it would or -might be desirable in the interests of the province to extend the provincial railway, known as the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, at present in operation between North Bay and Cochrane, in the said province to a suitable port on Hudson bay. That it may be found necessary or expedient to select for such Hudson bay terminus a point at or near the mouth of the Nelson river, and that as the estuary of the Nelson lies some distance westward of the proposed western or northwestern boundary of the province, the government desires that such arrangements he made as will enable the province, or such commission or public corporation as may be thereunto authorized on behalf of the province, to construct, maintain and operate that portion of the proposed extension of the said provincial railway which may be projected within the extended boundaries of the province of Manitoba for the purpose of reaching the terminus to he selected as aforesaid upon the waters of Hudson hay.
The prime minister states that he considers that reasonable provision should be made to give effect to this request on the part of Ontario in so far as it is within the authority of the government and parliament of Canada, and, therefore, recommends that:-
1.	The government of Your Boval Highness be authorized to transfer to the government of Ontario or to a minister of that government or to a commission as may he authorized or required by the government of the province of Ontario on behalf of the province, in so far as the lands hereinafter mentioned or described shall he vested in His Majesty in the right of the Dominion.
(a) A parcel of land of a uniform width of five miles commencing at a point to be determined by the government of Ontario on the proposed eastern boundary of Manitoba, within fifty miles of the point of intersection of the said boundary with the shore line of Hudson hay, and extending from the said proposed eastern boundary of Manitoba to the Nelson river, but so that no portion o-f the said parcel of land shall he more than fifty miles in a direct line from the shore of Hudson hay; also such further parcels of land not exceeding in width one-half mile upon the east side of the said river extending up river or along the shore of Hudson hay as may he necessary to entitle the province to a continuous water front of ten miles upon the Nelson river and Hudson hay, including the water front which will lie within the parcel five miles in width just hereinbefore mentioned or described with such right, interest or easement in the river-bed upon tile eastern side and the foreshore contiguous to the land so to be transferred, as may he necessary or reasonably required for the erection, maintenance and operation of docks, elevators, or other structures for the purposes of the said railway, provided, however, that the total combined frontage o-f the said two parcels of land upon Nelson river and Hudson bay shall not exceed ten miles.

(b) If the terminus of the Hudson Bay railway he established at Fort Churchill, and if the government of Ontario prefer to make Fort Churchill the terminus -of their said railway, a right of way two hundred feet in width from any point on the Nelson river to the nearest available point on the Hudson Bay railway, so that the provincial railway may connect with the Hudson Bay railway at that point, Your Royal Highness' government in that event agreeing for running powers over the Hudson Bay railway.
2.	Your Royal Highness' government undertake in the event of the extension of the said provincial railway beyond the limits of Ontario, to promote such legislation as may be necessary within the powers of the parliament of Canada, to authorize such extension and the construction, maintenance and operation of the railway within the province of Manitoba, with powers to construct and operate telegraph and telephone lines, docks, elevators or other structures of every kind, to develop and operate water-powers, and generally to do all things necessary or convenient for the operation of the said railway.
3.	A period of five years he allowed to the government of Ontario within which to select and designate the said lands intended to he transferred as aforesaid, and to notify the location thereof to Your Royal Highness' government, and that this order shall cease to be effective if such location be not made and duly notified within the said period.
The Prime Minister further recommends that, if the government of Ontario assent to the foregoing recommendations the necessary legislation for the purpose of carrying them into effect shall be submitted to parliament as soon as practicable thereafter.
The committee, concurring herein, submit the same for approval.
(Sgd.) RODOLPHE BOUDREAU, Clerk of the Privy Council.
I might say in addition, that I tinder-stand that an arrangement has been made between the government of Ontario and the government of Manitoba that if the railway shall be 'constructed 'along the strip of land which it is thus proposed to transfer to the province of Ontario for that purpose, the province of Manitoba will agree to exempt the railway and structures connected with it from provincial taxation. This land will, of course, be within the province of Manitoba and will be subject to the provincial legislation; but, so far as ownership is concerned, it will be in some corporation, public body or minister selected by the province of Ontario. And, so far as we understand, there is no constitutional difficulty in bringing that about, inasmuch as it is competent for the province of Ontario to own land in the province of Manitoba or any other province of the Dominion, just as it would be competent for Ontario to own land or buildings in the city of London or any part of the United Kingdom. Under the arrangement which is made it will be entirely competent for the province of Ontario, should the government of that province see fit to do so, to extend the Timiska-ming and Northern Ontario railway to the shores of Hudson bay. And in doing so it will have the co-operation of this government, and not only of this government but,
I believe, also of the government of Manitoba, because the government of that province realizes that the extension of a great railway like that to the shore of Hudson bay would be eminently in the interest not only of the province of Ontario but of the province of Manitoba as well.
I did not follow very closely what the Prime Minister said. Is the transfer of this land contingent upon railway construction, or is it contingent merely for railway construction?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is to go to the province of Ontario for the purpose of railway construction if the province of Ontario determines to extend the railway to the shores of Hudson bay; and when the land is once located and transferred to the province of Ontario-which must be done within five years-it becomes absolutely vested in Ontario and is not contingent upon the construction oPthe railway.

It seems difficult at first sight to completely realize this arrangement as stated by my right hon. friend, and involved in the order in council which he has read to the House. But it seems to me an extraordinary jumble, one of the most extraordinary that ever came before parliament.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Might I remind the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), that it is not permissible to debate a Bill on the first reading. Rule 49 is as follows:
When any Bill is presented by a member, in pursuance of an order of the House, or is brought from the Senate, the question, ' That this Bill be now read a first time,' shall be decided without amendment or debate.
If I understand it correctly an explanation should take place on the proposal to introduce the Bill, but other discussion of a Bill does not take place on the first reading.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, I bow to your ruling. But I have seen, and so have you, again and again, discussion upon the first reading of a Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think the rule might be waived if the right hon. gentleman desires to make any observations.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to ask the unanimous consent of the House, because then it will not be establishing a precedent which might be inconvenient should it be necessary to enforce the rule in the future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Carried.

I have only to say, Mr. Speaker, that the legislation which was introduced by my right hon. friend seems to be of a most extraordinary character. There has been a difference of opinion, naturally, between the provinces of Ontario and Manitoba as to the location of the boundary line, each endeavouring to have the line extended as far as it could in its own favour. My hon. friend behind me (Mr. Guthrie), has taken the view that the province of Ontario did not get its share. I have heard this idea before; and, having heard it, we of the late administration, thought it desirable to give a decision in which we took the side neither of Ontario nor of Manitoba, but looked at the matter only with a view to the Dominion at large, and concluded that the best division as between the provinces was to fix the 89th meridian of longitude; the territory to the west of that point to be given to the province of Manitoba, and that to the east to Ontario. But my right hon. friend takes out of what is given to Manitoba a strip of land ten miles wide and gives it to the province of Ontario.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Five miles wide.
Well, _ it matters little, whether five or ten miles. At all events, the province of Ontario is allowed under this arrangement to encroach upon the province of Manitoba to the extent of five miles.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My right hon. friend is mistaken. The grant is being made to the province of Ontario just as it might be made to any individual or corporation for the purposes of the construction of. a railway, but the land is not the less within the boundaries of Manitoba. But, inasmuch as we are not handing over the Crown lands to the province of Manitoba but retaining control of them, and as Ontario desires a port on Hudson bay, we are granting to Ontario within the limits of Manitoba a right of way five miles in width from the eastern boundary of Manitoba to this port on Hudson bay.

I understood that.. But I see a differeince beftween making a grant to a province and to an individual. Any grant to an individual or company must become subject to the legislative power of the province in which the grant is made. In this case such a company would be subject to the jurisdiction of the law of Manitoba. Do I understand that the great province of Ontario is to be subject to the laws of Manitoba and to become liable to the serious obligation involved in this arrangement? My right hon. friend stated a moment ago that he proposed legislation to hand Mr. SPEAKER.
over the natural resources of the provinces to each of these provinces-though he said also that he was not going to give them to Manitoba-and he disposed of five miles of the resources of Manitoba in favour of Ontario. How Manitoba will be satisfied with that is more than I can say.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I can say that Manitoba is perfectly satisfied.

I am sure that the government of Manitoba is perfectly satisfactory. But the government of Manitoba is not exactly the people of Manitoba. The government of Manitoba will be satisfied with anything that the right hon. gentleman offers them; but that the people of Manitoba are satisfied, there may be some reason to doubt. At all events we shall have the new problem in the Dominion of Canada of the great province of Ontario-the banner province as it likes to style itself becoming subject to Manitoba. We have heard that there have been considerable difficulties between Mr. Roblin and Sir James Whitney. All that is done now,-Sir James Whitney becomes the subject to Mr. Roblin.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is very very well satisfied with this arrangement. But I should have thought so old a parliamentarian as he is might have concealed his disappointment much more cleverly than he has done. Under the circumstances, his heat, is very natural, and we are not at all disturbed by it.
For the extending of the Timiskaming & Northern Ontario railway through Manitoba territory these 5 miles have been set apart just in the same way as they might be set apart for any great railway corporation desiring to build a line through the province of Manitoba to a port on Hudson bay. It is to be expected that any province would welcome the construction of such a line if built by any of the railway corporations of this country and I do not know why Manitoba should not welcome the construction of such a line by the great sister province of Ontario. I beiieve Manitoba will welcome it. As to the difficulty with regard to jurisdiction, my right hon. friend perhaps forgets that the Intercolonial Railway of Canada, extends through the provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and that the Canadian government has a very considerable mileage in Prince Edward Island. My right hon. friend knows that each one of those provinces has jurisdiction within the territory through which those lines of railway run, and I do not see any greater incongruity in the somewhat alarming picture which he endeavoured to draw, than there would be in having the Intercolonial railway of Canada, run through those four different provinces, and perhaps in the future through

other provinces of Canada. There will be no difficulty in working out the proposal, at least none is apprehended by those who have given it a great deal of consideration. It gives to Ontario a port on Hudson bay and if the Timiskaming & Northern Ontario railway should be constructed to that port, it would be an advantage not only to Ontario, which will thus secure the desired port, but to the province of Manitoba, and to every province of Canada that that should be brought about.
Does my right hon. friend think that under the British North America Act the province of Ontario could build a railway in another province?

I have not the slightest doubt that the province of Ontario can do it, and I have not a doubt that the province of Ontario will do it, will extend that railway to Hudson bay when that northern country is more fully developed than at present.

I understand my right hon. friend to say that the government of Manitoba was perfectly satisfied with the arrangement, but I did not understand him. to say whether the government of Ontario had consented to it.

The government of Ontario has assented to this arrangement and the government of Manitoba has assented to this arrangement, and every one has assented to it, except my hon. friends on the other side of the House.
I understand then that there is some correspondence which has not been brought down.
I think not.
I found nothing in the correspondence brought down showing the consent of Ontario or Manitoba to this new arrangement.

I do not think there is any correspondence on the subject. The government of Ontario has been represented here by a member of that government, who came and consulted with us on the subject. The government of Manitoba was represented here also by two members of that government, who came and consulted with us on the same subject.
All this has been verbal then?
It has all been verbal, but none the less satisfactory.
Do we understand that the title to the lands east of the boundary between Manitoba and Ontario is to go to the Ontario government or is it reserved to the Dominion?

In extending the boundaries of the province of Manitoba the Crown reserves, as was done in the case of Alberta and Saskatchewan, the title to the public domain which has not passed to private hands. Therefore the Crown, holding title to the public domain in the district indicated in the order in council, proposes to make a grant of a strip five miles in width from the eastern boundary of the province of Manitoba to the mouth of the Nelson river. The point at which that strip is to begin has not been precisely defined.
I was asking in regard to the title of lands in what would be New Ontario; does the federal government exercise the title or is it given to the province?
It passes as the other lands within the province of Ontario. It is to be administered by the Crown on the advice of the government of Ontario.
In the right of Ontario?

Of course, my hon. friend understands that there is never any transfer made in such cases because the land is vested in the Crown in the one case as much as in the other. The only question is by whose advice shall that land be administered, by the advice of the federal government or by the advice of the provincial government. This land, like the rest of the land within the limits of Ontario, will be administered by the Crown on the advice of the provincial government.
And on the other side of Manitoba it will be administered by the federal government.
Who will have jurisdiction over these five miles? Will it be the Dominion government or the government of Ontario or the government of Manitoba?
It will be subject to the legislative jurisdiction of the province of Manitoba just as any other portion of land within the boundaries of that province.
Then will the hon. gentleman tell me who owns the land? Is it owned by Manitoba or Ontario or the Dominion government?
It never has been owned by Manitoba, it is at present owned by the federal government and as soon as this grant is passed it will be owned by the Ontario government.
What considerations induced the government to establish the width of five miles for this right * of way?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We gave consideration to it and concluded that five miles would be a convenient strip.

Is it the intention of the government to appoint additional judges for the circuit court of Montreal? I see there is a great agitation in Montreal about this and I have tried since the beginning of the session to get an answer from the hon. gentleman. I notice that the members of the bar of Montreal are very insistent and many delegations have called on the hon. gentleman or at least many letters have been sent to him. Has he given a decision?
Mr. ' DOHERTY. I have not had any delegation nor have I had a large number of letters. I have had communications from a representative committee of the bar of Montreal upon the subject and, co-operating with that committee, I have given the very best consideration in my power to the problem presented in connection with the circuit court of Montreal and I have to thank that committee for having devoted a great deal of time and consideration to the subject.
That committee have agreed to a suggestion made by me, and 1 understand that the Prime Minister and Attorney General of the province to whom that suggestion was communicated has no objection to it. It has been agreed that it would be desirable, before proceeding to appoint the three additional judges who have been suggested for the circuit of Montreal, to endeavour, by selecting three judges from the rural districts in Quebec where there is the least work to be done, to dispose of the arrears that have accumulated in the circuit court. It is the intention of the government to ask the House to vote such additional funds as may be necessary to provide for any expense that may be incurred, and if the arrangement can be carried out it will place us in a position to start the present court with a clean sheet. If I mistake not, a measure has already been -introduced into the Quebec legislature, intended to provide for the simplification in some respects of the procedure of the circuit court, with a view to enabling the court to deal with cases more expeditiously. It is hoped that if the circuit court is given an opportunity of starting with a clean sheet, and its operations are further facilitated by a simplification of procedure, at all events, in certain cases, it will prove possible to carry on its Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
work without doubling the number of judges. The present idea is that there should not be any immediate increase in the number of judges, but that an endeavour should be made to ascertain whether the work can be satisfactorily carried on with the present number of judges. I may say that the hope I have that that may prove possible is not confined to myself. It is shared by the members of the Bar who, on the selection of their confreres, have been specially dealing with this matter of the business of the circuit court of Montreal. I may add further that I have had a conference with the present judges of the circuit court and they have expressed their satisfaction with this proposed arrangement and stated that, while they do not feel quite confident that even under this arrangement three judges will be sufficient, they do believe, after carefully going into the matter and coming to a conclusion, that once they are relieved of all these arrears and placed in the position that I have suggested, four judges will prove quite ample. In order to carry out this arrangement effectually, to obtain the results we desire, it will be necessary that we shall have the co-operation of the judges themselves, and they have expressed their perfect readiness to facilitate it and to cooperate with us. We need and I believe have further the good will of the members of the Bar and the sanction and approval of the government of Quebec. As I say, I have seen the communications between the Attorney General of Quebec and the committee of	the Bar to
which I have referred, in which that gentleman declares he has no objection to this endeavour being made to ascertain whether the problem that presents itself-and which, as I think everybody knows who knows anything about the administration of justice in Montreal is a serious problem-may not be more satisfactorily settled in this manner than it would be by merely appointing three additional judges to the circuit court and leave the matter in its present position. I would not like to give rise to any hopes that might later on be disappointed, but I think I may add that it is hoped that if this plan can be carried out, and if the circuit court can be carried on with the present number of judges, or only with four, possibly this House may look more favourably upon a proposition in future to increase the salaries of the judges of the court.

subtopic: DISMISSAL OF POSTMASTER AT CRYSTAL BEACH, ONTARIO.
DISMISSAL OF POSTMASTER AT CRYSTAL BEACH, ONTARIO.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the House goes into Committee of Supply I wjsh to bring up a question which I referred to about two weeks ago when the

hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) was not in his seat. It is a fact that the Postmaster General has dismissed in the county of Welland a young man by the name of A. or E. W. Buck, postmaster at Crystal Beach, and he has appointed a United States citizen to his place named Rebstock. There is no reason why my friend, Mr. Buck, who has held the position for many years should have been dismissed. The Postmaster General has received, I know, a large petition signed in favour of that young man retaining the position. He was not a partisan, he is not a politician and he never took any part in politics. Why the hon. gentleman saw fit to dismiss him I cannot understand. There was a large petition in favour of him retaining the position as postmaster and retaining the post office in the building where it has been situated in the past. I would not object so seriously to the dismissal of this officer if the Postmaster General had not appointed a United States citizen to fill his place. After all the waving of the flag by hon. gentlemen opposite I cannot quite understand why the Postmaster General should dismiss a good strong healthy Canadian citizen who will wave the Union Jack and appoint a fellow who is a United States citizen and who waves the Stars and Stripes. If the Postmaster General can explain that satisfactorily to me I will submit, but I doubt if he can. I would ask the Postmaster General to reconsider his decision in regard to the matter. The hon. gentleman dismissed the postmaster at Bridgeburg and reappointed a good Conservative. I did not make any complaint about that because I had that man dismissed some years ago and appointed a new man in his place. Therefore, he has simply restored the status quo. I am not objecting to that particularly. I think he made a mistake there, but I do ask that the Postmaster General should reconsider his position in regard to the Crystal Beach postmaster and reinstate a young man of good ability, and good habits and a Canadian citizen who has taken no part in politics.

speechtext: He is not a good citizen then.

subtopic: DISMISSAL OF POSTMASTER AT CRYSTAL BEACH, ONTARIO.
speechtext:
Some one says he is not a good citizen if he does not take part in politics. If he does take part in politics he is dismissed-so what is he to do?
I would ask the Postmaster General to look into the question of the dismissal of this postmaster and if he has to appoint any person in lieu of the man whom he dismissed and who should not have been dismissed, let him appoint some man who will wave the Union Jack instead of the Star Spangled Banner.
Mr.' PELLETIER. My hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) has stated that I reappointed a man whom he got dismissed without reason or investigation and the inference is that he admits he was wrong when he did that, and that I am right in making restitution. Has the hon. gentleman (Mr. German) any remorse for having deprived this man of his office during fifteen years?

subtopic: DISMISSAL OF POSTMASTER AT CRYSTAL BEACH, ONTARIO.

subtopic: DISMISSAL OF POSTMASTER AT CRYSTAL BEACH, ONTARIO.

subtopic: DISMISSAL OF POSTMASTER AT CRYSTAL BEACH, ONTARIO.

subtopic: DISMISSAL OF POSTMASTER AT CRYSTAL BEACH, ONTARIO.
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman has told us that he had not much fault to find with the reappointment of the man who had been dismissed.

The hon. gentleman from Welland was strong against reciprocity at one time, but he has now joined the party which is keeping reciprocity as one of its platform planks.
