Interior Department-Immigration contingencies-Canadian and British and foreign agencies and general immigration expenses, $500,000.
['No, not till Thursday.']

I wish to call the attention of the minister to certain regulations of his department which, in my opinion, operate very unjustly. The regulation now is that, if a foreigner starts for Canada he ' cannot remain in any intervening country, say the United States, for a week or two, and then come into Canada. This is a very serious matter, and I would like the minister to consider it. . I shall give one instance as an example of what is happening continually. About two years ago the Ontario Iron and Steel company employed a foreman from Pittsburg who was an expert iron worker. He had worked in the Pittsburg mills for several years, he had never become a United States citizen, he being a Swede. He came to Welland and he had to put up seventy dollars as security that he would go back to the United States within thirty days.
This mam stayed for thirty days. He had to go back or lose his $70. He could not stay in Canada unless he was a United States citizen. That is happening continually. There are good men, who would make excellent citizens of Canada, who have come from a foreign country and have lived in the United States for a year or two or three years; they have not become naturalized as citizens of the United States, and they cannot come into Canada and stay here. This is the most absurd problem in connection with the immigration matters that is confronting the Minister of the Interior at this moment. I have talked it oveT with the chief immigration officer, Mr. Scott, and he sees the difficulty. The only way out of it that I can. see is to 'allow the immigration officers some	degree of discretion in the
matter, if you have the right kind of officers, as>
you have in Welland, because I saw that they were appointed. Make the regulations more elastic and give the officers some sort of discretion. This is not the first time that I have 'called this hard and fast rule to the- attention of the Minister of the Interior. I called it to the attention of the former Minister of the Interior. I hope that the present minister will see some way of getting over a very serious difficulty that stands in the way <k our getting first-class settlers into Canada.

I want to .supplement the remarks which my hon. friend from Welland has just made. I can understand that, with the hard and fast regulations which Mr. PELLETIER.
the United; States has against us, there should be something along the same line in Canada. But it does seem ridiculous that persons coming from one part of Canada through the United States to. another part of Canada, should, under the regulations of the Immigration Department, be disturbed and put to the trouble of proving exactly who and what they are, and going through a course of sprouts which, if nothing else, is humiliating to the person who is subjected to this treatment. A short time ago I brought to the attention of the minister a case in which an officer, acting entirely in accordance with a memorial that had been sent out a day or two previously, had stopped a person who had come from Winnipeg, bad passed through the United States, and was coining to Sarnia, and had almost turned him back because some slight part of the regulations promulgated by the department had not been lived up to. Having regard to the regulations of the United States in regard to our workmen going into their country, I think we should have as high a wall against them as they have against us; but when you have a set of officers, as you have on the border, who are above the ordinary intelligence, .and who realize that they hold a more or less delicate office, in which a mistake on their part might lead to trouble between us and the United States, I think the minister should allow them to a certain extent to use their discretion. In some of the smaller centres, it is necessary at 'certain times to bring in labourers to perform local work, and in those oases I think the immigration officers ought to have power for a certain length of time to allow labourers to come in, in order that not only public works, but private 'enterprise, should not be kept back. I think it would be well that both the Department of the Interior and the Department of Labour should take this matter up, and see if the immigration regulations cannot be so framed that they will work more smoothly with regard to people who come to Canada with the intention of becoming good citizens and helping the country along.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I appreciate the force of the argument made by my hon. friend from Welland and my hon. .friend from West Lambton; but I am free to confess that I am not 'sufficiently conversant with the regulations to give the hon. gentlemen an answer off-hand. While the regulations may entail a certain amount of hardship,
I am sure that they were not adopted without some good and sufficient reason in the judgment of the department. I shall be glad, however, to take the matter up at me very earliest opportunity with the officers of the department, and see if some modifications along the lines suggested,

consistent with safety to the administration of this very delicate matter, cannot be made in the regulations.

I do not wish to criticise for a moment the administration of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Rogers), I do feel more like criticising the administration of his predecessor, because I took the matter up with him, and wanted him to do something but I could not get him to act. All I want is that the present minister will take this matter into consideration and decide upon some beneficial action. This situation, as I understand it was created in order to keep the Hindus out of British Columbia. But that does not apply here. This is a grievance which must be remedied, and it will be remedied, I am quite sure, by the minister.

I think these troubles are largely caused by want of judgment on the part of the officer. A case came under my notice the other day where a lady who had lived all her life in a Canadian town along side the border paid a visit to the United States. On returning to Canada she was stopped by an officer who would not allow her to pass. Fortunately there was another officer present who knew this lady, anid so she was allowed to proceed. She was a very respectable, well dressed lady, and there was no reason whatever for the indignity to which she was exposed. The trouhle is that a lot of messengers have been taken out of this House and appointed to .positions on the border. I think if good officers were appointed there would foe no trouble whatever. It is simply due to the stupid officers that were appointed by the late gouvern-ment.

I do not at all agree with my hon. friend from London, in the remarks which he has made concerning the officers. It is not at all, in my opinion, a question of the fitness of the officers, .but the responsibility lies with the regulations which have been made in the past, due perhaps to certain exigencies which arose. From my experience, which has been very considerable, along the border, the officers have been men above the ordinary intelligence, but they have simply done these things from a desire to live up to the regulations, and thought they were only carrying out their duty in that regard.
Do you consider a man is fit for such a position if he refuses to admit to Canada a respectable lady who lives here?
The officers have to act according to the regulations.
I do not think such conduct is the indication of intelligence on the part if the officer.

I cannot allow the statement of the hon. member for London to go uncontradicted, because I know these officers, I realise that they would like to use a certain amount of discretion, and discrimination, but they are_ tied down hard and fast by the regulations, and as I have already said I tried to get the exMinister of the Interior to change them, but he would not do it, and he deserved to be turned out I think. I hope the present minister will do better and make these regulations more elastic so that the officers in whom he has confidence may exercise some discretionary power.
If they do not give efficient service put them out.

I do not think the minister should take such an extreme course in the case of officers who are intelligent and efficient. Let these officers have -some power of discretion, and let the regulations be sufficiently elastic so that an intelligent immigration officer can admit a foreigner possessed of means; who is on his wray from the United -States into Canada. Under the regulations at present the officer cannot do that.

"I agree with the arguments presented by the member for Welland (Mr. German) and the member for Lambton (Mr. Pardee). Undoubtedly a great many very objectionable cases occur at present in' connection with the officers questioning people who are coming into Canada. Only last Saturday I was coming across the border and saw a poor woman being stopped, and one time I was afraid she was going to 'be put off the train by the officer. It turned out afterwards that although she could not speak very good English -she lived a short distance from the border at a village called Sherkston, where she lived with her family. I believe these officers are painstaking and careful and do anything they possibly can to assist immigrants, and it may be the regulations are too strict. But at the same time I call attention to the fact that these troubles do not all exist on the Canadian side. I live close to the border, as my hon. friend from Welland does, and travel backwards and forwards to Buffalo very often, and I think he will agree with me that we see more objectionable cases on the American than on the Canadian side.
That is quite right.

If some international arrangement could be made between Canada and the United States under which there could be a change in the regulations with respect to people who have to cross backwards and forwards, it would be a

I would like to call the minister's attention to the fact that some of the officers in the port of Sherbrooke are not very conversant with the French language. Trains of the Boston and Maine and Grand Trunk railways enter Canada through to Sherbrooke from all points in New England. The New England states are inhabited largely, as you know, by French population, and during the summer months their relatives in the eastern townships go down to visit them. Sometimes aged relatives go there and spend a few weeks, but when they return home they experience a good deal of trouble. I have a case in mind which happened last summer of' an old French settler returning from a visit to his son in the state of Maine, but who was turned back at a point below Sherbrooke and had to go back to his son before he could get home. These cases are quite frequent. I would impress _ the minister with the necessity that all immigration and customs officers, for instance, in eastern townships, should be thoroughly conversant with both languages, I think that it is a fair request to make to the minister who knows the importance of the French language as he speaks it very well himself.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know who the officers are at Sherbrooke, and I am not conversant with the conditions to which he refers. But I certainly can appreciate the point that it would be very advisable that the officers in charge should speak both languages. I shall be very glad indeed to see if we cannot arrange that at the earliest possible moment.

Living as I do near the border, between the province of New Brunswick and the state of Maine, I am in a position to know that Americans are dealt with very fairly by our people. They are allowed to come with their teams or to walk across the boundary line, and our immigration agents are very considerate in dealing with these visitors. But it is entirely different when we go to the other side. At St. Leonard when an international bridge was under construction I went there to see the work. I crossed on

the ferry, and when I landed on the American side I had to give a long account of myself to the United States immigration officer before I was allowed to proceed, I explained that I wished to stay there for only about ten minutes, but he told me that I must give my pedigree or he would not allow me to cross. Other Canadians there have had a similar experience. Canadians walking or driving to the other side of the line have to give an account of themselves. If a man has his wife with him, he has to give an account for her; if they have children with them, it must be explained to whom the children belong. It is very annoying to our New Bruns-wickers. If the minister could bring about arrangements under which people from our side could be allowed to drive or walk across on telling the immigration officer their names and what they are going for, it would be an advantage to many of our people.

This will probably be my only opportunity to bring to the attention of the minister the facts with regard to a matter of importance to the people I represent. There is an agent of the Department of Immigration at the port of North Sydney, and quite a number of immigrants from the other side of the Atlantic arrive at that place. But in case of those who are sick a different situation arises from that at Halifax or Montreal. The immigrant from Liverpool goes direct to Halifax, and he can be sent back, I presume, if the officers deem that course proper. But immigrants coming tp the port of North Sydney generally come from St. John's, Newfoundland. Restrictions upon immigration such as are known here are not in force in Newfoundland. Immigrants land in Newfoundland whose real destination is Canada.
After staying in Newfoundland for as long as they please, they take the train from St. John's to Port aux Basques thence cross in the steamer ' Bruce ' to North Sydney. It often happens that immigrants arrive there suffering from trachoma. The immigration officer at North Sydney is not in a position to send them back to the old country, because they do not come to North Sydney from the old country, but from Newfoundland. The only thing he can do, is to send them back to Newfoundland. But to send an immigrant to Port aux Basques is to send him to a place where there are no hospitals, and where he cannot get treatment. Sometimes cases arrive involving no little distress. A wife may arrive with her children to join the husband and father, who may have been in Canada for years preparing a home for them. But if one of them has trachoma, they may all have to be sent back to Newfoundland, and the husband,

though a Canadian citizen, can do nothing for them. But at North Sydney we have excellent doctors, and two excellent hospitals, one at North Sydney and one a mile and a half further down, with a tramway from the terminal wharf to both hospitals. If the regulations permitted it, we could treat these people on the spot. If it turned out, after a fair term of treatment that a cure could not be effected, the immigrant might then be deported. But in some eases those sent to Newfoundland afterwards find their way into Canada without complying with the regulations. These people are mostly Assyrians. Many of them are already in Canada. We find them honest, industrious citizens, willing to do any work that comes their way. All I ask is that these people should be put on the same footing as Europeans in regard to this matter. We are anxious to have them in Nova Scotia, for we need people to work in our mines or about our steel works, and we find these are good people. I hope the minister will give this matter consideration and place these Assyrians on the same footing as Europeans coming into Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The point the hon. gentleman raises is a rather important one. Some of the hon. members who have participated in the discussion this evening have pointed cut the difficulties in connection with immigrants coming from the United States. It is true, we need to have fairly close regulations to prevent people coming in who are undesirable. And I understand that some attempt has been practised in connection with their finding their way around through Newfoundland to avoid certain regulations they would meet if entering by other ports.
For that reason the point raised by my hon. friend is rather a difficult one but the chief officer of the department is present and has heard what my hon. friend has said; it will have very careful consideration in order, if possible, to remedy the trouble and remain consistent with our rules and regulations. I understand we have a doctor at North Sydney who looks after any person coming in who requires medical attendance.
He is not permitted to treat them?
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is permitted to examine and see what is the matter and if there is nothing serious the matter he passes them on to some other doctor.
If he finds they have trachoma he is not permitted to treat them but must send them out of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In that case I understand he returns them to Newfoundland.
And they cannot get treatment where they are sent.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is unfortunate for them. However, it is a matter that is worth looking into.

In the early part of the session I made some suggestions in regard to improving the immigration system and I hope the minister will be able to say to-night that he has adopted those suggestions. One of them was that the inspection should take place before the immigrants go on board the vessels.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is reasonable precaution taken in that way in view of the fact that all immigrants are examined by the ship's doctors and by the board of trade doctors before they are allowed to take passage for Canada. In that way the department feels they are fairly well protected. Less than I per cent of the immigrants have been returned.

If the same care was taken in inspecting them before they embark at Liverpool, the trachoma would be discovered there and that would relieve the troubles we are experiencing at Montreal. The expense would be great but surely it is worth while to go to any expense. The introduction of cholera to this country some years ago was owing to lack of inspection on the other side.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When we looked into this matter we found that the question arose whether we had authority to undertake the inspection on the other side. The cases of trachoma that have been reported are very few.
Has the department immigration hospitals in St. John and Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

In granting aid to the provinces in the matter of immigration, does the minister intend to vote money directly to each province to supplement expenditures made by the provinces for immigration work, or will the aid merely be limited to the payment of salaries of persons named by , the provincial governments to attend to immigration work in England?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It would not be wise for the government to make a direct grant, because you have to keep control of your whole machinery to make it as effective as it should be. We are suggesting to the provinces that we are prepared to carry out any reasonable policy that they will recommend that will be in keeping with that effort to improve, if possible, the conditions of the different provinces, and we

shall endeavour to circulate literature that in consultation with them we will agree upon as being the most desirable for each province.
I understand that one office is occupied by the provincial and federal immigration branch at Toronto. Where is the office, and who pays the rent?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The office is in the Union station and we pay the rent.

I am interested in this matter of immigration work, especially in the project of co-operation with the provinces which my hon. friend has put forward as the leading feature of his immigration policy. What is the intention in regard to the number of provincial agents to be appointed and paid by the Dominion, and are these agents to be nominated by the provincial governments?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know that we have any special rules as to nomination of officers. We have not accepted any nominations or asked any government to nominate any special officer, but we have asked them to give us all the information they possibly can. I thought we ought to have about two agents for each province to work up this matter of co-operation and work together. That was the suggestion with relation to the maritime provinces, which, with Ontario, have taken the most active interest in the plan.
The work in the prairie provinces has been pretty actively canvassed and in so far as the western country is concerned my hon. friend quite understands that we will give it every possible attention in order to continue as aggressively as we possibly can the policy in that direction in co-operation with the provinces, or in any other form that will be best calculated to bring in all the immigrants that we can secure.
Will the agents be sent abroad or will they remain in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a point in Tegard to which we will take advice from the provinces concerned and we will be guided by their judgment.
Will this force of provincial agents be in addition to the Dominion force that is now at work m Europe?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it is extra over and above the officers now engaged.
That would mean the addition of eighteen salaried agents to the staff at work in England and on the continent?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, two for each province.

It would be a very important addition to the cost of the Immigra-Mr. ROGERS.
tion Department and I will risk the expression of the idea that the expenditure of such a large sum as would be necessary under that proposal with the special view of introducing legislation into the eastern provinces where there is no free land, nor the same opportunity as there is in the prairie provinces, will certainly not produce the same result to the Dominion as like effort or like expense would if directed towards the prairie provinces where the opportunities at present exist.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I can appreciate what my hon. friend says in respect, of the western provinces and their possibilities. At the same time we must all realize the feeling that exists in the maritime provinces with respect to the matter of immigration. They have certainly not received much attention in this regard. In the province of New Brunswick they have adopted a very aggressive policy involving the purchasing of considerable tracts of land and dividing it up something in the form suggested by the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr.. McKenzie) when he was discussing the same thing in respect to the province of Nova Scotia. I certainly think it is worth while for the department to lend what assistance they can to the provinces which are so desirous to secure immigration and which are putting forth such an effort as Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island are. We would be failing in our duty in administering the immigration Work of this country if we did not lend that assistance that their energies appear to entitle them to. If it does not turn out as they expect it would be their misfortune and we would be very sorry but at the same time they have possibilities that entitle them to the consideration that we are suggesting.

When Mr. Hawkes was in the maritime provinces conferring with the governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in connection with immigration matters, a suggestion was made to him by the Secretary of Immigration for the government of Nova Scotia as a means of inducing immigration. There was brought to his attention the idea of organizing a corporation sufficiently strong to purchase a great area of vacant or abandoned farming lands in that province and to help along intending settlers who might eventually determine to locate on this land. I think I mentioned this suggestion to the minister during the debate on the resolution of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes). I know that such a thing is now receiving the consideration of some people m Nova Scotia with t'he view of organizing a company for that purpose. I would like to inquire of the minister if he would consider it a prac-

t-ical thing from his view point to aid a corporation of that kind in some form or another, such as a guarantee of interest upon bonds, or the payment of a subsidy according to the results, and if it would be possible to enter into any contract with the department. That suggestion has been made, I know, to the Department of the Interior by the government of'Nova Scotia. Possibly the minister has not had an opportunity of seeing it or of giving it consideration. I would like to know if any suggestion in that form would be apt to meet with the favour of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not seen or heard of a proposition of that kind as coming from the government or as a suggestion in the department up to the present time. I would rather fear that the suggestion might be surrounded with a certain amount of difficulty in connection with the department being a party to any undertaking of this kind which might be regarded as speculative in its nature. I would want to have that matter very carefully considered before I would venture to make any hon. friend anything like a definite answer. I have not heard of it yet and I have not had under consideration the representations, which he said have been made to the department.
I think they were made to Mr. Hawkes, as a matter of fact.
In the case of agents who will specially represent the various provinces, are they selected bv the provincial governments or will they be selected by the Immigration Department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We propose to consult every government and agree with them as to what agent we will select and as to who will be a desirable and useful man as publicity man for the province that he represents. We propose to invite every government to give us their advice and join in the recommendation of the man who will be useful to carry on the work.
As a matter of fact the federal government will actually engage the man and pay him?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is right.
And he will actually be under the federal government's supervision from start to finish?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is right.
I want to know if the $50 as laid down in the regulations is in force during this season?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, until the end of this month. The money qualification for immigrants other than Asiatics is $50 from the 1st of November to the 1st of March 124
and $25 from the 1st March to the end of October, just the same as it has been.
When the estimates were up before I made an inquiry in regard to the closing of offices in Great Britain and I was informed that none had been closed. Have there been any changes in England?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No changes.
And the same on tb* continent?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No change either.
Has the Boston office been opened?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, but we hope to open it on the 1st of March.
Who are the officials to be appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They have not been named yet.
I have been informed that the immigration agent at Edmonton has been dismissed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What is his name?
Webster. I would be glad to know what was the reason of his dismissal.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not remember the case now, but I will supply the information to the hon. gentleman to-morrow.

Mr. Webster was a gentleman of very considerable standing in the community when he was appointed, and I believe he was a very competent agent. Mr. Webster was a Liberal, but I am well aware there were no grounds for his dismissal because of partisanship. He certainly did not show any partisanship during the recent election. I am therefore, entirely at a loss to understand on what ground he has been dismissed. I want to place on record the facts in connection with the appointment of the man put in his place. I understand that the man who is to be appointed is one W. H. Clegg, who was president of the Conservative Association in Edmonton during the last election, and who was a party to an attemot to discredit me in the elections by giving an order for the manufacture of a ballot box which was put before the public as having been made in my interest, and improperly made for the purpose of misdirecting the results of the election. This is the man who has been appointed in Mr. Webster's place, and I must say that I do not think the appointment reflects any credit upon the minister or upon the department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am very sorry to learn the information which my hon. friend has imparted to the House. I will have the matter looked into and if the information



is well founded I will deal with it in the proper manner.

Some years ago there were appointed in different towns and villages of Ontario a number of agents whose duty was supposed to be to bring in farm hands or domestic servants, and some of these agents were very active and some of them did little or nothing. They were paid at the rate of two dollars per head for each farm hand or domestic they induced to come into the country. Now, in my view these agents have not been a very great success, to say the least of it, and I wish to know if it is intended to continue them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The returns for last year show that 4,224 males, 2,144 females and 157 children were distributed by these agents, in the province of Ontario. We have about seventy-five of these agents and the amount paid them last year was $5,152. I discussed this question with Mr. Duff, Minister of Agriculture for Ontario, a short time ago, and although he is thoroughly informed in matters of this kind, he was not in a position to say definitely and off-hand whether, in his judgment, it was a wise thing to discontinue the agents. He is making inquiries into the matter, and we expect to hear from him in the near future, when I shall be glad to communicate his views to my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson).

Judging from the fact that $5,152 was paid to these local distributing agents in Ontario last year, it would seem that 2,576 farm hands and domestics were placed by them in the province. A return brought down to the House some time ago shows that about two hundred and fifty of these agents were appointed throughout Ontario in 1907 and that the number has been reduced from year to year until last year there weTe eighty-eight. The demand of western Canada has drawn heavily on some of the oldest and best agricultural counties in the province of Ontario, and consequently there has been in some of these counties quite a decrease in the population. In my opinion, these local distributing agents have proven nothing less than an absolute failure in carrying out the business for which they were supposed to be appointed. The fact is that many of the Ontario counties which are most in need of people have not received one man or one woman through these agencies during the past two years. During the last ten years there has been a decrease of 3,476 in the population of the county of Dufferin, and not one person was placed in that county in the last two years by these agents. The same remark applies to Lennox and Addington, where there has been a decrease of 2,965.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In the county of Prince Edward, the population is less now by 714 than it was ten years ago, and not a single person was placed in that county through the medium of these local agents. In the county of Lambton, where the population in ten years has decreased by 5,380, there was just one person placed there by the local agency last year and nine in the year 1910. I do not believe there is any excuse for continuing a system of that kind, which in my opinion was devised for no other than political purposes. The province of Ontario has given liberally of its people to meet the demand of western Canada, and, Sir, it is the duty of this government to see that justice is done to that province with respect to this question. You may talk as you please about the demands of the maritime provinces and of western Canada, but, if this heavy dram on Ontario is continued, disaster will overtake the province, there is, in my opinion, danger of opening and developing the west more rapidly than the circumstances appertaining to the whole country would justify.
According to a return brought down there were 4,177 people placed by these agents in Ontario in the last two years. In twenty-one counties there were 1,450 people placed; yet in one county alone there were placed more than half of that number or 767, leaving 683 for the other twenty counties. Surely nobody can defend such a system as that; there is no equality or right of justice in it. Many of these counties are so handicapped to-day by the labour situation that many of the farms are not producing one half what they otherwise would do, and are used for grazing purposes because of the lack of labour. For instance, the county of Lamb-ton received only ten men in two years, and yet, notwithstanding the increase of the towns and cities, it has fallen off in population 5,380 in ten years. The county of Oxford showed a falling off of 1,032 people in ten years, yet it received only 125 in two years. Prescott received only 5 last year and none in 1910. The county of Durham received none in 1910 and four in 1911; yet there is a falling off there of 1,555. Middlesex received six in 1910 and 15 in 1911, and shows a falling off of 4,285. The census returns show an alarming condition of affairs in the province of Ontario, and the absolute necessity of the government seeing that something is done to meet the conditions that have arisen in that province.
A few days ago I urged on the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he was putting the grain Bill through, to do something to offset the spread of noxious weeds in the province of Ontario and provide for the destruction of weed seeds in screenings at the elevators, and thus prevent them being fed on the farms.

The absence of farm labour and the spread of noxious weeds in Ontario demand the consideration of the government. I do not believe that this government can afford to place the responsibility on any other shoulders than their own. I do not think they can _ depute their responsibilities to the provincial government or to any one else. I believe it is their first duty to see that in the older provinces that are annually denuded of farm labourers by the excursions to western Canada to harvest the crops there, that something is done to meet the conditions that exist, as a result of the policy that has been in force for many years. I do not object to these people going to western Canada. We are glad to nave our people go and settle in that country; but I believe that the previous government lost sight of the fact that it was their duty to see that other people took their places in the older provinces, where they would find the conditions more congenial and the training they would receive such as better to equip them for their experience in the newer country. I am glad the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) has brought up the matter of the local distributing agents in Ontario. Any one who knows the circumstances of their appointment and the manner in which they have discharged their duties knows that they have not been satisfactory. I understand that they were to receive applications from farmers and forward them to the superintendent of immigration to Ottawa, who was to send them to government agents in the old land and they to the boking agent there. This would entail a delay of several months before the farmers could be supplied. That policy has proven so unsatisfactory that very few of the booking agents to-day care to have men sent out in that way. I believe it is the duty of the government to see that there is a labour bureau establishment in every province of Canada, and that the booking agents in the old country are kept in touch with the conditions here. The labour bureau would receive applications from the farmers, and the immigration authorities would have absolute knowledge of the conditions in this country, and would see that men were sent out and placed by the bureau which would be in direct touch with farmers. I know as a matter of fact that at the present time the provincial department of immigration in Ontario has about 800 applications for men'; yet we have in force a regulation preventing immigrants from coming here between the months of November and March unless they have $50 in their possession. As.far as Ontario is concerned, I do not think it is advisable to enforce these regulations, particularly in face of the conditions that exist in this province at the present time. In 21 of the very best counties of the province of Ontario, there has been a falling off in the popula-1244
tion of 56,352 people, and the fanners are handicapped by the lack of farm labourers. There is a great outcry in the newspapers that the farmers of Canada are not producing enough to meet the requirements of the people. Why do we devote all our energies to the growing of wheat for the people of Europe, and fail to look after conditions in our own country, and to see that we do not have to import butter from Australia and New Zealand and eggs from Kansas and potatoes from Ireland as at present. Our friends opposite were very anxious a few months ago that reciprocity should be adopted, not for the relief of the farmer but for the relief of the consumer; but if they had done their duty by the older provinces, the conditions that are in existence here would not be in existence. I would therefore earnestly urge the minister to see that different methods are adopted, and that the province of Ontario receives at least equal treatment to that extended to the other provinces, and to see that the whole energy of the government is not devoted to western Canada as it has been heretofore.
Will the hon. gentleman please inform the minister and the House, if he can, how emigration from the older provinces can be prevented?

I have heard it stated-I do not know whether it is correct or not, or to what degree it is correct -that it was the practice some time ago in 'the province of Ontario to secure farm Labour, employ that Labour for a few months during the summer, and when the crops were all harvested, to permit that Labour to go away. If that is true it is a very unfair and unjust thing to Ontario or any other province.

I may tell the hon. gentleman that that statement is not correct. I have been connected with immigration work in the province of Ontario for nearly three years-and -at no month in the year have we been able to supply the demand for farm labourers in that province. That may seem unreasonable. A few years ago there were people in the city otf Toronto clamouring for assistance from the city authorities, yet those people would not go and work on a farm, although there was an abundance of such work to be had. If they were not qualified for farm work they would not be of any use on a farm. There are applications on the boobs of the Department of Immigration -at Toronto, -as I said a few minutes ago, ito the number of upwards of 800, at the present time. Many of these -applicants are 'asking for married men by the year, undertaking to provide them with houses, offering wages of at least $300 or $350 and more per year, and free fuel, free milk, a garden and other things. There is in the old country an abundance of such labour to be had. Last year the Ontario government advanced upwards of $25,000 to assist farm laborers and domestic servants to come out here, and place them on farms in Ontario, the provincial government is still pursuing that policy. Why should they -be compelled to do that ? Is it not the duty of the federal lauthori-ties to see that that is done, and to see that these demands are met, thus freeing the provincial governments from the necessity of entering on work of that kind? I may say that two years ago I was compelled to cable to a booking agent of the old country because the Dominion regulations were so strictly enforced by the late government as to prevent a number of men accepted by an Ontario government agent from coming out here and assure them of employment. I was told that the booking -agents had been threatened with the loss of the bonus which was paid to them if they continued to send -immigrants to the provincial authorities -and not to the local distributing -agents. But notwithstanding that, we find1 from the return brought down, that many of the best counties, counties that are most in need of men, are not getting one single man through the medium of the machinery which has been in existence in Canada for many years past.
Does the Ontario government or the federal government conduct any system of assisted immigration, or do immigrants coming out to Canada for employment have to pay their own fares?
The provincial government has been advancing $20 towards paying the fare of each farm labourer that came here.

I have had some little experience in regard to importation from the old country, not of farm labour, but of a different class of labour, and I must say that assisted immigration has been, so far as my experience is concerned, a failure. I have paid out a good deal of money for assisted immigration in connection with institutions with which I am interested, and I do not think I would be very far astray in saying that in nine cases out of ten these immigrants jumped their bonds, beat us out of the money, and proved very poor labour indeed. Therefore, I am not a very strong advocate of assisted immigration. I believe the proper class of immigrants to come to this country are men that will pay their own way. They will make better help and be more dependent on their exertions than immigrants who are assisted by ttenevolent or manufacturing institutions, or by the government, be it provincial or Dominion. My experience has been that assisted immigrants have 'been a complete 'and 'absolute failure.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I would like to say a word in connection with the information my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) has been good enough to give. We can well understand that the views of a gentleman who has had such a large and varied experience as he has had in the past in connection with immigration are of great practical importance, not only to the minister, but also to the department which carries on immigration work. I have listened -with much attention to the hon. gentleman's statement as to how matters have been working in the province of Ontario, and I am bound to think that perhaps these local agents, as they are called, have not been the greatest possible success so far as regards contributing anything to the immigration policy in that province. I find on glancing over the return that 2,000 o-f these immigrants were distributed by the Salvation Army, and I am glad to say-in so far as the west is concerned, at all events-that the officers of the Army have been very satisfactory, very energetic and very honest in their business dealings in connection with the immigration woTk which they undertook. In my judgment, it would not be desirable to discontinue in any form whatever the efforts which they are now making with respect to immigration work. I appreciate very much what the hon. member for South Oxford has been good enough to say in connection with immigration, a matter which is of such deep interest to himself personally, and I hope he will do me the honour of calling on me some time in the near future so that we may have an opportunity of discussing in more detailed form

the views which he holds and gathering more detailed information on the subject with the idea of doing the best we can on immigration work in Ontario.

If the figures are available, would the minister state the number of persons excluded from Canada last year coming from Great Britain, from the United States, from the continent of Europe and from Asia?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Persons excluded last year:	British, 247; United States, 21,466;
European, 607; Asiatics, 60. Total, 22,580.
I would like to have the number deported, if that can be given.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: 1 have not that at hand, but will be glad to give it later.

Possibly at some other time, when the minister's estimates are up, these figures can be given. I wish merely to get them on record. I ask also with regard to the Boyce-Sneed case in Winnipeg. These two parties come from Texas, and one of them was deported while the other was not. On what grounds was one of them allowed to remain in the country?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The immigration officer in Winnipeg, when I was there last Christmas, gave me the explanation verbally, and his statement, as I recollect it, was that the woman was deported on the ground that she had just come out of an asylum, and under the Act such people are subject to deportation. In the case of the man we had not the same right in the judgment of the officer, and, therefore, he did not order the deportation of the man.
Does not the minister think that both man and woman were subject to deportation regardless of the fact that one of them had lately been in a lunatic asylum?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am free to say I am inclined to agree with the hon. gentleman. But Mr. Bruce Walker, the officer in charge, did not take that action. I do not know what reason influenced him. Perhaps he thought he was going to save the life of the man; perhaps he did.
I would like to ask a number of questions with regard to Asiatic immigration, if convenient. ' How many Japanese arrived within the last calendar year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There were 727 men, and 337 women.
How many Japanese are estimated to be in Canada now?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The figures are not available.
How many Chinese arrived in the past calendar year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The number was, men 6,794; women, 79.
How many Chinese were exempt from the head tax?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have not the number, but I have the class of people exempt.
Tlie members of the diplomatic corps or other government representatives, their suite?, their servants; consuls and consular agents; the children born in Canada of parents of Chinese origin who have left Canada for educational or other purposes on substantiating their identity to the satisfaction of the officer of the port or place where they seek to enter on their return; [DOT]merchants, their wives and minor children; wives and minor children of clergymen, tourists, men of science, subject to such regulation as may from time to time he made by the government; duly certificated teachers.
In connection with the Japanese students, would the minister give a statement on a future occasion of the number of Japanese returned to Japan, and the same of the Chinese returned to China?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Can the minister give me an idea of the means now taken to check the arrival of Chinese, to see that they comply with the law with regard to the head tax.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are examined at the ocean port under the Chinese Act.
Are there special officers to deal with the Chinese?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are dealt with by the immigration officers.
Under special instructions under the Chinese Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
How many Hindus arrived during the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There were 13 men and 1 woman.
I have seen in the papers a statement that two Hindu women had arrived and were held for deportation. Have they been deported?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They arrived and were held for deportation, and their time was up on the 6th of February, but the time was extended in order that we might ascertain whether they came by direct passage or otherwise. When we get that information we shall be able to decide what course to take.
Is there any special regulation to prevent Hindu women from coming in?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Hindu women can come in the same as Hindu men?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
So, if the women in this case are rejected, it is because they did not comply with the ordinary regulation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Are there many Hindu women in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Very few-half-a-dozen or so.

How many Hindus are resident in Canada?
Mr.* ROGERS. From 2,300 to 2,500.
How many is it supposed returned during the past year to India?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not that information.
Would ic be in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, we can supply it very readily.
Would the minister make any statement as to his conclusions in regard to the relaxing of the regulations for the admission of Hindu women, the wives of Hindus living in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have had a special officer investigating those conditions and as far as we can judge from the information we have been able to obtain about 5,200 Hindus have come to Canada and to-day we have less than 2,500 left so that they are evidently finding out for themselves that either the climate or conditions are not suited to their wants. Some of their number were anxious to promote immigration and increase their numbers in Canada and to bring as they claimed their wives. But on investigations the report I get is that the class of Hindus we have in British Columbia are not a class who would possibly bring their wives to settle in that province. I do not of course mean that in every case; I am speaking in general terms. The police of Vancouver complain rather bitterly that some of the Hindus are rather a troublesome class and the health officers of Vancouver make a similar complaint that they are not a desirable class of settlers to have if it is possible to avoid doing so. In view of the condition and class of Hindu that we happen to have in_ Canada I do not think there is any chance of women coming out to take up their homes here and continue as residents in Canada. I am speaking only from the information handed me by the special officer detailed to ascertain this Mr. OLIVER.
information. I think that 300 of these Hindus left Canada last year, but I hope to have the report of the special officer in a short time and to submit to the House.
The committee may assume that it is not the intention of the minister to relax the conditions in regard to Hindu women?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not at present, no.

Can the minister explain the apparent fact that the number of Japanese who have arrived in the past year is in excess of the number provided for in the understanding with the Empire of Japan? I think the understanding is that about 400 labouring people may be admitted in a year. Last year 727 entered. Of course the difference may be made up of Japanese of other classes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In 1911 we had 427 and
in this year apparently 727.

It is a serious question. If the arrangement made is being adhered to by the government of Japan it is perfectly satisfactory but if not it is desirable that parliament should be advised of the fact. There is really a total of over a thousand.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I shall look into that.
Is there any change in the regulations regarding the admission of Chinese that would increase the exemptions from the head tax formerly in force?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No there has been no change.
Is the Chinese immigration increasing?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To some extent, but not very largely.
What is the appropriation of $75,000 which is not required for 1912-13?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is for seed grain. We will have a supplementary for seed grain this year.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. ROGERS moved the adjournment of the House.
What is the order of business for to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We will take up government Bills.
Which will have precedence?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We will take up probably the Tariff Commission Bill. I think that will be ready to go on to-morrow.
The Grain Bill is first on the list.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Probably the Grain Bill too. I expect my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be ready to go on with that.
And if not that, the Tariff Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If not that, the Tariff Commission.
And the highways?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and then we will go into the estimates if we get -through with those.
The boundaries question will not go on to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, not till Thursday.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.30 a.m. Wednesday.
Wednesday, February 28, 1912.
